2. Adl (Adalat) — Divine Justice. Allah is perfectly just; He does not and cannot act unjustly. This is an active attribute: Allah’s justice is a guarantor of moral order. This replaces al-Qadr as a named Root because Shi’a scholars, concerned about predestination undermining human accountability, prefer to emphasise justice.

3. Nubuwwah — Prophethood. Allah sent messengers to guide humanity. Muhammad is the final prophet.

4. Imamah — Leadership. After Muhammad, the community should be led by a line of divinely appointed Imams from the family of the Prophet (Ahl-ul-Bayt). The Imam is believed to be sinless and divinely guided. Twelver Shi’a Muslims believe in twelve such Imams; Sevener (Ismaili) Shi’a follow the first seven.

5. Mi’ad — Resurrection and the Day of Judgement. All people will be raised and judged. Mi’ad is essentially equivalent to Yawm al-Din in Sunni belief.

Twelver Shi’a Muslims (Ithna’ashariyya) are the majority of Shi’a, dominant in Iran, Iraq and parts of Lebanon. They recognise twelve Imams, the last of whom (Muhammad al-Mahdi) is believed to have gone into divine occultation and will return at the end of time.

Sevener (Ismaili) Shi’a Muslims follow the first seven Imams. They accept Ismail ibn Jafar as the seventh Imam rather than his younger brother Musa al-Kazim, whom Twelvers follow. The Aga Khan is the current hereditary leader of the Nizari Ismaili community, the largest surviving Ismaili branch.

Tawhid — The Oneness of Allah

Tawhid is the single most important belief in Islam. It holds that Allah is absolutely One — undivided, unique, without partners, children or equals. Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas) is the foundational Qur’anic text: it teaches that Allah is One, eternal and self-sufficient, was not born and has no offspring, and nothing is comparable to Him. Muslims recite this surah daily; it summarises the whole of Tawhid in four verses.

The opposite of Tawhid is Shirk (associating anything with Allah). Shirk is described in the Qur’an as the one sin Allah will not forgive if a person dies without repenting of it. This explains why Islamic art traditionally avoids depictions of Allah or the Prophet, using calligraphy and geometric patterns instead.

The Nature and Qualities of Allah

Muslims believe Allah possesses qualities revealed throughout the Qur’an. Key divine attributes include:

  • Omnipotence (all-powerful): Allah created the universe from nothing and sustains all life. Nothing is beyond His power.
  • Beneficence: Allah is supremely good and generous. His generosity extends to all creation.
  • Mercy (Ar-Rahman, Ar-Rahim): These two divine names both translate as “merciful” but are distinct. Ar-Rahman refers to Allah’s universal, boundless mercy that extends to all creation; Ar-Rahim refers to His particular and ongoing mercy towards believers. Every surah of the Qur’an (except one) opens with the phrase Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim (“In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful”).
  • Transcendence: Allah is beyond and above the physical world; He is not limited by time or space.
  • Immanence: At the same time, Allah is intimately close to His creation. The Qur’an states He is “closer to you than your jugular vein” (Surah 50:16).
Key Fact

Surah 16:35–36 is the Edexcel-named anchor for Allah’s oneness and prophethood: it declares that Allah sent a messenger to every nation, commanding: “Worship Allah and avoid false gods.” This verse links Tawhid to Risalah and underpins both the first and fourth articles of Sunni belief. In Shi’a Islam, Adalat (justice) is treated as a distinct Root of Religion, reflecting Shi’a theological emphasis on human moral accountability.

Comparing Muslim belief in Tawhid with Christian belief about the nature of God is a rich area for 12-mark Discuss answers.

  • Islam: God is absolutely one and indivisible. Any suggestion of a Trinity is rejected as Shirk. Allah has no son.
  • Christianity: God is one being in three persons — Father, Son and Holy Spirit (the Trinity). Christians affirm monotheism but understand God’s nature as Trinitarian. Catholics ground this in the Nicene Creed and the Catechism of the Catholic Church.
  • Judaism: Like Islam, Judaism insists on the absolute unity of God (the Shema: “The Lord our God, the Lord is One” — Deuteronomy 6:4) and strongly rejects any Trinitarian formula.

lesson_title: Risalah, Holy Books, Angels and Predestination
content_html:
Risalah — Prophethood

Risalah means prophethood. Muslims believe Allah did not leave humanity without guidance — He sent prophets to every nation at different times throughout history. Prophets are human beings chosen by Allah; they are not divine, but they are sinless (ma’sum) in the delivery of their message and are perfectly obedient to God. The Qur’an names 25 prophets, though Muslim tradition holds there were many more. Surah 2:136 instructs believers: “We believe in Allah and what was revealed to us and what was revealed to Ibrahim, Isma’il, Ishaq, Ya’qub, and the Tribes — and what was given to Musa and Isa and all the other prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them.”

Adam was the first human and the first prophet. Allah created Adam from clay and breathed life into him. In Islam, Adam’s sin in the Garden is not inherited by humanity — he repented, was forgiven, and every person is born in a state of fitrah (natural purity). There is no doctrine of original sin in Islam.

Ibrahim (Abraham) is known as Khalilullah — the Friend of Allah. He demonstrated perfect submission by being willing to sacrifice his son when commanded by Allah, who intervened and provided a ram instead. Most Muslim scholars identify the son as Isma’il, though the Qur’an does not name him in this narrative. Ibrahim also rebuilt the Ka’aba in Makkah with Isma’il, establishing the site of annual pilgrimage.

Musa (Moses) received the Tawrat (Torah) and led the Israelites from Egypt. Dawud (David) received the Zabur (Psalms). Isa (Jesus) received the Injil (Gospel) and is regarded in Islam as one of the greatest prophets — born of the virgin Maryam through divine intervention, the Messiah, who performed miracles by Allah’s permission.

Muhammad (born c.570 CE, died 632 CE) is the final prophet — the Seal of the Prophets (Khatam an-Nabiyyin). No prophet will follow him. He received the Qur’an through the angel Jibril over approximately 23 years, beginning in 610 CE. The Hijra (migration from Makkah to Madinah) in 622 CE marks the start of the Islamic calendar.

Key Fact

Surah 2:136 is the Edexcel-named anchor for Risalah. It establishes that Muslims believe in all prophets without distinction — this is what sets Islamic prophethood apart from the idea that only one tradition’s prophets matter. Surah 16:35–36 reinforces this, stating Allah sent a messenger to every nation commanding worship of Him alone.

Kutub — The Holy Books

Kutub means the holy books or scriptures. Muslims believe Allah revealed guidance to humanity through a series of scriptures. Surah 5:43–48 describes how each community received its own scripture and should live by it: “We revealed the Torah, containing guidance and light… We sent Isa, son of Maryam, in their footsteps… and gave him the Injil.” The passage goes on to say the Qur’an was sent to confirm and safeguard what came before.

Tawrat (Torah) — revealed to Musa (Moses). Muslims believe the original Tawrat was the word of Allah, but that it has been altered over time by human hands.

Zabur (Psalms) — revealed to Dawud (David). Again, Muslims hold the original to have been divine but believe the present form is not perfectly preserved.

Injil (Gospel) — revealed to Isa (Jesus). Muslims believe Isa received a pure revelation from Allah, distinct from the four Gospels in the New Testament, which are regarded as human accounts rather than the original divine text.

Qur’an — revealed to Muhammad through the angel Jibril over 23 years. Muslims believe the Qur’an is the final, complete and perfectly preserved word of Allah. Unlike previous scriptures, it has not been changed. Sahifah (scrolls) were also revealed to Ibrahim and Adam but are not preserved as independent texts today.

Malaikah — Angels

Malaikah (angels) are an article of faith in both Sunni and Shi’a Islam. Muslims believe angels were created from divine light, have no free will, do not eat or sleep, and obey Allah perfectly. They are neither male nor female. Believing in the angels is the second of the Six Beliefs of Sunni Islam.

Jibril (Gabriel) is the most important angel in Islamic teaching. He delivered the Qur’anic revelation to Muhammad and brought divine messages to earlier prophets including Ibrahim and Isa. He is known as the “trustworthy spirit” in the Qur’an.

Izra’il is the angel of death. Surah 32:11 refers to him: “The Angel of Death, who has been given charge of you, will take your souls.” Muslims believe Izra’il takes the soul from the body at the appointed moment of death — a moment pre-determined only by Allah.

Mika’il (Michael) is associated with mercy, rain, provisions and natural sustenance. He is responsible for the weather and natural phenomena that sustain life on earth.

Two further angels, Munkar and Nakir, are believed to question the deceased in the grave about their faith. Israfil is the angel who will blow the trumpet on the Day of Judgement.

Key Fact

Surah 32:11 is the Edexcel-named anchor for belief in the angel Izra’il (the Angel of Death): “The Angel of Death, who has been given charge of you, will take your souls.” This verse connects Malaikah (angels) to Akhirah (the afterlife) — the angel’s role at death is the first step in the journey to judgement.

Al-Qadr — Predestination

Al-Qadr is the sixth article of Sunni faith. It means predestination — the belief that Allah has complete knowledge of past, present and future, and that everything that happens is within His will. A hadith recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari 78:685 states that an angel records four things about a person before birth: their provision, their lifespan, their deeds, and whether they will be fortunate or unfortunate. This is written on the “Preserved Tablet” (Lawh al-Mahfuz).

A common misconception is that al-Qadr means humans are puppets with no real choices. Most Sunni Muslims hold that Allah’s foreknowledge is absolute — He knows what every person will do before they do it — but that His knowing does not cause the action. Humans genuinely choose; they simply cannot surprise God. This is how human accountability on the Day of Judgement is preserved.

Shi’a Islam approaches this differently. Rather than naming al-Qadr as a Root of Religion, Shi’a theology names Adl (Divine Justice) — emphasising that because Allah is perfectly just, He would not hold humans accountable for actions they were forced to perform. This framing places the accent on human freedom and divine justice rather than on divine decree.

lesson_title: Akhirah: Life After Death and the Day of Judgement
content_html:
Akhirah — Belief in Life After Death

Akhirah means “the hereafter” or life after death. It is one of the core beliefs in both Sunni and Shi’a Islam. Muslims believe that this earthly life is temporary — a test and a preparation. The real, eternal life begins after death. Everything a person does in this life will be examined on the Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Din).

Surah 17:49–72 addresses the question of resurrection directly. The passage confronts the sceptical claim that decayed bones could not be revived, and asserts that Allah, who created humanity the first time, is entirely capable of creating again. The surah describes the journey of the soul after death, from initial disbelief through to the scales of judgement, the record of deeds and the dividing of humanity into those destined for Jannah and those for Jahannam.

Key Fact

The starred spec point (1.8*) means Akhirah is a likely anchor for 12-mark Discuss questions that ask you to compare Islamic and another tradition’s views of the afterlife. Surah 17:49–72 is the named Qur’anic anchor for Muslim teaching on resurrection and judgement.

Death and the Barzakh

After death, Muslims believe the soul enters Barzakh (the barrier or intermediate state). In Barzakh, the soul waits until the Day of Judgement. During this time, two angels — Munkar and Nakir — are believed to question the deceased about their faith. The righteous experience a peaceful Barzakh; those who have done wrong may experience suffering.

The Day of Judgement

On the Day of Judgement, the angel Israfil will blow a trumpet, all of creation will be destroyed and then all people will be resurrected. Every person will stand before Allah and give an account of their life. Islamic teaching describes several features of this judgement:

  • Each person’s deeds are recorded by the angels Kiraman Katibin (“noble scribes”) throughout their life.
  • The Mizan (scales) will weigh every person’s good and bad deeds.
  • Each person will receive a record of their deeds — in their right hand (those destined for paradise) or behind their back or in their left hand (those destined for hell).
  • The Sirat (the bridge over hell) must be crossed. The righteous cross it easily; the wicked fall into Jahannam.

Jannah — Paradise

Jannah is the Islamic concept of paradise — a place of eternal peace, beauty and fulfilment. The Qur’an describes Jannah in vivid terms: cool shade, flowing rivers, rich provision, companionship and, most importantly, the direct experience of Allah’s presence (the Beatific Vision-equivalent in Islamic theology, called ru’yat Allah). Entry to Jannah is by Allah’s mercy, not by human deeds alone — deeds are the indicator of faith, but the final decision belongs to Allah.

Jahannam — Hell

Jahannam is the Islamic concept of hell. It is described in the Qur’an as a place of fire and suffering. Muslim scholars differ on whether Jahannam is eternal for all its inhabitants. Sunni mainstream views hold that non-believers remain in hell permanently, while some Muslims who have sinned but still held faith may be punished for a time before ultimately entering Jannah by Allah’s mercy. Jahannam is not described as a place of torture for its own sake — it is described as the natural consequence of a life lived in rejection of Allah.

Belief in Akhirah motivates Muslims to act ethically in the knowledge that everything they do is being recorded. It gives purpose to suffering: if life is a test, hardship has meaning. It provides comfort in the face of death and injustice — even if wrongs are not righted in this life, they will be addressed by Allah on the Day of Judgement. It also encourages generosity and justice, since how a person treats others will be weighed on the Mizan.

This is a starred comparison spec point — examiners may ask you to compare Islamic and another tradition’s afterlife beliefs in a 12-mark Discuss question.

  • Islam: physical resurrection on the Day of Judgement; deeds weighed on the Mizan; Jannah (paradise) or Jahannam (hell) as eternal destinations. Entry to Jannah is by Allah’s mercy. No concept of reincarnation.
  • Catholic Christianity: resurrection of the body at the Last Judgement; Purgatory as an intermediate state of purification for the faithful; Heaven, Purgatory and Hell as possible destinations. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (CCC 1030–1032) describes Purgatory. Islam has no equivalent to Purgatory, though the concept of Barzakh shares some structural similarity as an intermediate state.
  • Hinduism/Buddhism (for contrast): reincarnation (samsara) and the eventual release from the cycle (moksha/nirvana). Islam and Christianity both reject reincarnation.

lesson_title: The Five Pillars and Ten Obligatory Acts
content_html:
The Five Pillars of Sunni Islam

Islam is built on five core practices known as the Five Pillars. These are not optional extras — they are fard (compulsory) for every adult Muslim of sound mind. Together they shape a Muslim’s daily life, social relationships and relationship with Allah. The Prophet Muhammad described Islam as being “built upon five things” (Hadith, Sahih al-Bukhari). Surah 3:17–21 praises those who are patient, truthful, devout, and charitable — qualities embodied by the Five Pillars.

Key Fact

The Five Pillars: Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salah (five daily prayers), Zakah (2.5% of savings given to those in need), Sawm (fasting during Ramadan), Hajj (pilgrimage to Makkah at least once). This is the foundational framework of Sunni practice.

Shahadah — Declaration of Faith

The Shahadah is the declaration: “There is no God but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah.” It is the most fundamental act of Islamic faith. Reciting it sincerely and with understanding is the act that makes a person Muslim. It is whispered in a newborn’s ear, said at regular intervals in prayer and at the hour of death. Surah 3:17–21 describes those who consistently bear witness (“shahada”) to Allah’s oneness as among the most praiseworthy of believers.

Salah — Prayer

Salah is compulsory prayer five times a day: Fajr (before sunrise), Zuhr (after midday), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (after sunset) and Isha (night). Before praying, Muslims perform wudu (ritual washing). On Fridays, Sunni Muslim men are expected to pray Jummah (the Friday congregational prayer) at the mosque. Surah 29:45 states: “Recite what has been revealed to you of the Scripture; keep up the prayer — prayer restrains outrageous and unacceptable behaviour.” Surah 15:98–99 connects glorification of Allah in prayer with certainty of faith. Shi’a Muslims perform the same five prayers but may combine them into three prayer times during the day.

Sawm — Fasting

Sawm involves complete fasting during the holy month of Ramadan. Muslims abstain from all food, drink, smoking and sexual relations from dawn to sunset. Surah 2:183–185 commands: “You who believe, fasting is prescribed for you, as it was prescribed for those before you, so that you may be mindful of God.” Within Ramadan, the Laylat al-Qadr (Night of Power) commemorates the first revelation of the Qur’an to Muhammad and is described in the Qur’an as better than a thousand months of worship. Those who cannot fast (due to illness, pregnancy or travel) may break their fast and compensate later. Ramadan ends with the festival of Id-ul-Fitr.

Zakah — Almsgiving

Zakah means “purification” or “growth.” It requires every Muslim whose savings exceed the nisab (minimum threshold) to give 2.5% of their annual savings to those in need. Surah 9:58–60 specifies eight categories of those entitled to receive Zakah, including the poor, the indebted and travellers in need. Zakah purifies the giver’s remaining wealth from greed, supports the poor and reduces inequality within the ummah (global Muslim community).

Hajj — Pilgrimage

Hajj takes place in the twelfth month of the Islamic calendar and must be performed at least once in a lifetime by every Muslim who is physically and financially able. Surah 2:124–130 describes Ibrahim and Isma’il building the Ka’aba and establishing the rites of pilgrimage. Surah 22:25–30 describes the sacred sites and the command to proclaim Hajj to all people. Hajj rites include walking around the Ka’aba seven times (tawaf), walking between the hills of Safa and Marwa, standing on the plain of Arafat (wuquf), and symbolically stoning the devil. Hajj creates a profound sense of equality and unity — all pilgrims wear identical white garments (ihram), erasing distinctions of wealth and rank.

Spec point 2.3 on Salah is starred, making it a comparison target for Discuss questions.

  • Islam: Salah is compulsory five times daily; all pray in Arabic using set movements; facing Makkah (qibla); preceded by wudu. Jummah (Friday prayer) is a communal obligation for men.
  • Catholic Christianity: The Mass is the central act of worship â€” the Eucharist (the source and summit of Catholic life, Lumen Gentium 7). Catholics attend Sunday Mass as an obligation. Prayer takes many forms: formal (the Divine Office) and informal. No single fixed time structure equivalent to the five daily prayers.
  • General Christianity: Worship varies widely â€” liturgical (set structure, e.g. Anglican) and non-liturgical (free-form, e.g. Baptist). Prayer is encouraged but not prescribed at fixed times in the way Islamic Salah is.

The Ten Obligatory Acts of Shi’a Islam

Shi’a Muslims have their own framework of obligatory acts. While the Five Pillars are broadly shared, Shi’a Islam lists Ten Obligatory Acts (Furu ad-Din — branches of religion). These include Salah, Sawm, Zakah and Hajj (shared with Sunni Islam), but add several distinctively Shi’a duties: Khums (a 20% tax on surplus income), Jihad (striving in the way of Allah), Amr-bil-Maroof (commanding what is right), and Nahy-anil-Munkar (forbidding what is wrong). Khums is particularly significant: Surah 8:41 specifies that a fifth of certain gains should be set aside “for Allah and the Messenger,” which Shi’a Muslims understand as a continuing obligation paid to the Imam’s representatives (the religious scholars).

Key Fact

Khums (20% of surplus income) is a Shi’a-specific obligation distinct from Sunni Zakah (2.5% of savings above nisab). Khums is paid to the Imam’s representatives (religious scholars) for religious and charitable purposes. Both Zakah and Khums serve to reduce inequality within the ummah, but they operate on different rates and through different channels.

The Five Pillars are the universal Sunni framework of practice. The Ten Obligatory Acts of Shi’a Islam (Wajibat) include the Five Pillars (Salah, Sawm, Zakah, Hajj, and Shahadah through Walayah) plus additional obligations: Khums (20% levy), Jihad, commanding good, forbidding evil, and love/disavowal (Tawallah and Tabarra). Some scholars count the Ten differently, but the spec names Khums as the distinctive Shi’a addition. The underlying logic is the same: both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims structure their lives around prescribed acts of worship that express submission to Allah.

lesson_title: Jihad and Islamic Festivals
content_html:
Jihad — Striving in the Way of Allah

The word jihad means “struggle” or “striving.” It does not mean “holy war” — that is a common mistranslation. Every Muslim is engaged in jihad whenever they strive to be a better person, resist temptation, act justly or work for a fairer society. Islam recognises two forms of jihad: greater jihad (al-jihad al-akbar) and lesser jihad (al-jihad al-asghar).

Key Fact

Greater jihad is the struggle against nafs (the lower self) — the daily effort to be honest, compassionate, self-disciplined and obedient to Allah. Classical scholars held that this inward struggle is the most difficult and most continuous form of jihad. Lesser jihad refers to defensive struggle to protect the Muslim community under conditions tightly constrained by Islamic jurisprudence.

Greater Jihad — The Inner Struggle

Greater jihad involves resisting the temptation to lie, be selfish, be unjust or neglect religious duties. It includes studying Islam, raising a family according to Islamic values, working honestly, caring for parents and being a good neighbour. Every act of worship — Salah, Sawm, Zakah — is itself a form of greater jihad, since each requires the believer to overcome laziness, selfishness or distraction to submit to Allah. Greater jihad is lifelong; it ends only at death.

Lesser Jihad — Conditions and Constraints

Lesser jihad refers to the use of force to defend the Muslim community, resist oppression or uphold justice. It is not a licence for aggression. Surah 2:190–194 sets clear conditions: “Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you but do not transgress, for Allah does not love transgressors.” The passage prohibits fighting those who do not fight, prohibits attacking during sacred months and commands that fighting must stop when the enemy ceases hostilities. Surah 22:39 permits Muslims who have been wronged to fight in self-defence: “Permission to fight is given to those who have been attacked.”

Classical Islamic jurisprudence lists conditions that must be met before lesser jihad is permissible:

  • There must be a legitimate cause — typically self-defence or the defence of those being oppressed.
  • All peaceful alternatives must have been exhausted first.
  • It must be declared by a legitimate authority (not by individuals acting alone).
  • Non-combatants — women, children, the elderly, clergy and those not fighting — must be protected. Destruction of crops and buildings is prohibited.
  • It must cease when the enemy stops fighting or offers peace (Surah 2:192–193).

These conditions mean that lesser jihad is constrained in classical Islamic teaching far more than media portrayals often suggest. Extremist interpretations that remove these conditions are rejected by mainstream Islamic scholars.

Reducing jihad to “holy war” misrepresents Islamic teaching in two ways. First, it ignores greater jihad, which classical scholars considered the more important form. Second, it strips lesser jihad of its strict conditions — making it sound like permission for unlimited violence, which the Qur’an explicitly prohibits. Surah 2:190 states: “do not transgress, for Allah does not love transgressors.” Exam answers that describe jihad only as “holy war” will score poorly; both forms must be covered.

Islamic Festivals

Islamic festivals unite the global ummah in shared acts of worship, remembrance and celebration. Four key festivals feature in the specification: Id-ul-Adha, Id-ul-Fitr, Id-ul-Ghadeer (Shi’a) and Ashura.

Id-ul-Adha — Festival of Sacrifice

Id-ul-Adha (the Festival of Sacrifice) is one of the two major Islamic festivals. It commemorates Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice his son at Allah’s command. Surah 37:77–111 recounts the story: Ibrahim was commanded in a dream to sacrifice his son; he informed his son, who submitted willingly. As Ibrahim prepared to act, Allah intervened and provided a ram as a substitute, rewarding Ibrahim’s faith with the announcement that he had fulfilled the vision. Most Muslim scholars identify the son as Isma’il, though the Qur’an does not name him in this passage — the identification is traditional, not explicitly stated. Id-ul-Adha takes place during the Hajj period and involves the sacrifice of an animal (qurbani), with meat shared among family, friends and the poor.

Id-ul-Fitr — Festival Marking the End of Ramadan

Id-ul-Fitr celebrates the successful completion of the month-long Ramadan fast. It begins with a communal prayer and sermon at the mosque. Muslims give Zakat al-Fitr (a special obligatory charity at Ramadan’s end) so that everyone in the community can celebrate. The festival continues with visiting family, feasting, wearing new or clean clothes, and giving gifts to children. Id-ul-Fitr is a celebration of gratitude to Allah for the strength to complete Sawm and a joyful acknowledgement of the community that fasted together.

Id-ul-Ghadeer — A Shi’a Festival

Id-ul-Ghadeer is one of the most important Shi’a festivals. It commemorates the event at Ghadir Khumm (on the return from the Prophet’s final Hajj in 632 CE) when, according to Shi’a belief, the Prophet Muhammad announced that Ali ibn Abi Talib was to be his rightful successor. Shi’a Muslims understand Surah 5:3 — “Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My blessing upon you” — as referring to this proclamation at Ghadir. Sunni Muslims interpret this verse differently, associating it with the completion of the Hajj rather than a specific designation of Ali. Id-ul-Ghadeer is therefore a specifically Shi’a festival with profound significance for the doctrine of Imamah.

Ashura — A Day of Contrasting Significance

Ashura falls on the tenth day of Muharram (the first month of the Islamic calendar) and holds very different significance for Sunni and Shi’a Muslims.

Sunni Ashura: For Sunni Muslims, Ashura is primarily a day of voluntary fasting. A hadith recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari reports that when the Prophet arrived in Madinah and observed the Jewish community fasting, he was told it was the day Moses was saved from Pharaoh. The Prophet reportedly said he had a stronger connection to Moses and encouraged fasting on this day. It is an act of gratitude rather than mourning.

Shi’a Ashura: For Shi’a Muslims, Ashura is the most solemn day of the year — a day of mourning and lamentation for the martyrdom of Imam Husayn (the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad and the third Shi’a Imam) at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. Husayn and his small band were killed by the forces of Caliph Yazid after refusing to pledge allegiance to what Shi’a Muslims regard as an unjust ruler. Ashura is marked with processions, passionate re-enactments (ta’ziyeh), lamentations and the retelling of Husayn’s sacrifice. The tragedy of Karbala is central to Shi’a religious identity and theology.

Key Fact

Islamic festivals in this spec: Id-ul-Fitr (end of Ramadan — Sunni and Shi’a), Id-ul-Adha (feast of sacrifice, Ibrahim — Sunni and Shi’a), Ashura (Husayn’s martyrdom at Karbala — primarily Shi’a), Id-ul-Ghadeer (Muhammad’s designation of Ali — Shi’a). Surah 37:77–111 is the Qur’anic account of Ibrahim’s sacrifice that Id-ul-Adha commemorates.

lesson_title: Sources of Authority and Muslim Identity
content_html:
Section 3: Sources of Wisdom and Authority

This lesson covers two major sections of the specification: the sources of wisdom and authority that Muslims turn to for guidance (Sections 3.1–3.8) and the forms of expression and ways of life that shape Muslim identity (Sections 4.1–4.8). Because this lesson spans 16 spec points, each section has been given a focused sweep with key anchors highlighted for exam use.

The Qur’an as a Source of Authority

The Qur’an is the primary source of authority in Islam. Muslims believe it is the direct, unchanged word of Allah. Surah 53:4–18 is the Edexcel anchor for the Qur’an’s authority: it describes the divine origin of the revelation (“It is nothing less than a revelation that is sent to him”) and the vision of the Prophet during which the revelation was transmitted. The Qur’an is used in daily life: in Salah (prayer recitation is in Arabic), in the home (reading for guidance and blessing), in the mosque (recited communally and individually), as a source of law, and as the foundation of Islamic education.

The Prophet Muhammad

The Prophet Muhammad is the second source of authority in Islam. His life provides the model (Sunnah) for how Muslims should live. Key events include: his birth c.570 CE in Makkah; the first revelation at age 40 in 610 CE; his mission in Makkah (610–622 CE) and the growing opposition he faced; the Hijrah (migration to Madinah in 622 CE), which marks year one of the Islamic calendar; his work in Madinah establishing the Muslim community; and his death in 632 CE.

Surah 48:26–29 praises the believers who accompanied the Prophet and describes the characteristics of his companions: firm against opponents, merciful to one another, performing prayer and seeking Allah’s approval. Surah 33:36–47 refers to the Prophet as the Seal of the Prophets and sets out his multiple roles: a witness, a bringer of good news and a warner. Muhammad’s significance today: Muslims follow his example in prayer, family life, business ethics and social conduct; his practice is recorded in the Hadith.

Ahl-ul-Bayt means “People of the House” — the Prophet’s household. Surah 33:32–34 addresses the Prophet’s household with specific instructions, which Shi’a Muslims interpret as confirming their special status and purity. For Shi’a Muslims, Caliph/Imam Ali and the Ahl-ul-Bayt are the rightful authorities after the Prophet. For Sunni Muslims, Ali is respected as the fourth of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, but not as a uniquely divinely appointed leader. This disagreement is the theological root of the Sunni–Shi’a split and continues to shape divergent approaches to religious authority.

The Hadith

The Hadith are the recorded sayings, actions and approvals of the Prophet Muhammad. They are the second major written source of Islamic guidance after the Qur’an. Each hadith has two parts: the isnad (the chain of transmitters going back to the Prophet) and the matn (the content or body of the report). Scholars assess a hadith’s authenticity by analysing the isnad: how trustworthy were the narrators? Were they contemporaries who could plausibly have witnessed the event?

Key Fact

The two most authoritative Sunni hadith collections are Sahih al-Bukhari (compiled by al-Bukhari, d.870 CE) and Sahih Muslim (compiled by Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, d.875 CE). Shi’a Islam relies on its own hadith canon, known as the Four Books, which centre on reports from the Imams as well as the Prophet. This reflects the Shi’a conviction that the Imams are authoritative sources alongside the Prophet.

Shari’ah Law

Shari’ah Law is Islamic law derived from the Qur’an and Hadith, developed through scholarship. It governs worship, family life, business, criminal justice and social conduct. Two key legal tools are: qiyas (analogical reasoning, where a Qur’anic or hadith ruling is extended to a new situation by identifying a shared principle) and ijma (scholarly consensus). Surah 4:115 is the Edexcel anchor: it warns against following a path other than “the path of the believers,” which scholars interpret as supporting the principle of ijma. Qadis (judges) and the ulema (scholars) are the trained experts who interpret and apply Shari’ah. Sunni Islam has four main legal schools (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i, Hanbali); Shi’a Islam follows its own Ja’fari school, which gives greater weight to the Imams’ teachings.

The Imam in Shi’a Islam

In Shi’a Islam, the Imam is not simply a prayer leader but a divinely guided religious and political authority, believed to be sinless (ma’sum) and infallible in matters of faith. Nass is the doctrine that the designation of each Imam was divinely appointed and explicitly transmitted. The twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, is believed by Twelver Shi’a to have gone into occultation (divine hiding) and will return at the end of time. The Hadith of the pond of Khumm (Ghadir Khumm) is regarded by Shi’a Muslims as the Prophet’s explicit designation of Ali as the first Imam. In Sunni Islam, an imam is a prayer leader; the role carries no divine appointment or inerrancy. Sahih al-Bukhari 73:34–37 discusses the qualities expected of a Sunni imam — a role of learning and community service rather than divine authority.

Section 4: Forms of Expression and Ways of Life

Muslim Identity

Muslim identity is expressed through the shared ummah — the global community of believers. From birth, community ceremonies mark a child as part of the ummah (the Adhan whispered in the newborn’s ear; the Aqiqah ceremony). Expectations of modesty in dress and behaviour are rooted in Surah 24:30–31, which instructs both men and women to “lower their gaze and guard their private parts” and (for women) to “not display their adornments except to their husbands.” Interpretations of modest dress vary widely: some Muslim women wear a hijab (headscarf), niqab or abaya; others interpret modesty as a matter of character rather than specific dress.

Halal (permitted) and haram (forbidden) govern all areas of Muslim life: food (pork and blood are haram; meat must be slaughtered in the name of Allah), finance (riba, or interest/usury, is haram — Islamic banking uses profit-sharing instead), and conduct. These categories derive from the Qur’an and the Sunnah.

The Mosque

The mosque (masjid) is the centre of Muslim community life. Sahih al-Bukhari 2:39 describes the Prophet’s own mosque in Madinah and the practices associated with congregational prayer, establishing the template for mosque use. Key architectural features include: the mihrab (prayer niche indicating the direction of Makkah), the minbar (pulpit for Friday sermons), the minaret (tower for the call to prayer), and an area for wudu (ritual washing). In some mosques, a separate area is provided for women. The mosque is used for: daily and Friday (Jummah) prayer, Qur’an classes, community events and Eid celebrations.

Calligraphy

Calligraphy is one of the most important art forms in Islam. Islamic art avoids depicting human or animal figures in religious contexts because of concerns about idolatry — Surah 21:51–62 records Ibrahim destroying the idols of his people, establishing the Islamic rejection of images as objects of devotion. Calligraphy fulfils the artistic impulse while directing attention to Allah’s word rather than created beings. Qur’anic verses, the names of Allah and the Shahadah are rendered in intricate scripts. Calligraphy appears on mosque walls, in the Qur’an and in Islamic decorative art worldwide.

Sufism — The Mystical Tradition

Sufism is the mystical tradition within Islam. Sufis seek direct personal experience of Allah, emphasising inner purification, love of God and spiritual closeness over outward religious performance alone. Sufism is organised into brotherhoods (tariqas) led by spiritual teachers called shaykhs. Central practices include dhikr (remembrance — the rhythmic repetition of Allah’s names or Qur’anic phrases) and periods of extended fasting. Surah 13:28 is the key Qur’anic anchor: “Verily, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest.”

Al-Ghazali (1058–1111 CE) was a Persian Islamic scholar, theologian and mystic. His most important work is the Ihya Ulum al-Din (Revival of the Religious Sciences) — a comprehensive guide to Islamic spirituality that integrates orthodox theology with Sufi practice. Al-Ghazali argued that Sufism was grounded in the Qur’an and the Sunnah, not in contradiction to them. He is credited with reconciling mysticism and orthodox scholarship within Sunni Islam. His Revival remains one of the most widely read works in Islamic literature.

Ibn al-Arabi (1165–1240 CE) was an Andalusian (Spanish-born) Sufi mystic and philosopher. He developed the influential and controversial concept of wahdat al-wujud (Unity of Being) — the idea that all existence is, in some sense, a reflection or manifestation of Allah’s being. This idea was contested by some orthodox scholars who felt it blurred the distinction between Creator and creation. Ibn al-Arabi wrote extensively on spiritual experience, the nature of prophecy and the inner dimensions of Islamic faith.

Rabi’a al-Adawiyya (c.714–801 CE) was a female Sufi saint from Basra (modern-day Iraq), one of the earliest and most celebrated figures in the Sufi tradition. She is especially known for her theology of pure love (mahabbah) for Allah — the idea that love for God should be free of any desire for paradise or fear of hell. Her poetry and teaching profoundly shaped the devotional dimension of Sufism. The fact that Rabi’a is a named female figure in the specification reflects Sufism’s relatively open approach to female spiritual authority.

Key Fact

The Edexcel-named Sufi figures are: al-Ghazali — Revival of the Religious Sciences; reconciled Sufism with orthodox Islam. Ibn al-Arabi — concept of Unity of Being (wahdat al-wujud). Rabi’a al-Adawiyya — pure love for Allah independent of reward or fear. Dhikr anchor: Surah 13:28.

Muslim Charity

Beyond the obligatory Zakah (and Shi’a Khums), Muslims are encouraged to give sadaqah (voluntary charity). Surah 2:271–274 praises those who give in charity, especially those who give secretly: “If you give charity openly, it is good, but if you give it secretly to the poor, that is better for you.” One named Muslim charity is Islamic Relief Worldwide, which works to relieve poverty and suffering in the UK and globally. Muslim charities ground their work in the Qur’anic command to care for the poor, the orphan and the traveller — reflecting the Islamic understanding that wealth belongs ultimately to Allah and must be shared justly within the ummah.

lesson_title: Catholic Beliefs: Trinity, Incarnation and Creation
content_html:
Who Is God? The Catholic Understanding of the Trinity

Catholic Christianity teaches that God is one being in three equal, co-eternal Persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This is the doctrine of the Trinity. It is not three separate gods but one God who exists in a communion of love.

The Trinity is expressed most precisely in the Nicene Creed, which Catholics recite at Mass. The Creed was finalised at the First Council of Nicaea in 325 CE and expanded at the First Council of Constantinople in 381 CE. It affirms the Father as creator, the Son as “God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God,” and the Holy Spirit as “the Lord, the giver of life.”

Key Fact

The Nicene Creed was agreed at the First Council of Nicaea (325 CE) and completed at the First Council of Constantinople (381 CE). It remains the foundational statement of Trinitarian faith for Catholics today.

The baptism of Jesus (Matthew 3:13–17) is a defining scriptural moment for the Trinity. All three Persons are simultaneously present: the Son is baptised in the Jordan, the Holy Spirit descends as a dove, and the Father speaks — “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.” Catholics see this event as a ‘living icon’ of the Trinitarian God.

Catholics begin every prayer by making the Sign of the Cross: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” The Trinity is invoked at baptism, marriage, and the final blessing at Mass. The doctrine is not abstract theology — it shapes how Catholics understand themselves as created in the image of a God who is, at his very nature, relational and loving.

Creation: The World as God’s Gift

Genesis 1–3 is the Catholic Church’s foundational text on creation. It teaches that God created the universe “in the beginning,” ordering it from chaos into beauty, and declaring it “very good.” Catholics do not hold a single required interpretation: some read Genesis literally, taking the six days as historical days; many read it metaphorically, seeing the text as conveying theological truth about God’s nature rather than a scientific account of origins.

What all Catholics affirm is that God is the uncaused Creator, that creation is good and purposeful, and that the universe depends entirely on God for its existence. The creation account reveals God as benevolent (actively willing the good of creation), omnipotent (creating by word alone), and eternal (existing before and beyond creation).

Human Dignity: Made in the Image of God

Genesis 1:27 states that human beings are created in the image of God — the Latin term is imago Dei. This is the foundation of Catholic teaching on human dignity: every person, regardless of race, gender or ability, carries inherent worth because they bear God’s image.

Genesis also gives human beings dominion over the earth. Catholic tradition distinguishes two interpretations. The older ‘dominion’ reading emphasises human authority over nature. The more recent stewardship model, emphasised in modern Catholic Social Teaching (including Laudato Si’ by Pope Francis), sees human beings as guardians of creation who are accountable to God for how they treat the natural world.

Key Fact

Every human person has inherent dignity because they are created in the imago Dei (image of God). Modern Catholic teaching favours stewardship over unrestricted dominion, understanding humans as guardians of God’s creation, not owners of it.

The Incarnation: God Becomes Human

The Incarnation is the belief that the Son of God — the second Person of the Trinity — became human in the person of Jesus of Nazareth. Catholics teach that Jesus is fully God and fully human: two natures in one Person. This paradox is not a contradiction but a mystery at the heart of Christian faith.

The scriptural foundation is the Prologue of John’s Gospel (John 1:1–18). John opens: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” The ‘Word’ (Greek: Logos) is the divine reason and creative power through which all things were made. Then John 1:14 declares: “And the Word became flesh and lived among us.” This is the Incarnation — the eternal Word of God entering human history as a baby in Bethlehem.

All mainstream Christian denominations affirm the Incarnation. Orthodox Christians share the Catholic understanding that Jesus is one Person with two natures (agreed at the Council of Chalcedon in 451 CE). Protestant traditions also affirm the Incarnation but place less emphasis on Mary’s role as Theotokos (God-bearer), a title Catholics and Orthodox use to stress that the one she bore is truly God. Some liberal Protestants understand the Incarnation more symbolically — as God’s deepest self-disclosure in a human life — rather than a metaphysical change in the eternal Son.

For Catholics, the Incarnation is not only the central event of history — it sanctifies all of human life. Because God became human, human flesh and human experience carry an extraordinary dignity. This is why Catholics treat the body with reverence, why care of the sick and dying is a sacred duty, and why the physical world matters spiritually.

lesson_title: Paschal Mystery, Salvation and Eschatology
content_html:
The Paschal Mystery: Death, Resurrection, Ascension

The Paschal Mystery refers to the cluster of saving events at the heart of Catholic faith: the suffering, death, resurrection and ascension of Jesus. The word ‘paschal’ derives from the Hebrew Pesach (Passover) — the Jewish feast recalling Israel’s liberation from slavery in Egypt. Catholics understand Jesus’ death and resurrection as a new Passover: liberation from sin and death.

Luke 24 is the key resurrection account in this section. It describes the empty tomb, the appearance of two angels, and the risen Jesus walking unrecognised with two disciples on the road to Emmaus before revealing himself in the breaking of bread. For Catholics, Luke 24 shows that the resurrection is not merely a spiritual symbol but a bodily event — Jesus walks, talks and eats.

Key Fact

The Paschal Mystery consists of four events: the suffering, death, resurrection and ascension of Jesus. The term derives from the Hebrew Passover (Pesach), linking Christ’s death to Israel’s liberation from Egypt.

Salvation and Grace

Salvation is the rescue of humanity from sin and its consequences. Catholics teach that all humans are affected by original sin — the disordered state introduced by the Fall — which separates human beings from God. Jesus’ death on the cross is understood as the atoning sacrifice that overcomes this separation, reconciling humanity with God.

Grace is God’s unearned gift — his very life shared with human beings. Catholics teach that it is through grace, not human effort alone, that salvation is achieved. John 3:16–21 states that God sent his Son not to condemn the world but so that those who believe might have eternal life. Acts 4:8–12 records Peter declaring that “there is salvation in no one else” but Jesus Christ.

Catholic teaching holds that grace is received through the sacraments (baptism, Eucharist, etc.) and through a life of faith and works. Protestant traditions, following the Reformation principle of sola fide (faith alone), emphasise that salvation is by faith only — no human work contributes to justification. Lutheran and Reformed theology stress that grace is entirely God’s initiative; Catholics agree grace is unearned but emphasise that humans must cooperate with it through the sacramental life of the Church.

Catholic Eschatology: Life After Death

Eschatology deals with the ‘last things’ — what happens at and after death. Catholic teaching covers five key realities: resurrection, judgement, heaven, hell and purgatory.

Resurrection: Catholics believe in the bodily resurrection of the dead at the Last Day. This is modelled on Christ’s own resurrection, which was bodily (the tomb was empty). The body and soul are reunited for the final judgement.

Judgement: Catholics teach both a particular judgement (immediately after each individual’s death) and a general judgement at the end of time. John 11:17–27 records Jesus telling Martha: “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live.” This is one of the most cited eschatological texts.

Heaven: The eternal state of perfect communion with God, achieved after judgement. 2 Corinthians 5:1–10 describes Paul’s confidence in “a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.”

Hell: Catholics teach that hell is a real possibility — the permanent state of those who, by their own free choice, have rejected God completely. The Church does not name any individual as damned but teaches that God respects human freedom, even to reject him.

Purgatory: A state of purification after death for those who die in God’s grace but still need to be freed from the consequences of sin. Catholics pray for the dead precisely because purgatory means death is not the end of spiritual growth.

Key Fact

Catholic eschatology includes five ‘last things’: resurrection, judgement, heaven, hell and purgatory. The Scriptural anchors are John 11:17–27 (resurrection and life) and 2 Corinthians 5:1–10 (the body in heaven).

This is the comparison-marked spec point (2A 1.8*) — examiners may ask you to contrast Catholic afterlife beliefs with another tradition:

  • Purgatory: Catholics and Orthodox Christians accept purgatory; most Protestant denominations do not. The Church of England’s 39 Articles explicitly reject purgatory as “a fond thing vainly invented.” For Protestants, the believer goes directly to heaven or hell at death.
  • Nature of resurrection: Some Protestant traditions emphasise a spiritual resurrection body; Catholic and Orthodox teaching is more explicitly physical — the same body, transformed and glorified.
  • Prayer for the dead: Catholics and Orthodox pray for the dead (Masses for the departed, prayers during Remembrance of All Souls). Most Protestant churches do not pray for the dead, since they do not accept purgatory.

lesson_title: Sacraments, the Mass and Catholic Prayer
content_html:
The Sacramental Vision of Reality

Catholic theology teaches that all of creation can mediate the presence of God — the world is not a barrier between humans and God but a channel through which God communicates. This is the ‘sacramental nature of reality.’ At its core are the seven sacraments: visible, physical actions through which God’s invisible grace is communicated.

The Catechism of the Catholic Church (CCC) 1210–1211 lists the seven sacraments: Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Penance (Reconciliation), Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders, and Matrimony. Each sacrament uses a physical sign (water, oil, bread, wine, the laying on of hands) and spoken words to effect what it signifies — the grace it conveys.

Key Fact

The seven sacraments (CCC 1210–1211) are: Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Penance/Reconciliation, Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders, and Matrimony. They are the primary channels of God’s grace in Catholic life.

Orthodox Christianity shares the Catholic understanding of seven sacraments (though Orthodox may use the term ‘mysteries’). Most Protestant churches recognise only two sacraments: baptism and the Lord’s Supper (Eucharist), on the grounds that only these two were explicitly commanded by Jesus with a physical element. Some Protestant traditions use the term ‘ordinance’ instead of ‘sacrament’, emphasising that these are acts of obedience to Christ rather than channels of grace in themselves. Quakers and the Salvation Army practise no sacraments at all, arguing that all of life is sacred and no special rite is needed.

The Mass: Source and Summit

The Mass (also called the Eucharist) is the most important Catholic act of worship. The Second Vatican Council document Lumen Gentium paragraph 7 describes the Eucharist as “the source and summit of the Christian life.” ‘Source’ means everything in Catholic spiritual life flows from the Mass; ‘summit’ means everything is directed back towards it.

The Mass has two main parts. The Liturgy of the Word consists of readings from Scripture, a psalm, the Gospel, and a homily (sermon). The Liturgy of the Eucharist includes the Offertory (bringing bread and wine), the Eucharistic Prayer (the priest consecrates the bread and wine), and Holy Communion (the congregation receives). Catholics believe that at the consecration the bread and wine become truly Christ’s body and blood — this is called transubstantiation.

This is the comparison-marked spec point (2A 2.2*). The contrast examiners expect:

  • Catholic liturgical worship follows a fixed structure (the Order of Mass), uses set prayers, is led by an ordained priest, and centres on the Eucharist. Lumen Gentium 7 calls the Eucharist ‘source and summit’ — nothing is more central.
  • Evangelical/Pentecostal worship is less-structured: spontaneous prayer, contemporary music, informal praise, emphasis on the Holy Spirit moving freely in the gathered congregation. There may be no set liturgy. The sermon (preaching the Word) often replaces the Eucharist as the centrepiece.
  • Protestant Reformed worship (Anglican, Methodist, Baptist) sits between these poles: some follow a liturgy (Book of Common Prayer in Anglicanism) while others are free-form. Only two sacraments are observed, and the Eucharist may be celebrated monthly rather than at every service.

Catholic Prayer

Prayer is described in Catholic tradition as ‘the raising of hearts and minds to God.’ The primary prayer taught by Jesus is the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:5–14), which combines adoration, petition and forgiveness.

Catholics also practise set (formulaic) prayer — fixed words said at certain times (e.g. the Hail Mary, the Rosary, the Angelus) — and informal (extempore) prayer, spoken in the believer’s own words.

Popular piety refers to devotional practices outside the official liturgy that are deeply embedded in Catholic culture. CCC 1674–1676 recognises and regulates popular piety. The three main forms the spec requires:

  • The Rosary: A set form of meditative prayer using beads, combining the Lord’s Prayer, the Hail Mary and the Glory Be while meditating on twenty ‘mysteries’ (events in Christ’s and Mary’s lives). It is one of the most widely practised Catholic devotions.
  • Eucharistic adoration: Prayer before the consecrated host (a large wafer) displayed in a monstrance. Catholics believe Christ is truly present in the consecrated host, so adoration is direct prayer before the Lord himself.
  • Stations of the Cross: Fourteen pictorial stations placed around a church, representing moments of Christ’s passion from condemnation to burial. The faithful move from station to station in prayer, entering imaginatively into Christ’s suffering. Often used during Lent.
Key Fact

Lumen Gentium paragraph 7 (Second Vatican Council) calls the Eucharist the “source and summit of the Christian life.” Source: all Catholic grace and identity flows from it. Summit: all Catholic life is ordered towards it. This is the single most important named source for the Mass in this paper.

lesson_title: Pilgrimage, Catholic Social Teaching and Mission
content_html:
Catholic Pilgrimage

Pilgrimage is a journey to a sacred place undertaken for spiritual purposes. The Catechism of the Catholic Church 2691–2696 recognises pilgrimage as a form of penance and devotion, an outward expression of the inward journey towards God.

The four pilgrimage sites specified in this unit are:

  • Jerusalem: The holiest city in Christianity, the site of Jesus’ crucifixion, burial and resurrection. Pilgrims visit the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the Via Dolorosa and the Garden of Gethsemane. Jerusalem has been a destination for Christian pilgrims since the earliest centuries.
  • Lourdes (France): In 1858, Bernadette Soubirous reported eighteen apparitions of Mary in a grotto at Lourdes. The Catechism recognises such Marian apparitions as private revelation. Millions of pilgrims visit each year, many seeking healing. The healing spring at Lourdes is associated with reported miraculous cures.
  • Rome: The seat of the papacy and the location of St Peter’s Basilica, built over the tomb of the Apostle Peter. Catholics make pilgrimage to Rome to visit the Holy See, the catacombs, and St Paul’s Basilica. A ‘Holy Year’ (Jubilee) declared by the pope gives pilgrims special indulgences.
  • Walsingham (England): England’s national Marian shrine, based on a vision in 1061 in which a noblewoman, Richeldis, was shown the House of the Annunciation and instructed to build a replica. Destroyed at the Reformation and restored in the twentieth century, it remains a major pilgrimage destination for both Catholics and Anglicans.

Catholics and Orthodox Christians strongly affirm pilgrimage as a spiritual discipline. Many Protestants are sceptical: the Reformation rejected the idea that visiting a physical place earns spiritual merit, arguing that God can be encountered anywhere and that Jesus himself said the Father seeks worshippers ‘in spirit and truth’ (John 4:23). However, many modern Protestants and evangelicals do make pilgrimage to Israel/Palestine for educational and devotional reasons without attaching indulgence value to it.

The Funeral Rite

The Catholic funeral rite is a full liturgical celebration. It takes place in three stages: in the home (reception of the body and prayer), in the church (the Funeral Mass, which is the central moment), and at the cemetery (the committal, entrusting the body to God). The rite serves three purposes: communion with the deceased (the Church prays for them); communion of the community (the grief is shared); and proclamation of eternal life.

The theologian and Archbishop of Westminster, Cardinal Vincent Nichols, wrote a widely circulated reflection titled ‘Preparing my funeral,’ which the spec names explicitly. Nichols emphasises that a Catholic funeral is not simply a memorial service but an act of worship that entrusts the deceased to God’s mercy and proclaims the resurrection.

Catholic Social Teaching

Catholic Social Teaching (CST) applies the Gospel to social and economic life. Its key principles include: human dignity, the common good, solidarity (care for all, especially the poor), and subsidiarity (decisions made at the most local level possible).

The key named document for this spec point is Evangelii Gaudium (The Joy of the Gospel), written by Pope Francis in 2013. Paragraphs 182–237 focus on “the inclusion of the poor in society”: Francis insists that the Church’s mission is inseparable from care for the marginalised. He writes of the “economy of exclusion” and calls Catholics to a “culture of encounter” with those on the margins.

The CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development) is the Catholic Church’s development agency in England and Wales. It works in partnership with local communities in the Global South on long-term development and emergency relief. CAFOD grounds its work in Matthew 25:31–46 (the Parable of the Sheep and Goats), in which Jesus identifies himself with “the least of these my brothers.”

Key Fact

Evangelii Gaudium was written by Pope Francis in 2013. Paragraphs 182–237 address “the inclusion of the poor in society.” Matthew 25:31–46 (Sheep and Goats) is the key Scripture underpinning CAFOD’s work.

Catholic Mission and Evangelism

Mission is the Church’s calling to spread the Good News of Jesus. Evangelism is the direct proclamation of the Gospel. Catholics distinguish mission (building the Kingdom of God in the world, including through justice and development) from evangelism (explicit verbal proclamation).

Evangelii Gaudium Chapter 5 sets out Pope Francis’s vision for missionary discipleship: every baptised Catholic is a missionary. Mission is not only the work of priests and religious orders — the whole Church is called to go out to the “existential peripheries.”

Catholic thinking has sometimes separated ‘mission’ (proclaiming the Gospel in words) from ‘social action’ (serving the poor). Pope Francis in Evangelii Gaudium insists the two cannot be separated: “An authentic faith... always involves a deep desire to change the world.” CAFOD embodies this integration — it does not proselytise (seek to convert) but works for justice as an expression of the Gospel. Critics argue that without explicit proclamation of Christ, social action is not distinctively Christian. The 12-mark Discuss question on this topic will require students to weigh these positions against each other.

Key Fact

The Catholic funeral rite serves three purposes: (1) communion with the deceased through prayer; (2) supporting the bereaved community; (3) proclaiming eternal life and the resurrection to all present.

lesson_title: Christian Beliefs: God, Creation and Jesus
content_html:
The Trinity: One God in Three Persons

Christianity teaches that there is one God who exists eternally as three distinct Persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. This is the doctrine of the Trinity. The three Persons are not three separate gods (polytheism) nor three modes of one God (modalism) — they are one God in a communion of being and love.

The Nicene Creed (325/381 CE) is Christianity’s most widely accepted doctrinal statement. It confesses the Father as creator of all things, the Son as “God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God,” and the Holy Spirit as “the Lord, the giver of life.” The Creed is used across Catholic, Orthodox and most mainline Protestant traditions, making it the closest thing to a universal Christian statement of belief.

Matthew 3:13–17 (the baptism of Jesus) shows all three Persons simultaneously: Jesus is baptised in the Jordan, the Holy Spirit descends as a dove, and the Father speaks from heaven — “This is my beloved Son.”

Key Fact

The Nicene Creed was agreed at Nicaea (325 CE) and Constantinople (381 CE). It is shared by Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches. Matthew 3:13–17 is the key scriptural showing of all three Persons at once.

Creation: God and the Universe

Genesis 1–3 is the foundational Christian text on creation. Genesis 1 presents creation as six days of ordered making, culminating in humanity as the pinnacle. Genesis 2 gives a second, more intimate account focused on the first humans and their relationship with God. Genesis 3 introduces the Fall.

Christians interpret Genesis in divergent ways. A literal reading takes the six days as historical days. A metaphorical reading treats Genesis as theological poetry that conveys truths about God’s nature (creative, purposeful, benevolent) rather than a scientific sequence. John 1:1–18 adds the dimension that creation happened ‘through the Word’ — the eternal Son was the agent through whom all things were made, “and without him not one thing came into being.”

The Incarnation: God Becomes Human

The Incarnation is the belief that the second Person of the Trinity, the eternal Son (the Word or Logos), became human in the person of Jesus. John 1:14 states: “And the Word became flesh and lived among us.” 1 Timothy 3:16 calls this “the mystery of our religion” — God was manifested in flesh.

The Incarnation has enormous implications. It means Jesus is not merely a great teacher or prophet: he is the eternal God of the universe who chose to live a human life, to suffer and die. For Christians, this act of divine self-giving is the greatest expression of God’s love.

The Council of Chalcedon (451 CE) defined Jesus as “truly God and truly man,” with two natures in one Person. Catholic, Orthodox and most mainline Protestant churches affirm this. Some liberal Protestant theologians read the Incarnation as metaphorical — describing God’s deepest engagement with humanity rather than a literal metaphysical event. The Nicene Creed is the common anchor: “For us and for our salvation he came down from heaven... and was made man.”

The Last Days of Jesus

Luke 22–24 contains the account of Jesus’ last days. The sequence is: the Last Supper (Jesus shares bread and wine with his disciples, saying “This is my body... this is my blood of the new covenant”); betrayal and arrest in Gethsemane; trial before the High Priest and Pilate; crucifixion on Golgotha; burial and then resurrection (the empty tomb and appearances to Mary, to the disciples on the Emmaus road, and to the eleven).

The Last Supper is the foundation of the Eucharist practised in churches today. The crucifixion and resurrection are together the central event of Christian history — the moment of salvation.

Salvation and Atonement

Salvation is the rescue of humanity from sin. Christians teach that sin — human rebellion against God’s will — separates humanity from God. Jesus’ death on the cross is understood as the means by which that separation is overcome.

Atonement theories explain how the cross achieves salvation. John 3:16 states: “God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.” Acts 4:8–12 records Peter asserting that “there is salvation in no one else” but Jesus Christ — a foundational claim about the uniqueness of Christ’s saving work.

Key Fact

John 3:16 — “God so loved the world that he gave his only Son” — is the key salvation verse. Acts 4:8–12 — Peter declares salvation is found in Christ alone. Both are essential 5-mark source references on salvation.

Christians agree that the cross achieves salvation but differ on how. Substitutionary atonement (popular in Reformed/evangelical Christianity): Jesus took humanity’s punishment in their place. Moral influence theory (associated with liberal Protestantism): the cross demonstrates God’s love so powerfully that it draws humanity to repentance. Christus Victor (common in Orthodox thinking): Jesus defeated the powers of sin, death and evil by dying and rising. All three agree that salvation comes through Christ; they differ on the mechanism.

lesson_title: Eschatology and the Problem of Evil
content_html:
What Is Eschatology?

Eschatology is the study of “last things” — death, judgement, and what happens after death. For Christians, eschatology is not morbid speculation but a source of hope: the belief that death is not the end, and that God will ultimately bring justice and renewal. This starred spec point (1.6*) requires students to compare Christian eschatological beliefs with those of another religion.

Resurrection, Judgement, Heaven and Hell

Most Christian traditions teach that after death, humans face judgement, and then enter either heaven or hell. Heaven is described as eternal life in the presence of God — a state of perfect joy, peace and communion with God. Hell is described as eternal separation from God. The 39 Articles of Religion (the foundational Anglican confession of faith) affirm belief in the resurrection of the body and eternal life, but do not specify the precise nature of hell. Some Christians interpret hell as eternal conscious punishment; others see it as the final annihilation of the unrepentant; still others (universalists) believe God will ultimately save all people.

2 Corinthians 5:1–10 is a key passage for Edexcel: Paul writes that believers groan in their earthly “tent” (the body), longing for a “heavenly dwelling” made by God. He says “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each of us may receive what is due to us for the things done while in the body.” This passage affirms both resurrection (a new, permanent body from God) and judgement (accountability for earthly life).

Key Fact

Purgatory is the Catholic and some Orthodox teaching that souls who die in a state of imperfect holiness undergo purification before entering heaven. It is not a second chance for the unrepentant but a process of preparation for those who die in God’s grace. Most Protestant traditions (as reflected in the 39 Articles, Article XXII) reject purgatory as “a fond thing vainly invented, and grounded upon no warranty of Scripture.” This denominational divergence is directly tested in Edexcel’s question on eschatology.

This lesson’s spec point is starred (1.6*), meaning students are expected to compare Christian eschatology with another tradition — the most likely comparison in the exam is Islam or Catholic Christianity. Key comparisons: Both Christianity and Islam teach bodily resurrection, final judgement, heaven (Paradise/Jannah in Islam) and hell (Jahannam). Both affirm that what happens after death is determined by one’s response to God during earthly life. Divergence 1 — Purgatory: Catholic Christianity has a doctrine of purgatory; Islam has no direct equivalent, though some scholars discuss the barzakh (an intermediate state between death and resurrection) as a period of waiting rather than purification. Divergence 2 — Nature of salvation: Christianity teaches salvation through faith in Jesus Christ (Acts 4:8–12). Islam teaches submission (islam) to Allah, with the balance of one’s deeds assessed on the Day of Judgement; there is no equivalent to the Christian doctrine of atonement through Christ’s death. Divergence 3 — The Trinity: Christian descriptions of heaven involve the beatific vision (seeing God as he is, including the Trinity); Islamic paradise does not involve a Trinitarian concept of God.

The Problem of Evil and Suffering

If God is omnipotent (all-powerful) and benevolent (completely good and loving), why does evil and suffering exist? This is called the problem of evil. Philosophers argue: if God were truly omnipotent, he could prevent suffering; if God were truly benevolent, he would want to prevent it; yet suffering exists. This creates a logical tension for Christian belief in God.

Christians distinguish two kinds of suffering. Moral evil (also called moral suffering) is evil caused by free human choices — war, murder, cruelty, theft. Natural evil is suffering caused by natural events — earthquakes, diseases, floods. Both challenge belief in a good God, but in different ways. Moral evil raises questions about why God gave humans free will knowing they would misuse it. Natural evil raises questions about why God designed a world that produces suffering independently of human choice.

Key Fact

Psalm 103 responds to the problem of evil with a declaration of God’s compassion: “The Lord is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in love.” Christians use this Psalm to argue that God’s love and care for the suffering is itself part of the answer to the problem — God does not stand aloof but suffers with humanity (especially revealed in the incarnation and crucifixion). Psalm 119 returns repeatedly to trusting God’s word even in affliction: “It was good for me to be afflicted so that I might learn your decrees” — suggesting that suffering has a spiritual purpose for the believer. The book of Job is a sustained biblical engagement with the problem: Job suffers catastrophically without deserving it, protests to God, and ultimately receives not an explanation but an encounter with God’s greatness.

Solutions to the Problem of Evil

Christians offer several responses to the problem of evil. The free will defence argues that God gave humans genuine freedom, which makes moral evil a human responsibility rather than God’s. A world with free will is considered better than a world of moral robots, even if free will is misused. This does not fully explain natural evil, however.

COMMON EXAM ERROR: Students frequently confuse these two theodicies. They are distinct and must not be attributed to the wrong thinker. Augustine (354–430 CE): Evil is the privation (absence) of good — it has no independent existence but is what happens when goodness is removed. The cause of evil is the misuse of free will, first by Satan, then by Adam and Eve (the Fall). This is the ‘free will theodicy’ or ‘Augustinian theodicy.’ Books: City of God, Confessions. Key contrast: creation was originally ‘very good’ (Genesis 1); evil entered through human sin. Augustine does NOT use the phrase ‘soul-making.’ Irenaeus (c.130–202 CE): Humans were created immature, made in the ‘image of God’ but not yet in his ‘likeness’ — they need to grow. Evil and suffering are the necessary conditions for moral and spiritual development. Modern development: John Hick (*Evil and the God of Love*, 1966) called this the ‘soul-making theodicy’ or the ‘vale of soul-making’. The world is not a paradise but a place where souls develop through facing challenges and suffering. Key contrast with Augustine: evil is not a consequence of a past Fall but a necessary feature for human growth. NEVER attribute ‘soul-making’ to Augustine.

lesson_title: Christian Worship, Sacraments and Prayer
content_html:
Forms of Christian Worship

Worship is how Christians express love and devotion to God. Christians worship in several distinct forms, and different denominations emphasise different approaches. This spec point is starred (2.1*), meaning students must compare Christian worship with that of another religion in the exam.

Liturgical worship follows a fixed, formal structure. Anglican services follow the Book of Common Prayer (or its modern successor, Common Worship); Catholic services follow the Roman Rite; Orthodox services follow centuries-old liturgical patterns. The advantage is that worshippers know what to expect, the service connects them to centuries of Christian tradition, and the same words unite Christians globally. Anglicans, Catholics and Orthodox all use liturgical worship as their primary form.

Non-liturgical worship is less structured and more flexible. It is common in Methodist, Baptist and many Reformed churches. There is no prescribed prayer book; sermons are central; hymns and readings are chosen to suit the congregation’s needs. Some Christians prefer this form because it allows the Spirit to guide the service rather than following a predetermined script.

Key Fact

The Book of Common Prayer (1662 version) is the historical service book of the Church of England, providing set liturgies for Morning Prayer, Evening Prayer, Holy Communion and other rites. It shaped Anglican worship for centuries and remains in use today, especially in traditional parish churches. Many Anglicans also use the modern Common Worship (2000) book. The Book of Common Prayer is a specific Edexcel-named source — knowing its name and denominational context is essential for 5-mark source questions.

Pentecostal churches (and charismatic congregations in other denominations) worship very differently from liturgical traditions. Services are spontaneous and led by the Spirit: worship includes contemporary music with guitars, drums and clapping; congregants may speak in tongues (glossolalia), give prophecies, pray aloud spontaneously and respond physically. There is no fixed order of service and no prayer book. Pentecostal worship has grown rapidly in the UK and globally — it is the fastest-growing Christian expression worldwide. The contrast between Pentecostal and Anglican/Catholic liturgical worship is a prime example for exam questions on denominational diversity.

This spec point is starred (2.1*) â€” students must compare Christian worship with another tradition. The most common exam comparison is with Islam. Similarities: Both Christian and Islamic worship include communal prayer, reading from sacred scripture, and acts of praise directed towards God. Friday Jumu'ah prayers in Islam and Sunday services in Christianity both serve as the primary communal worship event of the week. Differences: Islamic Salah is highly ritualised (five set times daily, specific bodily postures, Arabic recitation, ritual purity required); Christian worship varies enormously from the Pentecostal free-flowing to the Catholic Mass. Islamic worship is strictly non-sacramental; Christian worship often centres on sacramental acts (Eucharist, baptism). Islam explicitly rejects the use of music and images in worship in many traditions; Christianity has a rich tradition of sacred music and art.

Sacraments in Different Denominations

A sacrament is an outward, visible sign of an inward, spiritual reality. The number of sacraments is a significant denominational difference. Catholic and Orthodox Christians recognise seven sacraments: Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Penance (Reconciliation), Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders and Matrimony. Most Protestant churches recognise only two — Baptism and the Eucharist (Lord’s Supper) — because only these two were explicitly commanded by Jesus in the Gospels. The 39 Articles XXV–XXXVI are the Anglican doctrinal statement on sacraments: Article XXV affirms two sacraments “ordained of Christ our Lord in the Gospel” (Baptism and the Supper of the Lord) and describes the five other Catholic sacraments as “not to be counted for Sacraments of the Gospel.”

Baptism is the sacrament of initiation into the Christian community — widely practised across denominations. The mode and timing vary: Catholics, Anglicans and Orthodox baptise infants (paedo-baptism); Baptists and many evangelicals baptise only those who have made a personal declaration of faith (believer’s baptism). The meaning also varies: in Catholic and Orthodox theology, baptism washes away original sin and incorporates the person into the Body of Christ; in Protestant theology, it is primarily a sign of inclusion in the covenant community and a declaration of faith.

The Eucharist (also called Holy Communion, the Lord’s Supper or the Mass) is the other universally accepted sacrament. However, what happens during the Eucharist is one of Christianity’s most significant theological disputes. Catholics teach transubstantiation: the substance of the bread and wine is truly transformed into the body and blood of Christ, though the outward appearance remains. Most Protestants either hold a memorialist view (bread and wine are symbols only, recalling Christ’s sacrifice) or a spiritual presence view (Christ is genuinely but spiritually present in the sharing). The Anglican Thirty-Nine Articles deliberately leave room for both views.

Prayer: Set and Informal

Prayer is a central Christian practice. Jesus taught about prayer in Matthew 6:5–14: he warned against ostentatious public praying done to impress others, and instructed his followers to pray in private and to use a model he gave them — the Lord’s Prayer. Christians use two main types of prayer. Set prayers are written texts used repeatedly — for example, the Lord’s Prayer, the General Confession from the Book of Common Prayer, or prayers from liturgical books. They provide unity, connect worshippers to tradition, and are especially central in liturgical worship. Informal prayer uses the believer’s own words, allowing personal and spontaneous expression of faith.

Key Fact

The Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:9–13) is the model prayer Jesus gave his disciples. It is the one prayer shared by virtually all Christian denominations worldwide, said in liturgical services, at weddings, baptisms and funerals. Its structure includes: address to God as Father in heaven; hallowing of his name (praise); petition for God’s kingdom to come; request for daily bread (provision); request for forgiveness; and protection from temptation and evil. It teaches Christians that prayer should combine praise, submission to God’s will, requests for daily needs and forgiveness.

lesson_title: Pilgrimage, Festivals, Mission and the Worldwide Church
content_html:
Christian Pilgrimage

Pilgrimage is a journey made to a sacred place for spiritual reasons. Christians have practised pilgrimage since the earliest centuries. The spec names four sites:
