  • Jerusalem: The holiest site in Christianity, where Jesus was crucified, buried and raised. Pilgrims visit the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the Via Dolorosa and the Garden of Gethsemane. Jerusalem is also holy to Jews and Muslims, making it a place of both spiritual depth and ongoing geo-political complexity.
  • Iona (Scotland): A small island off the west coast of Scotland where St Columba founded a monastery in 563 CE. The Iona Community (founded 1938 by George MacLeod) has made it a centre of ecumenical spirituality and social justice Christianity. Pilgrims come for retreat, reflection and the experience of Celtic spirituality.
  • Taizé (France): An ecumenical community founded in 1940 by Brother Roger Schutz. Each year tens of thousands of young people from across the world visit Taizé for prayer, song and reconciliation. Its simple, repetitive chants have become widely used across denominations. Taizé emphasises unity between Catholics and Protestants.
  • Walsingham (England): England’s national Marian shrine, dating to 1061. After destruction at the Reformation, it was restored in the twentieth century and is now visited by both Catholics and Anglicans. It represents the healing of divisions between denominations.

Luke 2:41–43 provides a biblical basis for pilgrimage: the young Jesus goes with his parents to Jerusalem for the Passover, showing that visiting sacred sites is part of faithful Jewish (and, by extension, Christian) practice.

Catholics and Orthodox strongly affirm pilgrimage as spiritually meritorious. Protestant reformers (Luther, Calvin) were more cautious: they rejected the idea that visiting a physical location earns spiritual credit, arguing God is present everywhere. Modern Protestants vary: some travel to Israel for educational reasons without claiming spiritual merit; others, like those visiting Iona or Taizé, do so for community and renewal rather than indulgences.

Christian Festivals: Christmas and Easter

Christmas celebrates the Incarnation — God becoming human in Jesus. The liturgical season of Advent begins four Sundays before Christmas and is a time of spiritual preparation and expectation. Christmas Day (25 December in Western churches) celebrates the birth of Jesus. The Christmas story combines Matthew 2 (Magi, Herod, Egypt) and Luke 2 (shepherds, manger, Bethlehem).

Easter is the most important Christian festival, celebrating Christ’s resurrection. It is preceded by Holy Week: Palm Sunday (entry into Jerusalem), Maundy Thursday (Last Supper, washing of feet), Good Friday (crucifixion), Holy Saturday (the waiting), Easter Sunday (resurrection).

1 Corinthians 15:12–34 is Paul’s great defence of the resurrection: “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins.” Paul argues the entire Christian hope rests on the historical reality of the resurrection. Without it, Christianity collapses.

Key Fact

1 Corinthians 15:12–34: Paul argues that if Christ has not been raised, faith is “futile.” The resurrection of Jesus is the guarantee of Christians’ own future resurrection. Easter celebrates this as historical fact, not symbol.

Mission, Evangelism and the Future of the Church

Mission is the Church’s outward movement into the world. Evangelism is the direct proclamation of the Gospel. Mark 16:9–20 (the so-called ‘longer ending’) records the risen Jesus commissioning his disciples: “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.” The spec includes this as the basis for Christian missionary work.

The Local and Worldwide Church

The local church serves its immediate community. This includes: regular Sunday worship as the centre of Christian identity; outreach work (food banks, community cafes, debt counselling); ecumenism (working across denominations in shared projects); and pastoral care for individuals.

The worldwide Church works for reconciliation and supports persecuted Christians. Christian Aid is the named development agency in this spec. It works in partnership with local organisations across the Global South on relief and development, grounded in Matthew 25:31–46 (the Sheep and Goats): Christians are called to see Christ in “the least of these.”

Key Fact

Christian Aid operates in over 40 countries, tackling poverty through long-term development. Its work is grounded in Matthew 25:31–46. The local church’s community role includes food banks, outreach work and ecumenical partnerships.

These two sites are Edexcel-specific pilgrimage sites not commonly found in other GCSE specifications. Iona is significant as the birthplace of Scottish Christianity and a centre of Celtic spirituality and social justice. Taizé is significant as an ecumenical community drawing hundreds of thousands of young Christians annually, representing hope for unity between Catholic and Protestant churches. Both are alternatives to the traditional ‘relic-and-indulgence’ model of pilgrimage — their significance is more about community and spiritual renewal than seeking miraculous healing.

lesson_title: Core Muslim Beliefs and the Nature of Allah
content_html:
Tawhid: The Oneness of Allah

The single most fundamental belief in Islam is Tawhid (Arabic: ‘oneness’). Allah is one, indivisible, eternal and without any partner, associate or equal. Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas — ‘Sincerity’) states: “Say: He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor was born, nor is there any equivalent to Him.” Surah 112 is the most-recited summary of Tawhid and is used to correct any association of partners with Allah (shirk), which is considered the gravest sin in Islam.

The characteristics of Allah described in the Qur’an include: oneness (Tawhid), immanence (closeness to creation), transcendence (beyond creation), omnipotence (all-powerful), beneficence and mercy (Ar-Rahman, Ar-Rahim), fairness and justice. Surah 16:35–36 emphasises that Allah sent messengers to every community to call them to worship him alone.

In Shi’a Islam, divine justice has a special name: Adalat. It is listed as one of the Five Roots and underscores that God’s justice is perfect — he does not oppress, and human beings genuinely have free will because a just God must leave room for real moral choice.

Key Fact

Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas) is the Qur’anic anchor for Tawhid: Allah is “the One, the Eternal Refuge” who “neither begets nor was born.” Shirk (associating partners with Allah) is the greatest sin in Islam because it violates Tawhid directly.

The Six Beliefs of Sunni Islam

Sunni Islam organises its core beliefs into six beliefs, drawn from Kitab al-iman 1:4 (a hadith of the Prophet). They are:

  1. Belief in Allah (Tawhid — the oneness of God)
  2. Belief in his Angels (Malaikah) — pure, obedient spiritual beings
  3. Belief in his Holy Books (Kutub) — revelations sent to the prophets
  4. Belief in his Prophets (Risalah) — messengers from Adam to Muhammad
  5. Belief in the Day of Judgement (Akhirah) — the final reckoning and afterlife
  6. Belief in divine decree (al-Qadr) — Allah’s knowledge of and sovereignty over all events

Shi’a Islam uses a different organising structure: the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din:

  • Tawhid — the oneness of Allah (Surah 112)
  • ‘Adl (divine justice/Adalat) — Allah always acts justly; human beings have real moral freedom
  • Nubuwwah — prophethood; Allah communicated through a line of prophets ending with Muhammad
  • Imamah — the leadership of the Imams, direct successors to Muhammad from the Prophet’s family (Ahl al-Bayt); this is distinctive to Shi’a Islam
  • Mi’ad — the Day of Resurrection and Judgement

Critical distinction: The Five Roots are Shi’a. The Six Beliefs are Sunni. Do not conflate them in exam answers.

Risalah: Prophethood

Risalah is the belief in prophethood: that Allah chose specific human beings to receive and convey his guidance to the world. Surah 2:136 names the key prophets believed in by Muslims: “We believe in Allah, and in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, and in what was given to Moses, Jesus and the Prophets from their Lord.”

The named prophets in this spec are: Adam (the first human being and first prophet), Ibrahim (Abraham — friend of God, father of monotheism), Musa (Moses — who received the Tawrat/Torah), Isa (Jesus — regarded as a great prophet and the Messiah, born of the virgin Maryam, but not the Son of God) and Muhammad (the final and greatest prophet, ‘seal of the Prophets’).

The Holy Books (Kutub)

Muslims believe Allah revealed holy books to his prophets. The Kutub (holy books) include: the Qur’an (revealed to Muhammad, in Arabic, the final and uncorrupted revelation), the Tawrat (Torah, revealed to Musa/Moses), the Zabur (Psalms, revealed to Dawud/David), and the Injil (Gospel, revealed to Isa/Jesus). Muslims believe the earlier books became corrupted over time — the Qur’an alone remains in its original form and therefore has supreme authority.

Both Islam and Christianity affirm that God is one, all-powerful, all-knowing, and merciful. However, there are significant differences:

  • Tawhid vs Trinity: Islam emphatically rejects the Christian Trinity as shirk (associating partners with God). Surah 112 directly refutes any idea that God has offspring or equals. Christians argue that the Trinity is a refined understanding of monotheism — one God in three Persons — not polytheism, but Muslims regard this distinction as insufficient.
  • Prophethood of Isa: Islam affirms Jesus (Isa) as a great prophet, born of the Virgin Maryam, the Messiah, and a worker of miracles — but emphatically not the Son of God or divine. The Christian claim that Jesus is God incarnate is rejected in Islamic theology as a violation of Tawhid.
  • Personal relationship: Both traditions affirm that God/Allah is close to his creation. The Qur’an teaches that Allah is “closer to him [the human] than his jugular vein” (Surah 50:16). Christians express this through the Incarnation — God entering human experience directly in Jesus.
Key Fact

Muslims believe earlier books (Tawrat, Zabur, Injil) were gradually corrupted by human error or alteration. The Qur’an, revealed to Muhammad in Arabic and preserved in its original form, is the final, uncorrupted Word of Allah. This is why the Qur’an has supreme authority in Islam.

lesson_title: Angels, Predestination and Akhirah
content_html:
Malaikah: Angels in Islam

Malaikah (singular: malak) are angels — spiritual beings created by Allah from light (nur). They have no free will; they exist only to obey Allah. They are not depicted with wings or human form in Islamic theology, though the Qur’an uses figurative language. Angels are part of the unseen world (al-ghayb).

Three angels are named in the spec:

  • Jibril (Gabriel): the angel of revelation, through whom Allah communicated the Qur’an to Muhammad. Surah 2:97–98 states: “Whoever is an enemy of Jibril — it is he who has brought the Qur’an down upon your heart.” Jibril also appeared to Maryam to announce the birth of Isa.
  • Mika’il (Michael): the angel of sustenance and mercy, associated with rain, provision and natural phenomena that sustain life. Surah 2:98 mentions him alongside Jibril.
  • Izra’il: the angel of death, who takes the soul at the moment of death. Surah 32:11 states: “The angel of death who has been entrusted with you will take you, and then you will be returned to your Lord.” Izra’il serves as a reminder that death is controlled by Allah, not by chance.

The Qur’an also names Kiraman Katibin — the two recording angels assigned to every person, noting their deeds. These records will be opened on the Day of Judgement.

Key Fact

Three named angels: Jibril (revelation, Surah 2:97–98), Mika’il (sustenance, Surah 2:98), Izra’il (death, Surah 32:11). All are created from light, have no free will, and carry out Allah’s commands perfectly.

Al-Qadr: Predestination

Al-Qadr is the Arabic term for divine decree or predestination. Muslims believe that Allah has complete foreknowledge of all events and that nothing falls outside his will. The hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari 78:685 relates the Prophet Muhammad’s teaching that every human being is created with their fate ‘written’ by an angel before birth, including their provision, lifespan, deeds and whether they will enter paradise or the fire.

This doctrine is one of the Six Beliefs of Sunni Islam. It teaches that human beings are not independent agents operating outside Allah’s knowledge, but it does not eliminate human moral responsibility: Muslims are still judged on the basis of their choices.

Sunni and Shi’a approaches to predestination differ in emphasis:

  • Sunni Islam holds that al-Qadr is one of the Six Beliefs: Allah knows and decrees all things. Most Sunni theologians teach that both divine foreknowledge and genuine human free will coexist, though how this is possible is a theological mystery (taqdeer). Human beings choose and are accountable; Allah knows those choices in advance.
  • Shi’a Islam places greater emphasis on Adl (divine justice) as the governing principle. A just God would not predetermine a person’s actions and then punish them — therefore, humans must have genuine freedom. Shi’a theology generally stresses human free will more strongly than some Sunni accounts.

Akhirah: Life After Death

Akhirah means ‘the hereafter’ or ‘the afterlife.’ It encompasses the events that follow death: the intermediate state (barzakh), the resurrection, the Day of Judgement, and the final destinations of paradise (Jannah) or hell (Jahannam).

Surah 17:49–72 is the spec-named Qur’anic passage for Akhirah. It describes sceptics asking how God could resurrect decomposed bones, to which the answer is: “Say: Be you stones or iron, or [any] creation of that which is great within your breasts. And they will say, ‘Who will restore us?’ Say, ‘He who created you the first time.’” Allah, who created from nothing, can certainly resurrect the dead.

The sequence of events in Islamic eschatology:

  1. Death and Barzakh: After death the soul enters a waiting state (barzakh — the ‘barrier’ between this world and the Day of Judgement).
  2. Resurrection: On the Last Day, all souls are resurrected bodily.
  3. Judgement: Each person’s deeds are weighed on scales (mizan). The recording angels’ books are opened. Allah’s mercy also plays a decisive role — he may forgive those whose deeds are insufficient.
  4. Jannah or Jahannam: The righteous enter Jannah (paradise) — a garden of eternal bliss in the presence of Allah. The unrighteous enter Jahannam (hell) — a place of fire and separation from God.

This is the comparison-marked spec point (2C 1.8*):

  • Both traditions teach bodily resurrection, final judgement, paradise and a place of punishment. Both hold that earthly life shapes eternal destiny.
  • Islam: no purgatory or intermediate purification state (other than barzakh as a waiting state). Judgement is based on the weighing of deeds. The role of a mediating figure (like Christ in Christianity) is absent — Allah alone judges, though his mercy is decisive.
  • Christianity (Catholic): purgatory allows purification after death for those not fully ready for heaven. Salvation is achieved through faith in Christ, whose atoning death ‘pays’ for sin — a concept absent from Islam. Protestant Christianity rejects purgatory.
  • Key difference: Islamic judgement is more explicitly deed-based with direct divine mercy; Catholic Christianity builds in an intermediate purification stage and grounds salvation in Christ’s atonement.
Key Fact

Islamic eschatology sequence: death → barzakh (waiting state) → resurrection → judgement (deeds weighed on mizan) → Jannah (paradise) or Jahannam (hell). Surah 17:49–72 is the key Qur’anic passage on resurrection.

lesson_title: The Five Pillars and Ten Obligatory Acts
content_html:
The Five Pillars of Sunni Islam

Islam is built on five core practices known as the Five Pillars. These are not optional extras — they are fard (compulsory) for every adult Muslim of sound mind. Together they shape a Muslim’s daily life, social relationships and relationship with Allah. The Prophet Muhammad described Islam as being “built upon five things” (Hadith, Sahih al-Bukhari). Surah 3:17–21 praises those who are patient, truthful, devout, and charitable — qualities embodied by the Five Pillars.

Key Fact

The Five Pillars: Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salah (five daily prayers), Zakah (2.5% of savings given to those in need), Sawm (fasting during Ramadan), Hajj (pilgrimage to Makkah at least once). This is the foundational framework of Sunni practice.

Shahadah — Declaration of Faith

The Shahadah is the declaration: “There is no God but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah.” It is the most fundamental act of Islamic faith. Reciting it sincerely and with understanding is the act that makes a person Muslim. It is whispered in a newborn’s ear, said at regular intervals in prayer and at the hour of death. Surah 3:17–21 describes those who consistently bear witness (“shahada”) to Allah’s oneness as among the most praiseworthy of believers.

Salah — Prayer

Salah is compulsory prayer five times a day: Fajr (before sunrise), Zuhr (after midday), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (after sunset) and Isha (night). Before praying, Muslims perform wudu (ritual washing). On Fridays, Sunni Muslim men are expected to pray Jummah (the Friday congregational prayer) at the mosque. Surah 29:45 states: “Recite what has been revealed to you of the Scripture; keep up the prayer — prayer restrains outrageous and unacceptable behaviour.” Surah 15:98–99 connects glorification of Allah in prayer with certainty of faith. Shi’a Muslims perform the same five prayers but may combine them into three prayer times during the day.

Sawm — Fasting

Sawm involves complete fasting during the holy month of Ramadan. Muslims abstain from all food, drink, smoking and sexual relations from dawn to sunset. Surah 2:183–185 commands: “You who believe, fasting is prescribed for you, as it was prescribed for those before you, so that you may be mindful of God.” Within Ramadan, the Laylat al-Qadr (Night of Power) commemorates the first revelation of the Qur’an to Muhammad and is described in the Qur’an as better than a thousand months of worship. Those who cannot fast (due to illness, pregnancy or travel) may break their fast and compensate later. Ramadan ends with the festival of Id-ul-Fitr.

Zakah — Almsgiving

Zakah means “purification” or “growth.” It requires every Muslim whose savings exceed the nisab (minimum threshold) to give 2.5% of their annual savings to those in need. Surah 9:58–60 specifies eight categories of those entitled to receive Zakah, including the poor, the indebted and travellers in need. Zakah purifies the giver’s remaining wealth from greed, supports the poor and reduces inequality within the ummah (global Muslim community).

Hajj — Pilgrimage

Hajj takes place in the twelfth month of the Islamic calendar and must be performed at least once in a lifetime by every Muslim who is physically and financially able. Surah 2:124–130 describes Ibrahim and Isma’il building the Ka’aba and establishing the rites of pilgrimage. Surah 22:25–30 describes the sacred sites and the command to proclaim Hajj to all people. Hajj rites include walking around the Ka’aba seven times (tawaf), walking between the hills of Safa and Marwa, standing on the plain of Arafat (wuquf), and symbolically stoning the devil. Hajj creates a profound sense of equality and unity — all pilgrims wear identical white garments (ihram), erasing distinctions of wealth and rank.

Spec point 2.3 on Salah is starred, making it a comparison target for Discuss questions.

  • Islam: Salah is compulsory five times daily; all pray in Arabic using set movements; facing Makkah (qibla); preceded by wudu. Jummah (Friday prayer) is a communal obligation for men.
  • Catholic Christianity: The Mass is the central act of worship â€” the Eucharist (the source and summit of Catholic life, Lumen Gentium 7). Catholics attend Sunday Mass as an obligation. Prayer takes many forms: formal (the Divine Office) and informal. No single fixed time structure equivalent to the five daily prayers.
  • General Christianity: Worship varies widely â€” liturgical (set structure, e.g. Anglican) and non-liturgical (free-form, e.g. Baptist). Prayer is encouraged but not prescribed at fixed times in the way Islamic Salah is.

The Ten Obligatory Acts of Shi’a Islam

Shi’a Muslims have their own framework of obligatory acts. While the Five Pillars are broadly shared, Shi’a Islam lists Ten Obligatory Acts (Furu ad-Din — branches of religion). These include Salah, Sawm, Zakah and Hajj (shared with Sunni Islam), but add several distinctively Shi’a duties: Khums (a 20% tax on surplus income), Jihad (striving in the way of Allah), Amr-bil-Maroof (commanding what is right), and Nahy-anil-Munkar (forbidding what is wrong). Khums is particularly significant: Surah 8:41 specifies that a fifth of certain gains should be set aside “for Allah and the Messenger,” which Shi’a Muslims understand as a continuing obligation paid to the Imam’s representatives (the religious scholars).

Key Fact

Khums (20% of surplus income) is a Shi’a-specific obligation distinct from Sunni Zakah (2.5% of savings above nisab). Khums is paid to the Imam’s representatives (religious scholars) for religious and charitable purposes. Both Zakah and Khums serve to reduce inequality within the ummah, but they operate on different rates and through different channels.

The Five Pillars are the universal Sunni framework of practice. The Ten Obligatory Acts of Shi’a Islam (Wajibat) include the Five Pillars (Salah, Sawm, Zakah, Hajj, and Shahadah through Walayah) plus additional obligations: Khums (20% levy), Jihad, commanding good, forbidding evil, and love/disavowal (Tawallah and Tabarra). Some scholars count the Ten differently, but the spec names Khums as the distinctive Shi’a addition. The underlying logic is the same: both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims structure their lives around prescribed acts of worship that express submission to Allah.

lesson_title: Jihad and Islamic Festivals
content_html:
Jihad — Striving in the Way of Allah

The word jihad means “struggle” or “striving.” It does not mean “holy war” — that is a common mistranslation. Every Muslim is engaged in jihad whenever they strive to be a better person, resist temptation, act justly or work for a fairer society. Islam recognises two forms of jihad: greater jihad (al-jihad al-akbar) and lesser jihad (al-jihad al-asghar).

Key Fact

Greater jihad is the struggle against nafs (the lower self) — the daily effort to be honest, compassionate, self-disciplined and obedient to Allah. Classical scholars held that this inward struggle is the most difficult and most continuous form of jihad. Lesser jihad refers to defensive struggle to protect the Muslim community under conditions tightly constrained by Islamic jurisprudence.

Greater Jihad — The Inner Struggle

Greater jihad involves resisting the temptation to lie, be selfish, be unjust or neglect religious duties. It includes studying Islam, raising a family according to Islamic values, working honestly, caring for parents and being a good neighbour. Every act of worship — Salah, Sawm, Zakah — is itself a form of greater jihad, since each requires the believer to overcome laziness, selfishness or distraction to submit to Allah. Greater jihad is lifelong; it ends only at death.

Lesser Jihad — Conditions and Constraints

Lesser jihad refers to the use of force to defend the Muslim community, resist oppression or uphold justice. It is not a licence for aggression. Surah 2:190–194 sets clear conditions: “Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you but do not transgress, for Allah does not love transgressors.” The passage prohibits fighting those who do not fight, prohibits attacking during sacred months and commands that fighting must stop when the enemy ceases hostilities. Surah 22:39 permits Muslims who have been wronged to fight in self-defence: “Permission to fight is given to those who have been attacked.”

Classical Islamic jurisprudence lists conditions that must be met before lesser jihad is permissible:

  • There must be a legitimate cause — typically self-defence or the defence of those being oppressed.
  • All peaceful alternatives must have been exhausted first.
  • It must be declared by a legitimate authority (not by individuals acting alone).
  • Non-combatants — women, children, the elderly, clergy and those not fighting — must be protected. Destruction of crops and buildings is prohibited.
  • It must cease when the enemy stops fighting or offers peace (Surah 2:192–193).

These conditions mean that lesser jihad is constrained in classical Islamic teaching far more than media portrayals often suggest. Extremist interpretations that remove these conditions are rejected by mainstream Islamic scholars.

Reducing jihad to “holy war” misrepresents Islamic teaching in two ways. First, it ignores greater jihad, which classical scholars considered the more important form. Second, it strips lesser jihad of its strict conditions — making it sound like permission for unlimited violence, which the Qur’an explicitly prohibits. Surah 2:190 states: “do not transgress, for Allah does not love transgressors.” Exam answers that describe jihad only as “holy war” will score poorly; both forms must be covered.

Islamic Festivals

Islamic festivals unite the global ummah in shared acts of worship, remembrance and celebration. Four key festivals feature in the specification: Id-ul-Adha, Id-ul-Fitr, Id-ul-Ghadeer (Shi’a) and Ashura.

Id-ul-Adha — Festival of Sacrifice

Id-ul-Adha (the Festival of Sacrifice) is one of the two major Islamic festivals. It commemorates Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice his son at Allah’s command. Surah 37:77–111 recounts the story: Ibrahim was commanded in a dream to sacrifice his son; he informed his son, who submitted willingly. As Ibrahim prepared to act, Allah intervened and provided a ram as a substitute, rewarding Ibrahim’s faith with the announcement that he had fulfilled the vision. Most Muslim scholars identify the son as Isma’il, though the Qur’an does not name him in this passage — the identification is traditional, not explicitly stated. Id-ul-Adha takes place during the Hajj period and involves the sacrifice of an animal (qurbani), with meat shared among family, friends and the poor.

Id-ul-Fitr — Festival Marking the End of Ramadan

Id-ul-Fitr celebrates the successful completion of the month-long Ramadan fast. It begins with a communal prayer and sermon at the mosque. Muslims give Zakat al-Fitr (a special obligatory charity at Ramadan’s end) so that everyone in the community can celebrate. The festival continues with visiting family, feasting, wearing new or clean clothes, and giving gifts to children. Id-ul-Fitr is a celebration of gratitude to Allah for the strength to complete Sawm and a joyful acknowledgement of the community that fasted together.

Id-ul-Ghadeer — A Shi’a Festival

Id-ul-Ghadeer is one of the most important Shi’a festivals. It commemorates the event at Ghadir Khumm (on the return from the Prophet’s final Hajj in 632 CE) when, according to Shi’a belief, the Prophet Muhammad announced that Ali ibn Abi Talib was to be his rightful successor. Shi’a Muslims understand Surah 5:3 — “Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My blessing upon you” — as referring to this proclamation at Ghadir. Sunni Muslims interpret this verse differently, associating it with the completion of the Hajj rather than a specific designation of Ali. Id-ul-Ghadeer is therefore a specifically Shi’a festival with profound significance for the doctrine of Imamah.

Ashura — A Day of Contrasting Significance

Ashura falls on the tenth day of Muharram (the first month of the Islamic calendar) and holds very different significance for Sunni and Shi’a Muslims.

Sunni Ashura: For Sunni Muslims, Ashura is primarily a day of voluntary fasting. A hadith recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari reports that when the Prophet arrived in Madinah and observed the Jewish community fasting, he was told it was the day Moses was saved from Pharaoh. The Prophet reportedly said he had a stronger connection to Moses and encouraged fasting on this day. It is an act of gratitude rather than mourning.

Shi’a Ashura: For Shi’a Muslims, Ashura is the most solemn day of the year — a day of mourning and lamentation for the martyrdom of Imam Husayn (the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad and the third Shi’a Imam) at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. Husayn and his small band were killed by the forces of Caliph Yazid after refusing to pledge allegiance to what Shi’a Muslims regard as an unjust ruler. Ashura is marked with processions, passionate re-enactments (ta’ziyeh), lamentations and the retelling of Husayn’s sacrifice. The tragedy of Karbala is central to Shi’a religious identity and theology.

Key Fact

Islamic festivals in this spec: Id-ul-Fitr (end of Ramadan — Sunni and Shi’a), Id-ul-Adha (feast of sacrifice, Ibrahim — Sunni and Shi’a), Ashura (Husayn’s martyrdom at Karbala — primarily Shi’a), Id-ul-Ghadeer (Muhammad’s designation of Ali — Shi’a). Surah 37:77–111 is the Qur’anic account of Ibrahim’s sacrifice that Id-ul-Adha commemorates.

lesson_title: The Buddha, the Dhamma and the Three Marks of Existence
content_html:
The Life of the Buddha

Buddhism began with the life of the Buddha, Siddhattha Gotama, believed to have lived in what is now Nepal and northern India. The Buddhavamsa XXVI tells how Siddhattha was born into a noble family. A prophecy said he would either become a great king or a great spiritual teacher. His father, hoping to keep him on the kingly path, sheltered him from all suffering — surrounding him with luxury, beauty and youth.

Despite his father’s efforts, Siddhattha ventured outside the palace walls and encountered the Four Sights: an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering ascetic (a holy man living without possessions). The first three showed him the reality of suffering; the fourth showed him that a different path was possible. These encounters changed everything. Siddhattha left his palace, his wife and his infant son to pursue spiritual liberation.

Key Fact

According to the Buddhavamsa XXVI, the Four Sights were: an old man (ageing), a sick man (illness), a corpse (death) and a wandering ascetic (the possibility of transcending suffering). They prompted Siddhattha’s ‘great renunciation’ — leaving his privileged life to seek enlightenment.

Enlightenment and the Founding of the Sangha

After years of studying with teachers and practising extreme asceticism, Siddhattha concluded that neither luxury nor extreme self-denial led to liberation. He chose a Middle Way between the two. Sitting in meditation beneath a Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya, he attained enlightenment. He became the Buddha — the Awakened One.

After his enlightenment the Buddha travelled to the Deer Park at Isipatana (near modern Varanasi) and gave his first teaching to five former companions. This event is called the ‘Setting in Motion of the Wheel of the Dhamma’. From this gathering, the Sangha (the community) began to form. Together with the Buddha and the Dhamma (the teachings), the Sangha forms the Three Refuges — the foundation of Buddhist life.

Dependent Origination (Paticca-samuppada)

At the heart of the Buddha’s insight was paticca-samuppada, often translated as ‘dependent origination’ or conditionality. This teaching says that nothing exists on its own — everything arises because of other conditions, and when those conditions change, the thing itself changes or ceases. Ignorance leads to mental formations, which lead to consciousness, which leads to birth, ageing, sickness and death — a chain of twelve interconnected links that keeps beings caught in suffering.

Understanding dependent origination is liberating: if suffering arises from conditions, then changing those conditions can end suffering. This is the practical logic behind all Buddhist practice.

The Three Marks of Existence

The Buddha taught that all conditioned existence has three characteristics, known as the Three Marks of Existence:

Dukkha (suffering or unsatisfactoriness). Dukkha covers obvious physical pain, but also the subtler dissatisfaction of getting what we want but finding it does not truly satisfy, and the suffering caused by change — even pleasant things end.

Anicca (impermanence). Anicca means that nothing conditioned is permanent. Feelings, thoughts, relationships, physical health, the seasons — everything arises, changes and passes away. Clinging to things as if they were permanent is a fundamental cause of suffering.

Anatta (no fixed self). Anatta is perhaps the most challenging Mark. The Buddha taught that what we call ‘the self’ is not a fixed, permanent entity but a constantly changing collection of five aggregates (the khandas). There is no unchanging soul or essence at the core of a person.

The Milinda Panha (Questions of King Milinda) is an Edexcel-named anchor text. In it, the monk Nagasena explains anatta using the analogy of a chariot. He asks King Milinda: is the chariot the wheels? The axle? The frame? The pole? When you take away each component, no ‘chariot’ remains — the chariot only exists as a label given to the collection of parts. In the same way, what we call ‘a person’ is a collection of changing physical and mental processes. There is no fixed ‘self’ hidden inside. This is the teaching of anatta.

The story is not a denial that persons exist at all — Nagasena is clearly speaking to a real king. Rather, it shows that persons exist conventionally (as useful labels for collections of processes) but not ultimately (as fixed, eternal entities). This distinction is important for understanding Buddhist ethics and rebirth.

Key Fact

The Three Marks of Existence apply to all conditioned phenomena: dukkha (suffering/unsatisfactoriness), anicca (impermanence) and anatta (no fixed self). Understanding them deeply is essential for Buddhist practice because it removes the delusion that drives suffering.

Theravada Buddhism emphasises anatta strictly: there is no self at any level, and liberation involves the complete cessation of personal existence in nibbana. Mahayana Buddhism introduces the concept of sunyata (emptiness) — not just persons but all phenomena are empty of inherent existence. Some Mahayana traditions also speak of Buddha-nature (tathagatagarbha) as an innate capacity for awakening. These are not contradictions but different emphases on the same core insight.

This divergence matters for your 12-mark Discuss answers: a question about anatta or the self in Buddhism may expect you to contrast Theravada and Mahayana approaches.

lesson_title: The Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path
content_html:
The Four Noble Truths

After his enlightenment, the Buddha’s first formal teaching was the Four Noble Truths, delivered at the Deer Park at Isipatana and recorded in the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. This sutta is the foundational text for the Four Noble Truths — Edexcel names it as the anchor source across all four truths.

The Four Noble Truths function like a medical diagnosis: identify the illness, find its cause, confirm a cure exists, and prescribe the treatment.

First Truth: Dukkha (Suffering)

The First Truth is that life involves dukkha — suffering, unsatisfactoriness. The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta identifies three types: obvious physical and mental pain; the suffering caused by change (pleasant things pass away); and the subtle suffering of conditioned existence itself. This is not pessimism but an honest diagnosis. Recognising dukkha is the first step toward freedom from it.

Second Truth: Samudaya (The Cause of Suffering)

Samudaya means arising or origin. The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta’s Sermon at Benares identifies the root of suffering as tanha (craving, thirst). Tanha fuels the Three Poisons: greed (lobha), hatred (dosa) and delusion (moha). These three are depicted at the hub of the Wheel of Life as a pig, a snake and a cockerel — the three animals that pull all living beings around the cycle of rebirth.

Key Fact

The Three Poisons — greed (pig), hatred (snake) and delusion (cockerel) — are depicted at the centre of the Wheel of Life (Bhavachakra). They represent the root causes of tanha (craving), which is the Second Noble Truth’s explanation of why suffering arises. The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta is the named source for this teaching.

Theravada Buddhists treat the Wheel of Life as a map of the rebirth realms that beings cycle through due to kamma. The goal is to exit the wheel entirely by achieving nibbana. Mahayana Buddhists also use the Wheel but emphasise that the Bodhisattva freely enters the cycle of rebirth to assist others towards liberation. For Mahayana, the Three Poisons are not just personal obstacles but represent the delusions that affect all sentient beings. This divergence means a Mahayana Buddhist may engage with the world differently than a Theravada monk who withdraws from it.

Third Truth: Nirodha (Cessation)

Nirodha means cessation or stopping. The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta teaches that suffering can end: when tanha is completely extinguished, nibbana (nirvana in Sanskrit) is reached. Nibbana literally means ‘blowing out’ — as a flame is extinguished — but it is not simple nothingness. It is the end of conditioned suffering and the cessation of the causes that keep beings bound to samsara (the cycle of rebirth).

Key Fact

Nibbana (Third Noble Truth) is the goal of Buddhist practice. The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, as the anchor text, records that the Buddha described it as the cessation of tanha and the end of rebirth in samsara. Theravada sees nibbana as the complete liberation of an individual; Mahayana sees it as encompassing all beings through the Bodhisattva path. This comparison point (1.5*) is important for 12-mark Discuss questions.

This spec point (1.5*) requires comparison with Christianity. Key contrasts: Buddhism teaches nibbana — the cessation of the causes of rebirth — whereas Christianity teaches resurrection of the body and eternal life with God (e.g. John 11:25). Buddhism’s cycle of samsara (multiple rebirths) contrasts with the Christian idea of one earthly life followed by judgement. Buddhism does not require a creator God for liberation; Christian salvation is achieved through faith in Christ. Both traditions affirm that the present life shapes what comes after it — Buddhist kamma and Christian moral living — but the mechanisms and goals differ fundamentally.

Fourth Truth: Magga (The Path)

Magga means path. The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta teaches that the Middle Way — avoiding both extreme luxury and extreme self-denial — leads to nibbana. The specific path is the Eightfold Path: Right Understanding, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration.

These eight aspects group into the Threefold Way: sila (ethical conduct: Right Speech, Action, Livelihood), samadhi (mental development: Right Effort, Mindfulness, Concentration) and panna (wisdom: Right Understanding, Intention). All three support each other — ethical behaviour creates the conditions for meditation, which in turn deepens wisdom.

lesson_title: Human Life, Ethics and Worship in Buddhism
content_html:
Human Personality: The Five Khandas

Buddhist teaching rejects the idea of a permanent, fixed self (anatta). Instead, what we call a ‘person’ is a temporary combination of five groups of processes called the Five Khandas (also spelled skandhas): form (rupa), sensation (vedana), perception (sanna), mental formations (sankhara) and consciousness (vinnana). The Khandha Sutta teaches that none of these aggregates is permanent, controllable or a self. Together they create the experience of being a person, but there is no unchanging ‘self’ hiding inside them.

Sunyata (emptiness) is the Mahayana development of anatta. All phenomena — not just persons — are empty of inherent, independent existence. Everything arises in dependence on causes and conditions. This extends the Theravada insight about persons to the entire fabric of reality.

Tathagatagarbha (Buddha-nature) is a contrasting Mahayana idea: while sunyata emphasises what things are not (not inherently self-existing), tathagatagarbha teaches that all sentient beings have an innate capacity for awakening — a seed of Buddha-nature within them. This does not contradict anatta — Buddha-nature is not a fixed self but a dynamic potential.

Arahant and Bodhisattva Ideals

The two main Buddhist traditions have different ideals for the fully-realised practitioner. Theravada Buddhism honours the Arahant ideal: an individual who has completely eliminated the defilements and will enter nibbana at death. The Arahant follows the Four Noble Truths to individual liberation.

Mahayana Buddhism centres on the Bodhisattva ideal. A Bodhisattva generates the aspiration to achieve Buddhahood for the benefit of all living beings, not just themselves. They develop the Six Perfections (paramitas) — generosity, ethics, patience, effort, meditation and wisdom — over countless lifetimes. The Mahayana also includes belief in celestial Buddhas (such as Amitabha of the Pure Land) who can help beings achieve liberation.

Buddhist Ethics: Kamma, Metta and the Five Precepts

Kamma (karma in Sanskrit) is the teaching that intentional actions — physical, verbal and mental — have consequences. The Dhammapada verses 181–187 and the Khuddakapatha affirm that good actions accumulate merit and lead toward liberation, while harmful actions generate unfavourable consequences. Every deliberate act matters.

Metta (loving kindness) and karuna (compassion) are the two key Buddhist virtues. Metta involves actively cultivating goodwill toward all living beings without exception — even those we dislike. Karuna moves beyond goodwill to the active wish to relieve suffering.

Key Fact

The pancha sila (Five Precepts) are the ethical foundation for all Buddhists: (1) abstain from killing living beings; (2) abstain from taking what is not given; (3) abstain from sexual misconduct; (4) abstain from false speech; (5) abstain from intoxicants. These are undertakings, not commandments — Buddhists choose to observe them as part of their practice.

Meditation

Meditation (samadhi) is one of the three divisions of the Threefold Way and central to Buddhist practice. There are several main types:

Samatha (concentration or calm-abiding) involves focusing the mind on a single object — the breath, a visualisation or a phrase — until the mind becomes still and focused. This creates the stable foundation needed for deeper practice.

Metta bhavana (loving kindness meditation) develops metta by deliberately generating feelings of goodwill, starting with oneself and gradually extending to all beings.

Vipassana (insight) uses the stable mind developed through samatha to investigate the moment-to-moment arising and passing of experience, directly perceiving anicca (impermanence), dukkha and anatta. Mindfulness of breathing is a key vipassana technique. Zazen is the Zen (Mahayana) form of seated meditation — ‘just sitting’ in open awareness.

Chanting, Mantras and Devotion

Chanting is a devotional and meditative practice. The Dhammapada 1–2 affirms that the mind shapes all actions: “Mind is the forerunner of all actions” — chanting trains the mind. The Tiratana chant (‘I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha’) is used in Theravada Buddhism. Mahayana Buddhism includes the chant of Nam Myoho Renge Kyo in Nichiren Buddhism, and the recitation of Amitabha Buddha’s name in Pure Land practice.

Key Fact

The three key meditation types are: samatha (concentration — calms and focuses the mind), metta bhavana (loving kindness — develops goodwill toward all beings) and vipassana (insight — directly perceives the Three Marks). These distinctions are examined in 4-mark and 5-mark questions comparing types of meditation.

Students sometimes assume Buddhist mantra recitation and mala bead counting are equivalent to Christian prayer addressed to a personal God. This is not correct. Theravada Buddhism generally regards mantras and devotional articles (like shrines) as supports for mental training — the Namo Buddhaya mantra (‘Homage to the Buddha’) expresses reverence and cultivates recollection of the Buddha’s qualities. In Mahayana traditions (especially Tibetan), mantras are seen as having transformative power as sacred syllables. Mala beads count repetitions. Neither tradition addresses an omnipotent creator deity in these practices.

lesson_title: Buddhist Worship: Temples, Puja, Death Rites and Festivals
content_html:
Buddhist Places of Worship

Buddhists worship in a variety of settings depending on their tradition. A vihara is the traditional monastery-complex found in Theravada Buddhism — it typically includes a shrine room, meditation hall and library. The library’s importance reflects the Buddhist emphasis on wisdom and study, as noted in the Kimsila Sutta.

A gompa is a Tibetan monastery, typically featuring elaborate shrine rooms with thangka paintings, statues of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and space for ritual practice. Triratna Buddhism (a Western movement) uses community centres rather than traditional monasteries, making practice accessible to people in secular contexts. All three types share a shrine room as their heart.

Key Fact

Three main types of Buddhist place of worship: the vihara (Theravada monastery-complex), the gompa (Tibetan monastery) and the temple (broader term). The Kimsila Sutta (an Edexcel-named anchor text) describes how Buddhists should conduct themselves when visiting these places of worship — with reverence and a desire to learn.

Objects of Devotion: Buddharupas and Sacred Objects

A buddharupa is an image of the Buddha that serves as a focus for devotion and meditation. The Vakkali Sutta clarifies the theological point: Vakkali, who was ill and longing to see the Buddha, is told that seeing the Dhamma is seeing the Buddha — the physical image points beyond itself to the truth the Buddha realised. Buddhists do not worship the statue as an idol; they use it to focus their minds on the Buddha’s qualities.

Other devotional objects include the Bodhi tree (venerated at Bodh Gaya as the site of enlightenment), flowers, incense and candles offered at shrines. These offerings are not gift transactions but symbolic acts cultivating the offering of oneself to the path.

Puja

Puja refers to acts of worship and devotion. The Mangala Sutta is recited during Theravada puja as a source of blessings. Typical puja includes offering flowers (representing impermanence), incense (representing the spread of good reputation), candles or lamps (representing wisdom), and prostrations before the buddharupa. Puja can be performed in the vihara with the Sangha or at a home shrine.

This is the 2.6* comparison-marked spec point. Key contrasts: Buddhist puja focuses on expressing reverence and cultivating the practitioner’s mind — it does not address an omnipotent creator God; Christian worship (liturgical or non-liturgical) is prayer directed to the personal God of the Bible. Buddhist puja may involve offerings to a buddharupa but this is not equivalent to Catholic veneration of the Eucharist (Christ’s real presence). Both traditions use communal gathering to strengthen commitment to practice and provide support. A 12-mark Discuss answer comparing worship should develop the Christian side with a named source (e.g. the Lord’s Prayer in Matthew 6:9–13) and avoid caricature of either tradition.

Death and Mourning Rituals

Buddhist death rituals vary significantly between traditions but all reflect the teachings on impermanence (anicca) and kamma. In Theravada communities, monks chant suttas at the bedside of the dying, and after death merits are transferred to the deceased. The body may be cremated (reflecting the teaching that the body is impermanent).

In Tibetan Buddhism, the Tibetan Book of the Dead (Bardo Thodol) is read aloud to the recently deceased or dying person. It describes the stages of consciousness experienced between death and rebirth (the bardo states) and instructs the consciousness to recognise the clear light of reality and achieve liberation. This is unique to Tibetan Vajrayana Buddhism.

Festivals

Wesak (Vesak) is celebrated on the full moon in May/June and commemorates the Buddha’s birth, enlightenment and parinibbana (passing into nibbana). It is the most widely observed festival across Theravada Buddhism.

Key Fact

Key Edexcel-named festivals: Wesak (Theravada — Buddha’s birth/enlightenment/death); Vassa/Rain Retreat (Theravada — three-month monastic retreat with reference to Anapanasati Sutta); Kathina (Theravada — offering of robes to monks after Vassa); Uposatha days (Theravada — fortnightly days of precept-keeping and lay devotion); Hanamatsuri (Japanese/Mahayana — celebrates the Buddha’s birth in April); Obon (Japanese — festival honouring ancestors); Parinibbana Day (Mahayana — commemorates the Buddha’s death); Lama Tsong Khapa Day (Tibetan — commemorates the 15th century founder of the Gelug school).

Vassa (the Rain Retreat) is a three-month period during the monsoon season when monks remain in their monasteries, intensifying practice. The Anapanasati Sutta (on mindfulness of breathing) is associated with meditation practice during Vassa. At the end of Vassa, the Kathina ceremony takes place: laity offer robes and supplies to monks, generating merit and strengthening the lay-monastic relationship. Uposatha days fall on new and full moon days: lay Buddhists take eight precepts (more than the usual five) and visit the monastery for teaching and meditation. These three practices together show how the monastic calendar structures the religious life of Theravada communities.

lesson_title: Brahman, the Three Aspects of the Divine and the Deities
content_html:
The Nature of Brahman

Brahman is the foundational concept of Hindu theology. Brahman is not simply ‘God’ in the sense of a personal deity — it is the ultimate reality, the absolute truth, the ground of all existence. Everything that exists either is Brahman or comes from Brahman. The Katha Upanishad 2.2.6–8 describes Brahman as subtler than the subtlest, greater than the greatest, the self of all beings.

Nirguna and Saguna Brahman

Hindu tradition makes a crucial distinction between two ways of understanding Brahman:

Nirguna Brahman (‘without qualities’) is Brahman understood as utterly beyond human conception — formless, attributeless, beyond gender, beyond personality. The Taittiriya Upanishad 2.7.1–2 describes this as Brahman beyond speech and thought. This is the most philosophically abstract understanding of the divine in Hinduism.

Saguna Brahman (‘with qualities’) is Brahman understood through qualities, form and personality — the God who can be worshipped, prayed to, and related to personally. The Rig Veda 1.154.1–2 describes Vishnu in his Saguna form. Most popular Hindu worship engages with Saguna Brahman through the deities.

Belief in Vaikuntha (the spiritual world, especially Vishnu’s abode) is associated with Saguna Brahman — it gives devotees a personal destination for their devotion and after-life aspiration.

Key Fact

Nirguna Brahman (formless, attributeless — Taittiriya Upanishad 2.7.1–2) contrasts with Saguna Brahman (personal, with qualities — Rig Veda 1.154.1–2). These are not two different gods but two ways of approaching the same ultimate reality. Most Hindu worship engages with Saguna Brahman through the deities.

The Three Aspects of the Divine

The spec requires knowledge of three aspects of Brahman beyond the Nirguna/Saguna distinction. The Mundaka Upanishad 2.1 is the named source:

Brahman as the impersonal, all-pervading ultimate reality — present everywhere, in all things, non-personal. This corresponds to Nirguna Brahman.

Antaryami — ‘within the heart’. Brahman is not only everywhere externally but is the inner witness and controller within every individual being. This is the aspect of God as the inner guide — the divine that is closer to us than our own thoughts.

Bhagavan — ‘beyond, as a personal loving God’. Brahman experienced as a supreme personal being who transcends the created world yet relates to devotees lovingly. This is the God of devotion (bhakti), known especially through Vishnu/Krishna.

The spec requires awareness of divergent views within Hinduism. Shaivism emphasises Shiva as the supreme reality — the divine as cosmic destroyer-creator who transcends ordinary distinctions. Shiva’s role as destroyer represents not annihilation but transformation: the old must end for the new to begin. Vaishnavism emphasises Vishnu (or Krishna as his avatar) as the supreme personal God (Bhagavan), approached through bhakti (devotion). Both Shaivism and Vaishnavism acknowledge Brahman as the ultimate reality but express it through different divine personalities.

The Major Deities

Hindu murti (sacred images) represent the deities in their Saguna forms. Avatars are manifestations of Vishnu who descend to earth when dharma (cosmic order) is under threat.

Vishnu is the preserver and sustainer. The Rig Veda 1.22 describes his three cosmic strides that measure the universe. His major avatars include Rama and Krishna. Vishnu’s abode, Vaikuntha, is the ultimate destination for devoted Vaishnavas.

Shiva is the destroyer-transformer. He is depicted with a crescent moon, the Ganges flowing from his matted hair, a trident, and seated in meditation. In Shaivism he is the supreme being.

Key Fact

Shakti is the divine feminine power or energy. She is worshipped in multiple forms: Parvati (consort of Shiva, representing love and devotion), Lakshmi (consort of Vishnu, representing prosperity and grace), and in more powerful forms such as Durga and Kali in the Shakta tradition. The three main deities — Vishnu (preserver), Shiva (destroyer-transformer), and Brahma (creator) — together reflect the cycles of creation, preservation and transformation in Hindu cosmology.

lesson_title: Atman, Samsara and the Purpose of Life
content_html:
The Atman

One of the most important concepts in Hinduism is the atman. Unlike the Buddhist teaching of anatta (no fixed self), Hinduism teaches that each individual has an eternal self — the atman — which is divine in nature. The atman is not the ego or personality (which changes), but the deepest, unchanging core of what a person truly is.

The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4 teaches that the atman continues after death, taking a new body determined by a person’s actions (karma) in the current life. The atman is what transmigrates — it is not destroyed at death but moves from body to body through the cycle of rebirth.

The 1.5* comparison-marked spec point requires you to compare Hindu and Christian views on the afterlife, but Hinduism’s unique concept of atman is also compared with Buddhism in wider RS discussions. Key contrast with Buddhism: Hinduism affirms a permanent, transmigrating self (atman); Buddhism denies a permanent self (anatta) — what transmigrates is not a fixed self but a causal stream of consciousness and karma. For the Christian comparison: Christianity teaches bodily resurrection and a personal soul created by God; Hinduism teaches an eternal atman cycling through many lives until liberation (moksha). A 12-mark Discuss answer should develop the Christian side with at least one named source (e.g. John 11:25 on resurrection).

Karma and Samsara

Karma is the law of moral causation. Every intentional action produces a consequence — good actions create positive karma that leads to better future lives; harmful actions create negative karma leading to lower rebirths. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4 describes how at death a person’s karma shapes what body the atman takes next: “A man becomes good through good deeds and evil through evil deeds.”

Karma drives samsara — the endless cycle of birth, death and rebirth. As long as a person is driven by desires, attachments and ignorance, they continue to generate karma and remain in samsara. Samsara can span countless lives across different forms — human, animal, divine or hellish realms — depending on accumulated karma.

Key Fact

Moksha is liberation from samsara. It is the ultimate goal of Hindu spiritual practice. When all karma is exhausted and the atman recognises its true nature (as identical with Brahman, in Advaita Vedanta, or as eternally related to Bhagavan, in Vaishnavism), the cycle of rebirth ends. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4 is the named source linking karma, the atman and the process of rebirth and liberation.

The Four Aims of Life (Purusharthas)

Hindu teaching identifies four legitimate aims for human life, known as the Purusharthas:

Dharma (duty/righteousness) is the first and foundational aim — living according to one’s moral obligations, social responsibilities and cosmic order. The anatana dharma (eternal law/truth) is the broader cosmic principle that dharma reflects.

Artha (wealth/prosperity) is the pursuit of material success, legitimately earned within the bounds of dharma. Kama (pleasure/desire) is the enjoyment of life’s pleasures — including love, beauty and sensory experience — when pursued ethically. Moksha remains the ultimate aim.

The Bhagavad Gita 3.35 teaches the importance of following one’s own dharma rather than imitating another’s: “Better is one’s own dharma, though imperfectly performed, than the dharma of another well performed.” This verse underpins the concept of varnashrama dharma — the duties specific to each person’s social position and stage of life.

Key Fact

Bhagavad Gita 3.35 is the named source for dharma and varnashrama dharma. The Purusharthas (dharma, artha, kama, moksha) map out a complete life: ethical duty, material success, pleasure and ultimately spiritual liberation. Varnashrama dharma specifies duties according to social position (varna) and life stage (ashrama: student, householder, forest-dweller, renunciant).

Students often conflate varnashrama dharma with the hereditary caste system. The distinction matters for the exam. Varnashrama dharma in classical Hindu texts refers to duties appropriate to one’s social role (varna) and stage of life (ashrama). The Bhagavad Gita’s teaching focuses on carrying out one’s duties faithfully as an act of worship. However, in practice the varna system became the hereditary caste system, which Hindu reformers such as Gandhi challenged. Many modern Hindus distinguish between the ideal varnashrama dharma in scripture and the social inequalities of the caste system. The 12-mark Discuss question may ask whether following dharma is always morally right — this divergence is relevant.

lesson_title: Suffering, Cosmology and Hindu Worship
content_html:
Hindu Responses to Suffering

Hinduism offers several teachings about why suffering exists and how to respond to it. Key virtues include ahimsa (non-violence), respect, empathy, mind/sense control, humility and love. The Mahabharata 5.39 states that the highest dharma is not to harm any living being — this links ahimsa directly to dharma as an ethical foundation for responding to suffering.

Suffering in Hindu thought is ultimately explained by karma — actions in previous lives shape present experience. This does not mean Hindus accept suffering passively: dharmic living, devotion (bhakti) and spiritual practice (yoga) are all active responses to suffering that work to purify karma and move the atman toward liberation. Knowledge and wisdom (jnana) help Hindus understand the real from the unreal, reducing the delusion that generates fresh suffering.

Hindu Cosmology

Hindu cosmology is vast in scale and deeply philosophical. The Rig Veda 10.129 (the ‘Hymn of Creation’ or Nasadiya Sukta) reflects on the mystery of creation itself: before anything existed, there was neither being nor non-being; the universe arose from a primordial impulse of desire. This cosmological humility — acknowledging that even the gods may not know how creation began — is distinctive in Hindu scripture.

Time in Hindu cosmology is cyclical and vast. The universe passes through four ages called yugas: Satya Yuga (the golden age of truth and righteousness), Treta Yuga, Dvapara Yuga and Kali Yuga (the present age, characterised by moral decline and spiritual degeneration, described in the Mahabharata). Together these four yugas form a Mahayuga, and thousands of Mahayugas form an even larger cycle.

Key Fact

Three cosmological concepts: Prakriti (matter/nature — the material aspect of the universe), tri-guna (the three qualities of matter: sattva — purity/harmony, rajas — activity/passion, tamas — inertia/darkness) and maya (illusion — the power that causes beings to mistake the world of appearance for the ultimate reality of Brahman). The Rig Veda 10.129 is the named source for Hindu cosmological reflection.

Forms of Hindu Yoga

Yoga means ‘union’ in Sanskrit. In Hinduism it refers to the spiritual disciplines that unite the practitioner with Brahman. There are four main paths:

Karma yoga is the path of selfless action. The Bhagavad Gita 6.44–47 describes the value of persistent practice. Earlier in the Gita, Krishna teaches performing one’s duty without attachment to results — every action becomes an offering to God rather than a source of new karma-bondage.

Jnana yoga is the path of wisdom and knowledge — using intellectual discrimination to see through maya and perceive Brahman directly.

Raja yoga (astanga yoga) is the path of meditation. The Bhagavad Gita 6.20–31 describes the state of a yogi whose mind is completely still and sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self.

Bhakti yoga is the path of loving devotion to a personal deity. The Bhagavad Gita 9.13–27 describes how even a leaf, a flower, fruit or water offered with devotion is accepted by Krishna — making bhakti accessible to everyone regardless of social position. This is the most widely practised path in popular Hinduism.

Forms of Hindu Worship

Hindu worship takes many forms. The Bhagavad Gita 9.13–27 specifically describes worship through offering and devotion:

Puja is the ritual offering to the deity — flowers, food (prasad), water, incense and light. Havan is the sacred fire ceremony. Darshan is the auspicious sight of the deity — Hindus come to the temple not primarily to hear a sermon but to see the deity and receive their gaze in return.

Key Fact

Key worship forms: puja (ritual offering), havan (fire sacrifice), darshan (auspicious sight of deity), bhajan (devotional song), kirtan (communal chanting/singing) and japa (repetition of God’s name). All reflect the Bhagavad Gita 9.13–27 principle that sincere devotion in any form is accepted by Krishna.

Arti is the waving of small oil lamps or candles before the deity, accompanied by the ringing of bells and singing. It is performed morning and evening in temples and homes. The flame represents the light of divine knowledge and devotion. After arti, worshippers cup their hands over the flame and bring the warmth to their faces, symbolising receiving the deity’s blessing. Arti is the most universally practised Hindu devotional act — it is both deeply personal and communally unifying.

lesson_title: Hindu Festivals, Pilgrimage and Charity
content_html:
Hindu Sacred Festivals

Hindu festivals celebrate the divine through joyful community participation, remembering key events in the lives of deities and the triumph of dharma over adharma (unrighteousness). The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.3.28 contains the famous prayer “Lead us from darkness to light, from the unreal to the real, from death to immortality” — a text associated with festivals of light such as Diwali.

Key Fact

Edexcel-named Hindu festivals: Diwali (Festival of Lights — Rama’s return, light over darkness); Holi (spring festival of colours — triumph of devotion over evil, associated with Prahlad and Holika); Navratri (nine nights honouring the goddess Durga); Dussehra (Rama’s victory over Ravana); Ram Navami (Rama’s birthday); Ratha-yatra (chariot festival of Jagannath); Janmashtami (Krishna’s birthday); Raksha Bandhan (festival of the brother-sister bond).

Diwali (October/November) celebrates the return of Rama to Ayodhya after his defeat of Ravana — the people lit lamps to guide him home. It also marks the goddess Lakshmi’s blessing of homes with prosperity. The Festival of Lights recalls the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.3.28’s prayer for light over darkness. For Sikhs, Diwali also marks the release of Guru Hargobind from imprisonment.

Holi (spring) celebrates the story of Prahlad, a devoted follower of Vishnu, and his aunt Holika, who tried to kill him in fire but was herself destroyed — divine devotion protecting the faithful. Holi also celebrates the playfulness of Krishna with the gopis. The throwing of coloured powder represents joy, spring and the dissolution of social divisions.

Hindu Pilgrimage

Pilgrimage is central to Hindu practice. The Rig Veda 10.75 (the Nadi-Stuti hymn) praises the sacred rivers of India, especially the Ganges. The Ganges is regarded as a goddess (Ganga Mata) whose waters purify karma and confer blessings on those who bathe in them. The city of Varanasi (Kashi) on the Ganges is regarded as the holiest city — dying in Varanasi is believed to grant moksha because Shiva himself whispers the liberating mantra into the ear of the dying.

Vrindavana is the sacred town associated with the childhood of Krishna — pilgrims walk the circumambulation path to experience Krishna’s divine presence. Together Varanasi, Vrindavana and pilgrimage to the Ganges represent three distinct types of Hindu pilgrimage: to a sacred river, to a sacred city and to a deity’s birthplace.

Key Fact

The Rig Veda 10.75 praises the sacred rivers as sources of divine blessing. Pilgrimage to the Ganges is believed to purify karma. Varanasi is associated with Shiva and liberation at death. Vrindavana is associated with Krishna’s divine childhood. These are the three Edexcel-named pilgrimage sites.

Hindu Environmental Projects

Hindu environmental care flows from the belief that the natural world is a manifestation of Brahman and that dharma requires care for creation. The Rig Veda 10.87.16–19 contains a prayer for the protection of creation from harm, and is associated with the Hindu commitment to environmental care. Rivers and sacred places are especially protected because of their spiritual significance.

Cow protection (go-raksha) is a specific form of Hindu environmental and ethical commitment. Cows are regarded as sacred — symbols of abundance, motherhood and the earth itself. Many Hindu organisations run gaushalas (cow sanctuaries) and campaign against the beef trade. This is connected to ahimsa (non-violence) and the understanding that all creatures are manifestations of Brahman.

Hindu Charity Work

The Bhagavad Gita 3.10–12 teaches the principle of yajna (sacrifice and giving) as the foundation of cosmic and social life: the world is sustained by acts of giving, and those who do not share in this reciprocal generosity fail in their dharmic duty. Dana (charitable giving) is one of the most important dharmic duties for Hindus.

Hindu charity work is understood as seva (selfless service) — an expression of karma yoga (selfless action) and bhakti (devotion through service). Organisations such as the Sewa UK network support food banks, medical camps and women’s rights initiatives, reflecting the Bhagavad Gita 3.10–12 principle that service to others is service to God. The spec requires knowledge of one named Hindu charity working to promote wellbeing, social inclusion and women’s rights. Environmental organisations such as Friends of Vrindavan work to restore sacred forests and rivers near pilgrimage sites, combining dharmic duty, environmental ethics and seva.

lesson_title: The Nature of God, Shekhinah and the Messiah
content_html:
The Nature of the Almighty

The Edexcel spec uses the title ‘the Almighty’ as the formal name for God in Judaism. Jewish belief is centred on the absolute oneness of the Almighty — monotheism is foundational. The Almighty is One: not one of many gods, not a God with parts or persons, but the absolutely singular source and sustainer of all existence. This is stated in the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4): “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one.”

Genesis 2 is the named source for several of the Almighty’s key characteristics:

Creator: The Almighty is the Creator of all existence, bringing the universe into being from nothing (creation ex nihilo). Genesis 2 describes the Almighty forming man from the dust of the ground and breathing life into him — humanity has a special, intimate relationship with the Creator. Jews today see creation as a gift requiring responsible stewardship.

Law-Giver: The Almighty is the source of all moral and religious law. The Torah (especially the Ten Commandments in Exodus 20) represents the Almighty’s revealed law. Living according to the Almighty’s law is not merely a religious duty but the means by which Jewish individuals and communities reflect the divine will in everyday life.

Judge: The Almighty holds all humanity accountable for their actions. Jewish theology teaches that the Almighty sees all deeds, knows all intentions, and will judge righteously. This belief in divine justice motivates ethical living — if the Almighty judges, then moral behaviour ultimately matters.

Key Fact

The four Edexcel-named characteristics of the Almighty: One (absolute monotheism — Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4), Creator (Genesis 2), Law-Giver (Torah, Exodus 20), Judge (holds all humanity accountable). These characteristics are tested in 3-mark and 4-mark questions.

The Shekhinah

Shekhinah means ‘divine dwelling’ — the presence of the Almighty among the Jewish people. The named anchor text is 2 Chronicles 7:1–3, which describes the Shekhinah descending as a cloud and filling the Temple when Solomon dedicated it: “When Solomon had finished praying, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering… and the glory of the Lord filled the temple.” The priests could not enter because of the overwhelming divine presence.

The Shekhinah is both comforting and awesome. Jewish theology developed the concept to express how the transcendent, infinite Almighty can be encountered in human experience — in the Temple, in the synagogue, in the home, and wherever Jews gather to pray. For many Jews, the Shekhinah is also associated with the feminine aspect of the divine.

Orthodox Judaism maintains that the Shekhinah was uniquely present in the Temple and that its absence today (since the Temple’s destruction in 70 CE) is a mark of divine distance pending the Messianic age and the rebuilding of the Temple. The Shekhinah will return fully when the Messiah comes. Reform Judaism tends to understand the Shekhinah as God’s presence available in every genuine moment of prayer, community and ethical action — not waiting for a physical Temple. This makes the concept more immediately accessible but less tied to specific historical events.

The Messiah and the Messianic Age

Messiah comes from the Hebrew mashiach (‘anointed one’). In Judaism the Messiah is a future human king — not divine — from the lineage of King David who will redeem the Jewish people and bring a universal age of peace. The named anchor text is Jeremiah 23:5–8, which describes the Almighty promising to raise a righteous Branch from David’s line who will reign wisely and bring justice: “The days are coming… when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, a King who will reign wisely and do what is just and right in the land.”

The messianic age will involve: the ingathering of exiled Jews to Israel; the rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem; universal recognition of the Almighty; the end of war and injustice. Jews believe the Messianic age has not yet arrived — the world still contains war, injustice and suffering.

Key Fact

Orthodox Jews believe in a personal Messiah — a specific future individual from David’s line — who will physically rebuild the Temple and redeem the Jewish people. Reform Jews tend to reinterpret this as the ‘messianic age’: a future era of universal justice brought about through human effort and moral progress, without necessarily involving a specific individual. Jeremiah 23:5–8 is the named source for messianic hope.

Both Orthodox and Reform Judaism place responsibility on the Jewish people to actively work toward the conditions of the messianic age. Tikkun olam (‘repair of the world’) is the Jewish ethical concept that every act of justice, charity, compassion and righteousness contributes to repairing the broken world and hastening the time of redemption. This means the messianic hope is not passive waiting but active ethical engagement. A 12-mark Discuss answer on this topic should develop this active dimension alongside any divergence between Orthodox and Reform positions.

lesson_title: The Covenant and Jewish Moral Principles
content_html:
The Covenant with Abraham

The relationship between the Jewish people and the Almighty is fundamentally one of covenant. The first great covenant is the Abrahamic covenant, recorded in Genesis 17. The Almighty promised Abraham: a great nation of descendants; the land of Canaan (the Promised Land); and a special ongoing relationship between the Almighty and Abraham’s descendants. In return, Abraham and his male descendants were to observe circumcision as a physical sign of the covenant in every generation.

This covenant is unconditional in one sense — the Almighty’s promise to Abraham’s descendants stands regardless of their behaviour. But it is also relational: the Jewish people are called to live faithfully in response to the Almighty’s faithfulness. The Promised Land is both a concrete historical reality and a symbol of the relationship between the Almighty and the Jewish people.

The Sinai Covenant and the Ten Commandments

The second great covenant is the Sinai Covenant, recorded in Exodus 20. Through Moses, the Almighty gave the Jewish people the Decalogue (Ten Commandments). The Decalogue establishes both duties to the Almighty (no other gods, no idols, no misuse of the divine name, observe Shabbat, honour parents) and duties to fellow human beings (no murder, adultery, theft, false testimony or coveting).

Key Fact

Two key covenants: the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17 — land, descendants, relationship; sign = circumcision) and the Sinai Covenant (Exodus 20 — the Ten Commandments / Decalogue as the terms of the Jewish people’s relationship with the Almighty). Both are the foundation of Jewish identity and practice.

Sanctity of Life and Pikuach Nefesh

Jewish ethics places an exceptionally high value on human life. Sanctity of life means that every human life has infinite worth because it is created by the Almighty in His image. This principle leads directly to Pikuach Nefesh — the principle that preserving life (nefesh = soul/life) overrides nearly all other commandments.

The named anchor text is Talmud Yoma 83–84, which states that Shabbat laws may be broken to save a life: “If a person sees a child who has fallen into a well, he may break the Shabbat to save it.” In practice, Pikuach Nefesh means that a Jewish doctor can and must work on Shabbat to save a patient; a pregnant woman is not required to fast on Yom Kippur if it endangers her health.

Orthodox Judaism applies Pikuach Nefesh strictly and carefully — it suspends specific commandments only when there is a genuine, immediate threat to life. The principle does not override every inconvenience; Orthodox rabbis consider cases individually. Reform Judaism applies the principle more broadly: if keeping a commandment causes significant harm or suffering, Reform Jews may view this as a Pikuach Nefesh consideration. For example, Reform Jews are more likely to apply Pikuach Nefesh to mental health as well as physical health, which has implications for topics like fasting and end-of-life care.

The Mitzvot and Free Will

The Mitzvot (singular: mitzvah) are the 613 commandments in the Torah. They cover every aspect of Jewish life — worship, food, business, family relationships, charity and social justice. The named source is Mishneh Torah by Maimonides — specifically the Sefer Madda (Book of Knowledge), which establishes the philosophical foundations of the Mitzvot.

Crucially, the Mitzvot are observed through free will. The Almighty does not compel obedience. Humans have the capacity to choose righteousness or sin, and this makes obedience meaningful and disobedience culpable. Maimonides emphasises that the Almighty’s knowledge of future human choices does not remove human freedom — this is one of the deepest puzzles in Jewish theology.

Jewish Beliefs about Life after Death

Jewish beliefs about life after death are notably less defined than in Christianity or Islam. The Torah’s focus is primarily on living ethically in this world. The named source is Ecclesiastes 12, which reflects on the nature of human mortality and uses somewhat ambiguous language about the spirit returning to the Almighty who gave it. This ambiguity reflects the diversity of views within Judaism.

Key Fact

The 1.8* comparison-marked spec point requires comparison of Jewish and Christian afterlife beliefs. Orthodox Judaism affirms bodily resurrection (techiyat ha-meitim) as a key belief — the dead will be resurrected in the Messianic age. Orthodox Jews also believe in the World to Come (Olam Ha-Ba) and sometimes Gehinnom (a place of purification). Reform Judaism tends to de-emphasise physical resurrection, focusing instead on the spiritual legacy of how one lived. Ecclesiastes 12 (the spirit returns to the Almighty) is the named anchor source.

The 1.8* comparison-marked spec point. Key contrasts: Orthodox Judaism believes in resurrection of the body in the Messianic age; Christianity teaches resurrection through Christ as demonstrated in the resurrection of Jesus (John 11:25 — ‘I am the resurrection and the life’). Judaism does not have a highly developed doctrine of heaven and hell; Christianity has more defined teaching on these (John 3:16 on eternal life; the Catholic doctrine of purgatory). Both traditions see ethical living now as shaping what comes after death. Jewish afterlife belief is tied to collective redemption in the Messianic age; Christian afterlife is individual resurrection and judgment.

lesson_title: Jewish Worship: Synagogue, Prayer and Sacred Texts
content_html:
Jewish Public Worship

Jewish public worship takes place primarily in the synagogue. Psalm 116:12–19 asks “How can I repay the Lord for all his goodness to me?” — capturing the spirit of gratitude and obligation that motivates Jewish communal worship. Services in the synagogue involve prayer, readings from the Torah and Haftarah (Prophets), and a rabbi’s sermon. Communal prayer requires a minyan — a quorum of ten adult Jews (Orthodox Judaism requires ten adult males; Reform Judaism counts women equally).

The Tenakh and Talmud

The Tenakh is the Hebrew Bible — an acronym from Torah (Five Books: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy), Nevi’im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings). The Torah is the most sacred section, believed by Orthodox Jews to have been revealed directly by the Almighty to Moses at Sinai.
