The Catholic Church responds that its teaching is grounded in natural law (the purpose of sex as written into human nature) and in scripture, not merely in social convention, and that redefining marriage or sexuality ultimately harms human flourishing even if it appears liberating in the short term.

The Purpose and Importance of Family

For Catholics, the family is “the domestic church” — the first place where faith is lived and passed on. The primary purposes of marriage include procreation and the education of children in the faith. Familiaris Consortio (Pope John Paul II, 1981), sections 36–85, provides the most detailed modern Catholic teaching on the family. It describes the family as the “first and vital cell of society” and outlines four specific tasks: forming a community of persons, serving life, participating in the development of society, and sharing in the life and mission of the Church.

Catholics do not ignore the reality of diverse family structures in 21st-century society. The Church recognises that families today include nuclear, single-parent, same-sex parent, extended, and blended families. The Catholic response is pastoral rather than condemnatory — families who do not match the ideal are still offered the full support of the Church community, while the Church maintains its teaching about the ideal of marriage between a man and a woman.

Key Fact

Familiaris Consortio was written by Pope John Paul II in 1981. It describes the family as the “first and vital cell of society” and the “domestic church.” It gives four tasks of the family: community of persons, serving life, developing society, and sharing in the Church’s mission. Sections 36–85 cover the family directly.

Support from the Local Parish: Family Group Movement

The local Catholic parish supports families through family worship, sacramental preparation, parents’ classes, children’s groups and counselling. One concrete example the spec names is the Family Group Movement, founded in France in 1947. Small groups of families meet regularly for prayer, discussion and practical support, creating a community in which faith can be shared and family life strengthened. The Catechism 2226 also notes that parents are “the first educators” of their children in the faith — the parish exists to support them in that primary vocation, not to replace it.

Cohabitation (living together as an unmarried couple) is viewed negatively in official Catholic teaching, because the permanence and public commitment of marriage are seen as essential to the full meaning of the sexual relationship. Many non-religious people and some Protestants regard cohabitation as a reasonable way to test compatibility before marriage, and argue that committed relationships have the same moral value whether legally formalised or not. The Catholic Church responds that the absence of a binding commitment changes the nature of the relationship and undermines the conditions for genuine self-gift. It nevertheless recognises that pastoral sensitivity is required when working with cohabiting couples who may be seeking to grow closer to the Church.

lesson_title: Contraception, Divorce, Gender Equality and Discrimination
content_html:
Family Planning and Contraception

The Catholic Church teaches that artificial contraception is morally wrong. This position is most clearly stated in Humanae Vitae (1968), written by Pope Paul VI. The document argues that every act of sexual intercourse must remain open to both its unitive dimension (deepening love between spouses) and its procreative dimension (openness to new life). Deliberately removing the procreative dimension through artificial means — the contraceptive pill, condoms, sterilisation — violates the integrity of the sexual act as God intended it.

The Church does not oppose natural family planning (NFP), which works with the body’s natural fertility cycles. NFP methods (such as monitoring the woman’s cycle to identify fertile and infertile periods) are not considered contraception in the moral sense because no act of intercourse is deliberately made infertile — instead, couples abstain during fertile periods. Catholics who use NFP still respect the principle that each act of intercourse must remain open to life in principle.

Key Fact

Humanae Vitae was published in 1968 by Pope Paul VI. It forbids the use of artificial contraception on the grounds that the unitive and procreative dimensions of marriage cannot be artificially separated. It remains one of the most debated documents in modern Catholic history.

Most Protestant denominations, including the Church of England, accept artificial contraception as a responsible way to plan a family. They argue that responsible parenthood and the wellbeing of existing children and the mother are important factors that a fixed rule about every act cannot accommodate. From the perspective of situation ethics (Joseph Fletcher, 1966), each case should be decided by what maximises love (agape) — and for a couple in poverty or with health concerns, contraception may be the most loving choice. Humanists and atheists generally see contraception as a tool of responsible reproductive choice with no moral problem. Catholics respond that the Church’s teaching is not merely a rule but a statement about the nature of sexual love, and that following it requires virtue, not restriction.

Divorce, Annulment and Remarriage

Divorce is not recognised by the Catholic Church as a valid dissolution of a sacramental marriage. Because marriage is a sacrament — a permanent covenant before God — it cannot simply be dissolved by a civil court. The Catechism of the Catholic Church 2382–2386 acknowledges that civil divorce may sometimes be justified as a legal measure to protect financial and civil rights, particularly in cases of abuse or abandonment. But in Catholic teaching, the person remains married before God even after a civil divorce. Remarrying while a first spouse is still living is therefore regarded as adultery.

The Church does, however, offer the process of annulment. This is not the same as divorce — it does not dissolve a marriage but declares that a valid sacramental marriage never existed from the beginning, because one or both parties lacked the capacity, freedom or intention required for a valid marriage. If a marriage is annulled, both parties are free to marry in the Church. Annulments require an investigation by a Church tribunal and are not automatic.

Key Fact

Catechism 2382–2386: civil divorce does not dissolve a sacramental marriage before God. Remarriage after divorce without annulment is regarded as adultery. Annulment is the Church’s ruling that a valid sacramental marriage never existed — not a Catholic divorce. Distinction is crucial in the exam.

Equality of Men and Women in the Family

Catholic teaching holds that men and women are equal in dignity before God but have complementary roles in the family. Catechism 2207 states that the family is “the original cell of social life” and that within the family, both parents have essential roles. The Church values what it calls “the dignity of work within the home” — the contribution of whoever carries out domestic and childcare work, whether mother or father, is considered genuinely valuable and not less important than paid employment.

Pope John Paul II’s “theology of the body” (a series of catechetical lectures given 1979–1984) offers a deeper philosophical framework. John Paul II argued that the body itself is a “theology” — its sexual differentiation as male and female reflects the self-giving love that defines the Trinity and that finds its human expression in marriage. This approach respects the embodied difference between men and women while insisting on their equal dignity and worth.

Gender Prejudice and Discrimination

The Catholic Church officially opposes all forms of gender prejudice and discrimination. Catechism 1938 states that “every form of social or cultural discrimination in fundamental personal rights on the grounds of sex, race, color, social conditions, language, or religion must be curbed and eradicated as incompatible with God’s design.” This is a strong and explicit statement. Within Catholic families and communities, both men and women should be treated with equal respect and given equal opportunity to develop their gifts.

The question of the role of women in the Church is a point of divergence within Christianity. The Catholic and Orthodox churches do not ordain women as priests, arguing that Jesus chose only male apostles and that this reflects a permanent theological intention, not a cultural accident. The Church of England and most Protestant denominations do ordain women, arguing that the principle of equality in Christ (“there is neither male nor female” — Galatians 3:28, though not a spec reference for this route) outweighs the argument from historical practice. Catholics respond that women hold vitally important roles in the Church as religious sisters, catechists, liturgical ministers and leaders of lay movements, even without ordination.

Situation ethics, developed by Joseph Fletcher in 1966, argues that love (agape) should guide every moral decision contextually, without rigid rules. Applied to divorce, this might mean that if a marriage has irretrievably broken down and both parties are suffering, the most loving course is separation and the freedom to remarry. Applied to gender roles, situation ethicists would argue that whatever enables human beings to flourish and love one another is morally correct, regardless of traditional role boundaries. Catholics respond that situation ethics sounds compassionate but can justify almost any action if framed in terms of “love,” and that the natural law framework of Catholic ethics provides more reliable guidance for human flourishing over time than case-by-case judgement.

lesson_title: Revelation, Visions and Miracles in Islam
content_html:
Revelation in Islam

Revelation is fundamental to Islamic theology. Muslims believe that Allah has communicated his will to humanity through a succession of prophets and revealed books, culminating in the Qur’an as the final, complete and perfectly preserved revelation. Surah 34:46–50 addresses the prophet Muhammad directly: “I advise you only to one thing — that you stand up to Allah in pairs and alone, then reflect.” The passage makes clear that revelation comes from Allah alone, not from human invention or external inspiration. Muslims understand the Qur’an as the direct speech of Allah, transmitted through the angel Jibril to Muhammad over approximately 23 years (610–632 CE).

This understanding of the Qur’an as direct divine speech — not a book about God but God’s own words — distinguishes Islamic revelation from most Christian understandings of the Bible. For Sunni Muslims, the Qur’an is perfectly preserved and its Arabic text is the literal word of Allah; translations are always considered interpretations rather than the Qur’an itself. Shi’a Muslims share this fundamental conviction but may also attach great importance to the interpretive role of the Imams in understanding revelation. Sufi Muslims additionally emphasise the inner, experiential dimension of revelation — seeking not merely intellectual understanding of Allah’s words but transformative encounter with the divine reality they point to.

Key Fact

Surah 34:46–50 establishes that the message of Muhammad comes from Allah alone. Muslims believe the Qur’an is the direct speech of Allah transmitted through Jibril — not a human composition, which is why it carries absolute authority. The Arabic text is considered the literal word of Allah; translations are interpretations.

Visions in Islam

Visions are recognised in Islamic tradition as one of the ways in which Allah communicates. The Qur’an itself records a vision of the Virgin Mary: Surah 19:16–22 describes the angel Jibril appearing to Maryam in the form of a man, announcing the miraculous birth of Isa (Jesus). The passage presents this vision as a direct divine intervention — Jibril speaks and Maryam conceives Isa by divine command. For Muslims, this vision confirms both the reality of divine communication and the elevated status of Maryam and Isa within Islam.

Islamic tradition also includes the concept of ru’ya (true dreams) as a form of divine communication, particularly important in the Sufi tradition. The Prophet Muhammad is reported to have received early communications from Allah through true dreams. Sunni and Shi’a Muslims both recognise visions and true dreams as potentially real experiences of divine communication, though they exercise caution — not every claimed vision is accepted as genuine. The scholarly tradition requires such experiences to be consistent with the Qur’an and Sunnah.

The Qur’an as a Miracle

In Islam, the greatest miracle is not a dramatic supernatural event but the Qur’an itself. Surah 17:84–89 issues a challenge to those who doubt the divine origin of the Qur’an: “Say: if all of humanity and the jinn were to come together to produce the like of this Qur’an, they could not produce the like of it, even if they were to help one another.” This is known in Islamic theology as the Inimitability of the Qur’an (i’jaz al-Qur’an). Muslims point to the Qur’an’s literary perfection in Arabic, its internal consistency, its preservation without corruption over fourteen centuries, and its ability to transform individuals and communities as evidence that it cannot be of human origin.

Atheists and Humanists challenge Islamic claims about the Qur’an and visions on several grounds. First, they argue that beauty or complexity in a text is not evidence of divine authorship — many great works of literature are produced by human genius. Second, they point out that every religious tradition claims its own scriptures are uniquely authoritative, yet these claims are mutually contradictory — they cannot all be right, so the fact of the claim provides no proof. Third, visions (including those of Jibril appearing to Maryam and to Muhammad) may have natural psychological explanations rather than supernatural ones. Muslims respond that the inimitability challenge has stood for over 1,400 years without a convincing human response; that the consistency of the Qur’an’s themes and its preservation are themselves remarkable; and that the transformation it produces in believers’ lives is evidence of a real source beyond human invention.

Key Fact

The Inimitability of the Qur’an (i’jaz al-Qur’an) is stated in Surah 17:88: no human or group of humans could produce a text equal to the Qur’an. Muslims point to its Arabic literary perfection, 1,400-year preservation, and internal consistency as evidence of divine origin — making the Qur’an itself the primary miracle of Islam.

lesson_title: Religious Experience, Design and Cosmological Arguments
content_html:
Religious Experience in Islam

Muslims in the Sunni, Shi’a and Sufi traditions all affirm the possibility of religious experience as a real encounter with the divine. Surah 2:118 states: “Those who do not know say: ‘Why does Allah not speak to us directly, or why does a sign not come to us?’” — implying that signs and communication from Allah do occur, but those who have not experienced them may not recognise them. For Muslims, the history of prophecy is itself a record of divine-human encounter: Allah speaking to Ibrahim, Musa, Dawud, Isa and finally Muhammad.

Within Sunni Islam, religious experience is understood primarily through the lens of prophetic tradition — the prophets’ experiences are the model for understanding divine communication. Personal religious experiences are evaluated against the standard of Qur’an and Sunnah. Shi’a Islam attributes a special intercessory and illuminating role to the Imams, who are understood as having privileged access to divine guidance. Sufi Islam places the greatest emphasis on personal religious experience — practices like dhikr (rhythmic remembrance of Allah’s names) and sama (devotional music and poetry) are designed to bring the practitioner into direct awareness of Allah’s presence.

Atheists and Humanists argue that religious experiences are subjective inner states that cannot serve as objective evidence for Allah’s existence. They point out that people in every religious tradition report experiences they interpret as encounters with their own deity — this suggests that the experiences are culturally conditioned rather than genuine encounters with a particular divine being. Richard Dawkins and other atheist writers argue that the human brain is evolved to detect patterns and agency, which produces vivid experiences of presence and meaning even when no real agent is present. Muslims respond that the consistency of spiritual experience across diverse cultures and centuries, the moral transformation it produces, and the fact that such experiences have historically galvanised extraordinary lives points to a real source beyond the individual mind.

The Design Argument in Islam

The design argument is strongly supported by the Qur’an. Surah 2:164 lists the signs of Allah’s creative power: “In the creation of the heavens and the earth, in the alternation of night and day, in the ships that sail through the sea with what benefits people, in the water Allah sends down from the sky, giving life to the earth after it has died... in the movement of the winds, and the clouds that run their appointed courses between sky and earth — in all of these are signs for those who use their reason.”

This verse is a cornerstone of the Islamic design argument. Every feature of the natural world — the rotation of the earth, the water cycle, the ecosystem of living things — is understood as a ayat (sign) pointing to Allah. The intricate interdependence of natural systems, the fact that the universe’s physical constants are precisely tuned to permit life, and the beauty of living organisms all lead Muslims to conclude that a wise and powerful Creator designed them. Unlike Paley’s watchmaker analogy, which is a philosophical argument from analogy, the Islamic design argument is grounded in Qur’anic theology — creation is a witness to Allah because Allah himself says so.

Key Fact

Surah 2:164 lists the alternation of night and day, the water cycle, the movement of ships, the winds and clouds as signs (ayat) of Allah for those who reason. The Islamic design argument is rooted in this Qur’anic witness to creation, not just philosophical argument from analogy.

The Kalam Cosmological Argument

The most important cosmological argument in Islam is the kalam cosmological argument. The word kalam means “speech” or “rational theology” in Arabic. The argument was developed within the Islamic scholarly tradition, and its most famous formulation comes from al-Ghazali (1058–1111 CE), in his work Kitab al-lqtisad fil’ltiqad (“The Middle Path in Theology”).

The kalam argument runs as follows: (1) Everything that begins to exist has a cause. (2) The universe began to exist. (3) Therefore the universe has a cause. Al-Ghazali then argues that this cause must be timeless, uncaused, immensely powerful, and personal — because a non-personal cause could not “decide” to begin creating at a particular moment. Muslims identify this first cause with Allah.

Key Fact

The kalam cosmological argument: (1) Everything that begins to exist has a cause. (2) The universe began to exist. (3) Therefore the universe has a cause — identified as Allah. Developed by al-Ghazali (1058–1111 CE) in Kitab al-lqtisad fil’ltiqad. This is NOT the same as Aquinas’s Five Ways — Aquinas and al-Ghazali made distinct arguments in different intellectual traditions.

Students regularly confuse the kalam cosmological argument with Aquinas’s Five Ways. They are distinct in origin, structure and tradition. The kalam argument originates in Islamic rational theology (ilm al-kalam), with al-Ghazali (1058–1111 CE) as its most influential developer. Aquinas’s First Three Ways (motion, causation, contingency) originate in Catholic scholastic theology, drawing on Aristotle. The kalam argument focuses specifically on the beginning of the universe (“everything that begins to exist has a cause”); Aquinas’s Third Way focuses on contingency (“things might not exist”). Never attribute the kalam argument to Aquinas. In the Islam routes of your exam, al-Ghazali is the named figure — use his name and his text.

lesson_title: The Problem of Suffering in Islam
content_html:
The Problem of Suffering

One of the most searching challenges to religious belief is the existence of suffering. If Allah is all-powerful (qadeer), all-knowing (alim) and compassionate (rahman, rahim), why does suffering exist? The opening surah of the Qur’an — Al-Fatiha (Surah 1) — immediately names Allah as Ar-Rahman (the Most Compassionate) and Ar-Rahim (the Most Merciful). These attributes are fundamental to Islamic theology. The problem of suffering asks: how can a God defined by compassion allow disease, disaster, poverty and grief?

It is important to note that Islamic theology approaches this differently from Western Christian theodicy. Islam does not have an equivalent of Augustine’s free-will defence or Irenaeus’s soul-making theodicy as named frameworks. Instead, the Qur’an addresses suffering directly through themes of divine will, human purpose, and the nature of this world. Surah 2:151–177 — a long and theologically rich passage — teaches that suffering is woven into the fabric of human life and that the proper response is patience (sabr), prayer and practical action.

Key Fact

Ar-Rahman = the Most Compassionate — universal mercy extending to all creation. Ar-Rahim = the Most Merciful — particular mercy offered specifically to believers. Both names appear in the opening of every surah (the Basmala) and in Al-Fatiha (Surah 1). Distinction is worth a mark in source-of-wisdom questions.

Life as a Test: The Islamic Response

The most distinctive Muslim response to suffering is the concept of life as a test (dunya as imtihaan). Surah 2:155–157 (within the broader passage 2:151–177) explicitly teaches: “We will test you with something of fear and hunger, some loss in goods, lives and crops — but give glad tidings to those who patiently persevere, who say, when afflicted with calamity: ‘To Allah we belong, and to him we shall return.’” Suffering is not a sign of Allah’s absence or indifference — it is part of the divine test of this temporary world.

Muslims believe that this life (dunya) is temporary and that the real measure of a person will be revealed on the Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Qiyamah). Suffering in this life, however severe, is finite — it will end either in this world or at death. The promise of paradise (jannah) for those who remained faithful through suffering gives suffering a context of ultimate hope. This framework allows Muslims to accept hardship without despair, because they believe Allah’s justice and mercy will ultimately prevail.

Patience (Sabr)

Sabr (patience) is one of the most highly praised virtues in Islamic ethics and spirituality. The Qur’an repeatedly instructs believers to respond to suffering with sabr — patient endurance that trusts in Allah’s will. Surah 2:153 teaches: “O you who have believed, seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allah is with the patient.” This verse links sabr directly to prayer (salah) as the two primary responses to suffering. Sabr is not passive resignation — it involves active trust in Allah’s wisdom, alongside continuing to act righteously in the face of hardship.

Beyond accepting suffering with patience, Muslims are called to address it through prayer and charity. Prayer (du’a — supplicatory prayer, as distinct from the obligatory salah) allows Muslims to bring their pain and needs directly to Allah, trusting that he hears and may respond in ways that serve their ultimate good. Charity (sadaqah and obligatory Zakah) is a direct practical response to the suffering caused by poverty and inequality. By redistributing wealth, Muslims address the conditions that produce suffering rather than merely accepting it. Surah 2:177 is explicit: “Righteousness is... to spend of your substance, out of love for Him, for your kin, for orphans, for the needy, for the wayfarer, for those who ask.” This verse (within the 2:151–177 passage) makes charity an integral part of the faithful response to suffering.

Key Fact

Surah 2:153: “Seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allah is with the patient.” The concept of dunya as imtihaan (life as a test) means suffering is part of Allah’s purposeful trial — not a sign of his absence. Those who endure with sabr and maintain faith will receive Allah’s mercy and ultimate reward.

Atheists and Humanists challenge the “life as test” framework on several grounds. First, they argue that the scale of suffering — the Holocaust, childhood cancer, famine killing millions of children — is vastly disproportionate to any educational or testing purpose. Second, they question whether a perfectly just Allah would create a world whose “test” many people are effectively predestined to fail due to the circumstances of their birth. Third, the appeal to future paradise as compensation seems to make this life’s injustices ethically irrelevant. Muslims respond that the Day of Judgement is the ultimate measure of justice — Allah’s mercy and wisdom extend beyond what human beings can perceive in any individual case, and that the promise of Allah’s presence “with the patient” (Surah 2:153) is a promise of companionship in suffering, not just future reward.

lesson_title: Marriage, Sexual Relationships and Family in Islam
content_html:
Marriage in Islam

Marriage (nikah) is considered a fundamental Islamic institution. It is an act of worship and a sunna (practice) of the Prophet Muhammad, who is reported in hadith to have described marriage as “half of the deen (religion).” Surah 4 (An-Nisa, “the Women”) is the primary Qur’anic source for marriage law and ethics. It establishes rights and responsibilities between spouses, the conditions for valid marriage, and the framework for family life. Marriage in Islam is not a sacrament (as in Catholicism) but a legal contract (aqd) which, when entered into freely and with proper conditions, is pleasing to Allah and an expression of permissible love.

The purposes of Islamic marriage include companionship and emotional fulfilment, procreation, the strengthening of the ummah, and the channelling of sexual desire within a relationship approved by Allah. Cohabitation (living together outside marriage) is not accepted in Islamic teaching — sexual relationships outside marriage are regarded as morally wrong. Non-religious Humanists and atheists generally argue that committed relationships have equal value whether legally formalised or not; Muslims respond that the framework of marriage provides the security, commitment and public accountability that children and partners deserve.

Key Fact

Surah 4 (An-Nisa, “the Women”) is the primary Qur’anic source for marriage law and family ethics. Marriage in Islam is a legal contract (nikah) that channels sexual desire within Allah’s approved framework and serves the purpose of procreation, companionship and strengthening the ummah.

Sexual Relationships

Muslim teaching is clear that sexual relationships are only appropriate within marriage. Surah 23:5–11 praises the believers who “guard their private parts, except from their wives or those their right hands possess — for then they are not blameworthy.” This passage establishes the marital context as the only acceptable framework for sexual activity. Muslims believe this protects individuals from exploitation, ensures children are born into committed families, and reflects the divine order for human sexuality.

On same-sex relationships, classical Islamic jurisprudence regards these as impermissible, drawing on Qur’anic and hadith sources. This is a matter of significant debate in contemporary Islam: a small number of modern Muslim scholars and communities argue for a reinterpretation, but the mainstream Sunni and Shi’a scholarly tradition maintains the prohibition. Non-religious Humanists argue that loving, committed relationships between consenting adults are morally equal regardless of gender. Muslim responses emphasise that Islamic ethics are grounded in revelation rather than evolving social norms, and that human dignity requires a framework of divine guidance.

Within the Sunni tradition, all four main schools of law (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i, Hanbali) agree on the fundamental permissibility of temporary marriage (mut’ah) being forbidden, while they permit standard nikah. Shi’a Muslims, particularly Twelver Shi’as, permit mut’ah (temporary marriage for a specified period), which Sunnis do not accept. This divergence reflects deeper differences between Sunni and Shi’a jurisprudence and interpretation of the Prophet’s practice. In questions of polygyny (a man marrying up to four wives, subject to strict conditions), Surah 4:3 permits it “if you fear you cannot be just, then [marry] only one” — most contemporary Muslim families in the West are monogamous in practice, reflecting both local legal norms and a stricter reading of the “justice” condition.

The Purpose and Importance of the Family

The family is central to Islamic life. Surah 46:15–18 instructs children to honour their parents and describes the duty of care for ageing parents as an obligation. Procreation is an important purpose of marriage: the Muslim family is the unit through which the ummah is perpetuated and in which children are raised in the Islamic faith. Children have responsibilities to their parents and parents to their children; the family unit is the primary institution of social support, education and welfare in Islamic teaching.

Islamic family structures have traditionally been extended: grandparents, parents and children living together or in very close proximity, providing mutual support and ensuring that elderly members are cared for within the family rather than delegated to state institutions. The nuclear family structure common in the West is accepted but not ideally preferred — the extended family model better reflects Islamic values of kinship solidarity. The ummah extends the circle of support still further — the mosque community provides resources, counselling, childcare, and support for widows and orphans.

The Support of the Ummah

Surah 3:102–105 calls on believers to “hold fast to the rope of Allah and be not divided among yourselves” — a powerful image of the ummah as a single community bound together by faith, responsible for one another’s wellbeing. The mosque community supports families through rites of passage (Aqiqah at birth, nikah ceremonies, funeral prayers), Islamic education for children (maktab or madrasah), and financial support through Zakah and voluntary charitable networks. Blended and single-parent families are supported by the ummah with the same pastoral concern, recognising that diverse family structures exist in 21st-century society.

Key Fact

Surah 3:102–105 calls believers to “hold fast to the rope of Allah” and not be divided. The ummah is a community of mutual responsibility. The mosque supports families through rites of passage, Islamic education, Zakah distribution, and pastoral care for the vulnerable.

lesson_title: Contraception, Divorce, Gender Equality and Discrimination
content_html:
Family Planning and Contraception

The Catholic Church teaches that artificial contraception is morally wrong. This position is most clearly stated in Humanae Vitae (1968), written by Pope Paul VI. The document argues that every act of sexual intercourse must remain open to both its unitive dimension (deepening love between spouses) and its procreative dimension (openness to new life). Deliberately removing the procreative dimension through artificial means — the contraceptive pill, condoms, sterilisation — violates the integrity of the sexual act as God intended it.

The Church does not oppose natural family planning (NFP), which works with the body’s natural fertility cycles. NFP methods (such as monitoring the woman’s cycle to identify fertile and infertile periods) are not considered contraception in the moral sense because no act of intercourse is deliberately made infertile — instead, couples abstain during fertile periods. Catholics who use NFP still respect the principle that each act of intercourse must remain open to life in principle.

Key Fact

Humanae Vitae was published in 1968 by Pope Paul VI. It forbids the use of artificial contraception on the grounds that the unitive and procreative dimensions of marriage cannot be artificially separated. It remains one of the most debated documents in modern Catholic history.

Most Protestant denominations, including the Church of England, accept artificial contraception as a responsible way to plan a family. They argue that responsible parenthood and the wellbeing of existing children and the mother are important factors that a fixed rule about every act cannot accommodate. From the perspective of situation ethics (Joseph Fletcher, 1966), each case should be decided by what maximises love (agape) — and for a couple in poverty or with health concerns, contraception may be the most loving choice. Humanists and atheists generally see contraception as a tool of responsible reproductive choice with no moral problem. Catholics respond that the Church’s teaching is not merely a rule but a statement about the nature of sexual love, and that following it requires virtue, not restriction.

Divorce, Annulment and Remarriage

Divorce is not recognised by the Catholic Church as a valid dissolution of a sacramental marriage. Because marriage is a sacrament — a permanent covenant before God — it cannot simply be dissolved by a civil court. The Catechism of the Catholic Church 2382–2386 acknowledges that civil divorce may sometimes be justified as a legal measure to protect financial and civil rights, particularly in cases of abuse or abandonment. But in Catholic teaching, the person remains married before God even after a civil divorce. Remarrying while a first spouse is still living is therefore regarded as adultery.

The Church does, however, offer the process of annulment. This is not the same as divorce — it does not dissolve a marriage but declares that a valid sacramental marriage never existed from the beginning, because one or both parties lacked the capacity, freedom or intention required for a valid marriage. If a marriage is annulled, both parties are free to marry in the Church. Annulments require an investigation by a Church tribunal and are not automatic.

Key Fact

Catechism 2382–2386: civil divorce does not dissolve a sacramental marriage before God. Remarriage after divorce without annulment is regarded as adultery. Annulment is the Church’s ruling that a valid sacramental marriage never existed — not a Catholic divorce. Distinction is crucial in the exam.

Equality of Men and Women in the Family

Catholic teaching holds that men and women are equal in dignity before God but have complementary roles in the family. Catechism 2207 states that the family is “the original cell of social life” and that within the family, both parents have essential roles. The Church values what it calls “the dignity of work within the home” — the contribution of whoever carries out domestic and childcare work, whether mother or father, is considered genuinely valuable and not less important than paid employment.

Pope John Paul II’s “theology of the body” (a series of catechetical lectures given 1979–1984) offers a deeper philosophical framework. John Paul II argued that the body itself is a “theology” — its sexual differentiation as male and female reflects the self-giving love that defines the Trinity and that finds its human expression in marriage. This approach respects the embodied difference between men and women while insisting on their equal dignity and worth.

Gender Prejudice and Discrimination

The Catholic Church officially opposes all forms of gender prejudice and discrimination. Catechism 1938 states that “every form of social or cultural discrimination in fundamental personal rights on the grounds of sex, race, color, social conditions, language, or religion must be curbed and eradicated as incompatible with God’s design.” This is a strong and explicit statement. Within Catholic families and communities, both men and women should be treated with equal respect and given equal opportunity to develop their gifts.

The question of the role of women in the Church is a point of divergence within Christianity. The Catholic and Orthodox churches do not ordain women as priests, arguing that Jesus chose only male apostles and that this reflects a permanent theological intention, not a cultural accident. The Church of England and most Protestant denominations do ordain women, arguing that the principle of equality in Christ (“there is neither male nor female” — Galatians 3:28, though not a spec reference for this route) outweighs the argument from historical practice. Catholics respond that women hold vitally important roles in the Church as religious sisters, catechists, liturgical ministers and leaders of lay movements, even without ordination.

Situation ethics, developed by Joseph Fletcher in 1966, argues that love (agape) should guide every moral decision contextually, without rigid rules. Applied to divorce, this might mean that if a marriage has irretrievably broken down and both parties are suffering, the most loving course is separation and the freedom to remarry. Applied to gender roles, situation ethicists would argue that whatever enables human beings to flourish and love one another is morally correct, regardless of traditional role boundaries. Catholics respond that situation ethics sounds compassionate but can justify almost any action if framed in terms of “love,” and that the natural law framework of Catholic ethics provides more reliable guidance for human flourishing over time than case-by-case judgement.

lesson_title: Jesus as Messiah, Son of Man and the Baptism
content_html:
Who Was the Messiah Supposed to Be?

At the time of Jesus, Jewish people in first-century Palestine were eagerly waiting for a Messiah. The Hebrew word means “anointed one” — the same concept as the Greek “Christ.” But expectations varied widely. Many Jews hoped for a warrior king like David who would overthrow Roman rule by military force. Others anticipated a priestly or prophetic figure. What almost nobody expected was a suffering Messiah who would die at the hands of the very oppressors he was meant to defeat.

One of the most important Old Testament passages Christians use to understand Jesus’s role is Isaiah 53. This text describes a “suffering servant” who is “despised and rejected” and who carries the people’s suffering in his own body. Early Christians read this passage and saw Jesus in it — the Messiah was not a conquering general but someone who fulfils God’s purposes through self-giving suffering. This is one reason why Mark’s Gospel, from its very opening lines, is so theologically charged.

Key Fact

Mark’s Gospel opens at Mark 1:1 with the declaration: “The beginning of the gospel about Jesus Christ, the Son of God.” Within the first eleven verses, Mark establishes Jesus as Messiah (Christ), Son of God, and the one who fulfils the prophecies of Isaiah. The Gospel then immediately goes on to announce Jesus’s baptism — his public commissioning as God’s chosen servant.

The Title ‘Son of Man’

One of the most unusual and distinctive titles Jesus uses for himself in Mark is Son of Man. Unlike “Messiah,” which carried powerful political overtones, “Son of Man” was more ambiguous and allowed Jesus to define his mission on his own terms. It has two layers of meaning.

The first layer comes from Daniel 7:13, which describes a heavenly figure “like a son of man” coming before God (“the Ancient of Days”) on clouds of glory and receiving “dominion and glory and a kingdom.” This apocalyptic figure has cosmic authority. When Jesus calls himself Son of Man, he is linking his identity to this heavenly ruler — a being with divine backing and an eternal kingdom.

The second layer is more human and vulnerable. Jesus also uses the title “Son of Man” when speaking of his coming suffering and death (for example when predicting his passion). This deliberate ambiguity is central to Mark’s portrayal of Jesus — he is simultaneously the exalted cosmic Lord of Daniel’s vision and the servant who must suffer. Scholars refer to this as the “hidden” nature of Jesus’s identity, and it runs throughout the whole Gospel.

At the time of Jesus, Jewish expectations of the Messiah were diverse. The Pharisees hoped for a teacher who would purify Jewish law. The Zealots wanted a military revolutionary. The Essenes (the community behind the Dead Sea Scrolls) anticipated a priestly Messiah from the tribe of Levi. Most of these groups would have been confused or even offended by Jesus, whose Messiah-ship centred on suffering, service and a cross rather than triumph.

Christians today see Isaiah 53 as proof that Jesus fulfilled Old Testament prophecy in an unexpected way — the “suffering servant” model reframes what messianic victory looks like. From a Humanist or atheist perspective, this reinterpretation is a post-hoc rationalisation: the early Christian community read its experience of Jesus’s death back into the Hebrew scriptures rather than fulfilling a genuine prediction.

The Baptism of Jesus (Mark 1:2–11)

Mark’s Gospel begins with extraordinary speed. There is no nativity story, no birth narrative, no genealogy. Mark immediately introduces John the Baptist, then launches straight into the baptism of Jesus (Mark 1:2–11). This reflects Mark’s breathless, urgent style — the word “immediately” appears over forty times in the Gospel.

In Mark 1:2–8, John the Baptist appears in the desert “preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.” Mark describes him wearing camel’s hair and eating locusts and wild honey — evoking the prophet Elijah. John declares that the one coming after him is so much greater that John is not even worthy to untie his sandals. This prepares the reader for the arrival of Jesus.

The baptism itself (Mark 1:9–11) contains three theologically significant moments. First, as Jesus comes up out of the water, the heavens are “torn open” — a dramatic, even violent image of God breaking into the world. Second, the Holy Spirit descends “like a dove” on Jesus — marking him as the one on whom the Spirit rests, recalling Isaiah’s description of the Spirit-filled servant. Third, a voice from heaven declares: “You are my Son, whom I love; with you I am well pleased.” This is a divine commissioning — God publicly identifies Jesus at the very beginning of his public ministry.

Key Fact

The baptism passage (Mark 1:9–11) contains a Trinitarian moment: the Father speaks from heaven, the Son is baptised in the water, and the Holy Spirit descends as a dove. This is significant for Christian understanding of Jesus as divine — the Father himself confirms Jesus’s identity.

John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance — people went to be washed of their sins. This raises an obvious question for Christians: why did a sinless Jesus submit to it? Different Christian traditions offer different answers. Some say Jesus was baptised in solidarity with sinful humanity — identifying with the people he came to save. Others argue he was submitting to God’s plan to show that all righteousness should be fulfilled. Still others focus on the baptism as a public commissioning for ministry rather than a washing from sin.

From a non-religious perspective, the baptism narrative is a significant historical problem. John’s baptism implied that Jesus needed to repent, which contradicts the Christian claim that Jesus was sinless. Many historians consider the baptism to be one of the most historically reliable events in the Gospels precisely because the early Church would not have invented something so potentially embarrassing. This is known as the “criterion of embarrassment.”

Significance for Christians Today

The titles Messiah, Son of Man and Son of God remain central to Christian identity and worship. Christians affirm Jesus as the Christ at baptism, in creeds, and in prayer. The suffering-servant model of the Messiah shapes Christian ethics: if the Son of God came to serve and suffer rather than to dominate, then Christian life is called to the same pattern of self-giving. The baptism of Jesus is also foundational for Christian sacramental practice — most Christian denominations celebrate baptism as a sacrament of initiation, modelled on Jesus’s own.

lesson_title: Miracles of Jesus in Mark
content_html:
What Are Miracles and Why Do They Matter in Mark?

Mark’s Gospel contains more miracle stories per chapter than any other Gospel. Miracles serve two purposes in Mark: they demonstrate Jesus’s divine authority, and they provoke responses of faith, confusion or hostility. Mark divides the miracles into two types: nature miracles and healing miracles. Each type reveals a different dimension of who Jesus is.

The Calming of the Storm (Mark 4:35–41)

In Mark 4:35–41, Jesus and his disciples are crossing the Sea of Galilee when a violent squall erupts. The disciples panic; Jesus is asleep in the stern. They wake him crying, “Teacher, don’t you care if we drown?” Jesus stands up and commands the wind and waves: “Quiet! Be still!” The storm stops immediately. Jesus then turns to the disciples and asks: “Why are you so afraid? Do you still have no faith?” The disciples are terrified and ask: “Who is this? Even the wind and the waves obey him!”

This question — “Who is this?” — is the central question of the whole Gospel. The miracle shows Jesus exercising power over creation in a way that, in the Hebrew scriptures, belongs to God alone. In the Old Testament, God is repeatedly described as the one who stills the seas and calms the storms (for example in the Psalms). For Mark’s readers, the implication is clear: Jesus possesses divine power over nature.

The Feeding of the Five Thousand (Mark 6:32–44)

In Mark 6:32–44, a crowd of around five thousand men (plus women and children) has followed Jesus into a remote place. The disciples suggest sending them away to find food. Jesus tells the disciples to feed them. They protest — they have only five loaves of bread and two fish. Jesus takes the food, looks up to heaven, gives thanks and breaks the loaves. The disciples distribute them to the crowd; everyone eats and is satisfied. Twelve basketfuls of broken pieces are collected afterwards.

This miracle is packed with theological significance. It echoes Moses feeding the Israelites with manna in the wilderness. The action of taking, giving thanks, breaking and giving (the eucharistic actions) points forward to the Last Supper. The twelve baskets may represent the twelve tribes of Israel. Christians today see this as showing Jesus’s compassion for human physical need as well as his divine power.

Key Fact

Mark’s Gospel contains two feeding miracles. The feeding of the five thousand is in Mark 6:32–44. There is a separate feeding of four thousand in Mark 8:1–9. These are different events — don’t confuse them. The five thousand feeding has twelve baskets left over; the four thousand has seven. Only the feeding of the five thousand is specified in this part of the specification.

Walking on Water (Mark 6:45–52)

Immediately after the feeding, Jesus sends his disciples by boat to the other side of the lake and goes up a hillside to pray. In the night, he comes to them — walking on the water. The disciples are terrified, thinking he is a ghost. Jesus climbs in and the wind ceases. Mark adds the observation that “they were completely amazed, for they had not understood about the loaves; their hearts were hardened.” Even after witnessing the feeding miracle, the disciples still do not fully comprehend who Jesus is.

The walking on water reinforces Jesus’s authority over the natural world. The phrase “he was about to pass by them” may echo the Old Testament idea of God “passing by” (as with Moses in Exodus 33 and Elijah in 1 Kings 19). Mark uses these Old Testament echoes consistently to suggest that Jesus is the presence of God himself on earth.

Healing Miracles: Legion (Mark 5:1–20)

In Mark 5:1–20, Jesus encounters a man in the region of the Gerasenes who is possessed by many unclean spirits. The man lives among the tombs, cannot be controlled, and cries out day and night. The demons name themselves “Legion” — a Roman military term for up to six thousand soldiers — emphasising both their number and, for Jewish readers, their association with Roman occupation. Jesus drives the demons into a herd of pigs that rush into the lake. The formerly possessed man is found sitting, clothed and in his right mind. The townspeople beg Jesus to leave the region, apparently frightened by what has happened.

This miracle demonstrates Jesus’s authority over the spiritual world as well as the natural world. The man’s restoration — sitting, clothed and in his right mind — is a vivid image of the wholeness that Jesus brings. Christians see healing miracles as showing Jesus’s compassion and his power to restore people excluded from community.

Healing Miracles: Jairus’s Daughter (Mark 5:21–43)

In Mark 5:21–43, Jairus, a synagogue ruler, falls at Jesus’s feet and begs him to come and heal his twelve-year-old daughter who is dying. While they are on the way, messengers arrive to say the girl has already died. Jesus responds: “Don’t be afraid; just believe.” He arrives, finds the mourners weeping, and declares the child is only sleeping. They laugh at him. Taking only Peter, James and John (his inner circle of disciples), Jesus enters the girl’s room. He takes her hand and says “Talitha koum!” — an Aramaic phrase meaning “Little girl, get up.” She immediately stands up and walks. Jesus tells the family to give her something to eat.

This miracle is sandwiched around the healing of a woman with bleeding (Mark 5:25–34) — a literary technique Mark uses, called a “Markan sandwich,” to reinforce meaning. Both involve a twelve-year period: the woman has been ill for twelve years; the girl is twelve years old. Both involve an act of courageous faith. The raising of Jairus’s daughter pushes Jesus’s power to its most dramatic — he appears to reverse death itself.

Key Fact

The five miracle passages for this lesson: calming the storm (Mark 4:35–41), feeding the five thousand (Mark 6:32–44), walking on water (Mark 6:45–52), healing of Legion (Mark 5:1–20), and raising of Jairus’s daughter (Mark 5:21–43). Knowing which passage is which is essential — exam questions ask about specific miracles.

From a Humanist or atheist perspective, miracles are not evidence of divine power. They argue that the natural world operates according to scientific laws that do not have exceptions. What appeared miraculous in the first century can now be explained: mass psychological suggestion, misremembering, literary embellishment, or metaphor. The feeding of five thousand might symbolise the miracle of sharing rather than a multiplication of food. The storm calming may reflect the disciples’ experience of sudden peace rather than a physical intervention.

Christians respond in different ways. Some insist the miracles are literally true — God created the natural laws and can override them. Others argue the miracles are ‘signs’ whose deeper significance is theological, whether or not the physical events happened exactly as described. What matters, they argue, is what the miracles say about Jesus’s identity and mission.

Taken together, the miracles in Mark present Jesus as someone with authority over: the natural world (storm, feeding, water), the spirit world (Legion), disease (bleeding woman), and death (Jairus’s daughter). Each category escalates. For Mark, these miracles are not random acts of power but signs that the Kingdom of God is breaking into the world through Jesus. They also show his compassion: he is moved by a father’s grief, a sick woman’s desperation, a crowd’s hunger. The disciples’ persistent failure to understand (“their hearts were hardened”) serves as a warning to readers who might observe miracles and still not grasp who Jesus is.

lesson_title: Peter's Confession, the Transfiguration and Conflicts of Jesus
content_html:
Peter’s Confession at Caesarea Philippi (Mark 8:27–33)

Mark 8:27–33 is one of the most pivotal passages in the whole Gospel. Jesus and his disciples are travelling near Caesarea Philippi, a largely Gentile city in the far north of the region. Jesus asks: “Who do people say I am?” The disciples report various views — John the Baptist, Elijah, or one of the prophets. Then Jesus pushes further: “But what about you? Who do you say I am?”

Peter answers: “You are the Messiah.” It is the first time in Mark that a human being explicitly identifies Jesus with this title. For the reader, it is a moment of breakthrough. But what happens next is shocking. Jesus immediately begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise after three days. Peter takes Jesus aside and rebukes him. Jesus then rebukes Peter in the strongest terms: “Get behind me, Satan! You do not have in mind the concerns of God, but merely human concerns.” Peter had understood the title; he had completely misunderstood what the title meant.

Key Fact

Peter’s confession (“You are the Messiah”) at Caesarea Philippi (Mark 8:27–33) is the turning point of the Gospel. It marks the end of Jesus’s Galilean ministry and the beginning of his journey towards Jerusalem and the cross. Immediately after, Jesus teaches the first of three passion predictions — the Messiah must suffer.

The Messianic Secret

Throughout Mark’s Gospel, Jesus repeatedly commands people and demons to keep quiet about his identity. After healing the leper (Mark 1:44), he tells him to “say nothing to anyone.” After the raising of Jairus’s daughter, he gives “strict orders not to let anyone know about this.” When demons correctly identify him as the Son of God, he silences them. This pattern is called the messianic secret.

The German scholar William Wrede, writing in 1901, was the first to identify this as a deliberate theological device. He argued it was Mark’s way of explaining why Jesus was not widely recognised as the Messiah during his lifetime. Modern scholars suggest other interpretations: perhaps Jesus genuinely wanted to control how his mission was understood, or perhaps Mark is showing that Jesus’s identity can only be understood fully in light of the cross and resurrection — before that, any proclamation of “Messiah” would be dangerously misunderstood, as Peter’s rebuke demonstrates.

The Transfiguration (Mark 9:1–10)

Six days after Peter’s confession, Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain. There his appearance changes before them: his clothes become “dazzling white, whiter than anyone in the world could bleach them.” Moses and Elias appear and talk with Jesus. A cloud overshadows them, and a voice declares: “This is my Son, whom I love. Listen to him!”

The Transfiguration is a moment of divine disclosure. Moses represents the Law; Elias (Elijah) represents the prophets. Their appearance alongside Jesus signals that he is the fulfilment of both the Law and the Prophets — the whole of Israel’s scriptures point towards him. The divine voice echoes the baptism (Mark 1:11), but now adds the command “Listen to him!” — directing the disciples to take Jesus’s teaching about suffering seriously.

From a Humanist or atheist perspective, the Transfiguration is a visionary experience, not a literal supernatural event. Visions and altered states were common in the ancient world and were often interpreted as divine communication. The appearance of long-dead figures like Moses and Elijah cannot be verified by any independent evidence and does not constitute proof of Jesus’s divine identity. The story may be a later creation by the early Church to affirm its faith that Jesus was greater than Moses and Elijah.

Christians respond that the Transfiguration is confirmed by multiple witnesses (three disciples), is described with specific visual detail that does not read like symbolic invention, and is consistent with the disciples’ later proclamation of Jesus as Lord after the resurrection. For Christians, the event is a genuine glimpse of Jesus’s divine nature before the cross.

The Conflicts of Jesus

Mark’s Gospel shows Jesus in repeated conflict with the religious authorities. These controversies are not incidental — they build the case that ultimately leads to his arrest. Three key conflicts are in the specification.

In Mark 2:1–12, Jesus heals a paralysed man who is lowered through the roof by his friends. Crucially, Jesus first says “Son, your sins are forgiven.” The scribes immediately react inwardly: “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” Jesus perceives their thoughts and challenges them, then heals the man to show that “the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.” The miracle is theologically loaded: Jesus is doing something only God can do.

The Sabbath controversies in Mark 2:23–3:6 show Jesus’s disciples plucking grain on the Sabbath, and Jesus healing a man with a withered hand on the Sabbath. The Pharisees challenge both actions as unlawful. Jesus responds with the famous statement: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.” This claim to be “Lord of the Sabbath” is another assertion of divine authority — only God could claim ownership of the day God had established.

The cleansing of the Temple (Mark 11:15–18) is a dramatic act of prophetic protest. Jesus enters the Temple courts, overturns the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves, and drives everyone out. He quotes Isaiah 56:7 (“My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations”) and Jeremiah 7:11 (“You have made it a den of robbers”). The chief priests and scribes “began looking for a way to kill him.” This act is the trigger for the passion narrative.

Key Fact

In each conflict, Jesus asserts divine authority: to forgive sins (Mark 2:1–12), to redefine the Sabbath as “Lord of the Sabbath” (Mark 2:23–3:6), and to purify the Temple (Mark 11:15–18). Each provokes increasing hostility from the authorities, building the case against him that eventually leads to his death.

The scribes and Pharisees were not simply petty rule-enforcers. They were guardians of the Jewish covenant with God. The Torah was not just law — it was the sign of Israel’s special relationship with God. When Jesus claimed to forgive sins, he was doing what only God could do. When he called himself Lord of the Sabbath, he claimed a divine prerogative. When he disrupted the Temple, he threatened both the religious system and the economic arrangements that the priestly families depended upon. Each act was, from their perspective, a form of blasphemy or dangerous social disruption.

For Mark’s readers, these conflicts were not failures of communication but deliberate prophetic challenges. Jesus was not trying to keep the peace — he was announcing a new order, the Kingdom of God, which would require the old structures to give way.

lesson_title: The Last Days of Jesus and the Passion
content_html:
The Last Supper (Mark 14:12–31)

On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, Jesus instructs two of his disciples to prepare the Passover meal. The evening meal that follows (Mark 14:12–31) becomes one of the most theologically significant events in the whole New Testament. While they are eating, Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it and gives it to his disciples saying: “Take it; this is my body.” He then takes a cup, gives thanks and shares it, saying: “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.”

This is the institution of what Christians call the Eucharist. The language of “covenant” and blood echoes Exodus 24, where Moses sprinkled blood on the people to seal the covenant at Sinai. Jesus reframes the Passover — a celebration of liberation from Egypt — as a new covenant sealed with his own death. This passage is the scriptural foundation for Christian sacramental practice across all denominations.

Also in this passage, Jesus predicts that one of the Twelve will betray him. He predicts that all of them will “fall away” and specifically that Peter will deny him three times before the rooster crows twice. These predictions set the stage for the passion narrative that follows.

Key Fact

The Last Supper passage is Mark 14:12–31. The central actions are: Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and says “This is my body.” He takes the cup, gives thanks, shares it, and says “This is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many.” This is the basis for the Eucharist celebrated in churches worldwide.

Gethsemane (Mark 14:32–42)

After the meal, Jesus takes his disciples to the garden of Gethsemane on the Mount of Olives (Mark 14:32–42). He takes Peter, James and John deeper into the garden and tells them: “My soul is overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death. Stay here and keep watch.” He falls to the ground and prays: “Abba, Father, everything is possible for you. Take this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will.”

He returns to find the disciples asleep. He wakes them, returns to pray, comes back again and finds them sleeping again. A third time the same. This threefold pattern (like Peter’s threefold denial) is a literary device in Mark emphasising the disciples’ failure at the crucial moment. Jesus’s prayer — especially the address “Abba” (an intimate Aramaic term for Father) — shows a real human struggle with the prospect of death, while the submission “yet not what I will, but what you will” models obedient trust.

The Betrayal and Arrest (Mark 14:43–52)

While Jesus is still speaking, Judas Iscariot arrives with an armed crowd sent by the chief priests. Judas identifies Jesus with a kiss — the customary greeting between a student and his rabbi, now perverted into a signal for arrest. One of the bystanders draws a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest’s servant. Jesus challenges his arresting party: “Am I leading a rebellion, that you have come out with swords and clubs to capture me? Every day I was with you, teaching in the temple courts, and you did not arrest me.”

Mark then adds a striking detail found only in his Gospel: a young man following Jesus, wearing nothing but a linen garment, is seized. He flees naked, leaving his garment behind. Scholars debate whether this is the author’s subtle self-insertion into the story, a symbolic detail (nakedness as shame), or simply an eyewitness memory included for vividness.

The Trials (Mark 14:53–65; 15:1–15)

Jesus faces two separate trials. In Mark 14:53–65, he is brought before the High Priest and the Sanhedrin. Witnesses are produced but their testimony does not agree. Finally the High Priest asks directly: “Are you the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One?” Jesus answers: “I am.” He adds that they will see “the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Mighty One and coming on the clouds of heaven.” The High Priest tears his clothes and declares blasphemy. Jesus is condemned to death.

In Mark 15:1–15, Jesus is brought before Pilate. Pilate asks: “Are you the king of the Jews?” Jesus replies: “You have said so.” He gives no further answer, to Pilate’s amazement. Pilate offers to release a prisoner as was his custom at the festival — but the crowd, stirred up by the chief priests, call for Barabbas. Pilate asks what to do with Jesus; they shout “Crucify him!” Pilate, “wishing to satisfy the crowd,” hands Jesus over to be crucified.

In first-century Judaea, the Sanhedrin (Jewish ruling council) had authority over religious law but could not carry out the death penalty without Roman authorisation. This is why Jesus faces two trials: the Sanhedrin condemns him for blasphemy (Mark 14:53–65), and Pilate then must authorise the crucifixion (Mark 15:1–15). The Jewish authorities wanted Jesus dead but needed Rome to do it. This two-stage legal process is consistent with what historians know about Roman provincial governance.

Each trial has a different focus. The High Priest’s trial revolves around Jesus’s identity: “Are you the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One?” Pilate’s trial revolves around political threat: “Are you the king of the Jews?” The Sanhedrin charge is blasphemy; the Roman charge must be sedition against Caesar. Mark shows how the same claim — that Jesus is the Christ — is processed differently by Jewish religious law and Roman political law.

The Passion and Crucifixion (Mark 15:21–39)

Jesus is crucified at a place called Golgotha (“the place of the skull”) at nine in the morning. Mark notes that Simon of Cyrene is compelled to carry the cross. At midday, darkness covers the land for three hours. At three in the afternoon, Jesus cries out in Aramaic: “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” — which Mark translates as “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” This is the opening line of Psalm 22, a psalm that moves from abandonment to vindication.

Jesus utters a loud cry and breathes his last. At that moment, the curtain of the Temple is “torn in two from top to bottom” — a symbol that the barrier between God and humanity has been removed. Immediately the Roman centurion standing opposite Jesus says: “Surely this man was the Son of God!” In Mark’s Gospel, this is the first time a human being — not a demon — correctly identifies Jesus with this title while he is alive. And it is a Roman soldier, a Gentile outsider, who says it.

Key Fact

The centurion’s confession at the cross — “Surely this man was the Son of God” (Mark 15:39) — is the climax of Mark’s narrative on Jesus’s identity. It is spoken by a Gentile Roman soldier at the moment of death, not triumph. This reflects Mark’s whole theology: Jesus’s divine identity is revealed in and through the cross, not despite it.

The Resurrection: The Empty Tomb (Mark 16:1–8)

On the first day of the week, three women — Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome — come to the tomb to anoint the body. They find the stone already rolled away and a young man in white inside who tells them: “He has risen! He is not here. See the place where they laid him. But go, tell his disciples and Peter, ‘He is going ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you.’”

Mark’s Gospel ends at this point (16:8): “Trembling and bewildered, the women went out and fled from the tomb. They said nothing to anyone, because they were afraid.” This is the authentic ending of Mark. The abruptness is deliberate — the reader is left with the empty tomb, the proclamation, and the challenge to believe and follow. There is no appearance of the risen Jesus in the genuine Markan text. This ending has troubled Christians across the centuries, which is why later scribes added a “longer ending” (Mark 16:9–20) that most scholars consider a later addition, not part of the original Gospel.

The ending at 16:8 — with the women fleeing in fear — is theologically rich rather than incomplete. Mark has shown disciples who repeatedly fail, misunderstand and abandon Jesus. The women at the tomb are the disciples’ last chance, and they too fail to deliver the message. Yet the risen Jesus has gone ahead to Galilee. The open ending invites the reader to become the one who does go to Galilee, who does tell the disciples, who does follow. Some scholars argue Mark ended abruptly because the original last page of the scroll was lost; others argue the ending is deliberate.

Christians who find the ending abrupt are reassured by the other Gospels (Matthew, Luke and John), which all record resurrection appearances. But for students of Mark specifically, the challenge of the spec is to understand Mark 16:1–8 on its own terms — the empty tomb, the proclamation, and the challenge to respond in faith. This is the authentic Markan witness to the resurrection.

lesson_title: Discipleship: The Call, the Cost and Living It Today
content_html:
The Call of the Disciples

Discipleship in Mark’s Gospel begins with a simple, urgent invitation. In Mark 1:14–20, Jesus walks beside the Sea of Galilee and calls Simon and Andrew, then James and John. Each time, the response is immediate: “Immediately they left their nets and followed him.” There is no lengthy deliberation, no negotiation. The disciples abandon their livelihoods on the spot. In Mark 2:13–17, Jesus calls Levi, a tax collector — a figure despised as a Roman collaborator — with the same two words: “Follow me.” Levi gets up and follows.

This pattern communicates something important about what Mark means by discipleship: it is a total reorientation of life, not a part-time commitment. Scholars note that in the ancient world, students usually chose their rabbi; here, Jesus chooses his disciples. This reversal is deliberate. The disciples did not graduate to follow Jesus — they were called, often from ordinary working lives, and they left everything in response.

In Mark 6:7–13, Jesus sends out the Twelve on a mission. He sends them “two by two” and instructs them to “take nothing for the journey except a staff — no bread, no bag, no money in their belts.” They are to travel light, depend on the hospitality of others, and preach repentance. This commissioning extends the model: discipleship is not just internal formation but active participation in Jesus’s mission.

The Parables of Discipleship

Two parables in Mark address what discipleship looks like in practice.

The Parable of the Sower (Mark 4:1–20) describes four kinds of soil: the path (no response), rocky ground (initial enthusiasm that withers), thorny ground (choked by wealth and worries), and good soil (bearing fruit). Jesus explains that the seed is “the word.” The parable is a sobering map of how differently people receive the invitation to follow Jesus, and it connects directly to the Kingdom of God — the disciples are called to be “good soil,” remaining receptive to God’s word even when life makes it difficult.

The Parable of the Tenants (Mark 12:1–12) is a allegory about Israel’s history of rejecting God’s messengers. The vineyard owner sends servants (the prophets) and finally his “beloved son” (Jesus). Each is rejected or killed. The parable ends with the owner’s judgement on the tenants. For Christians, this parable shows that true discipleship means recognising the Son and accepting the cost of that recognition, even when rejection and suffering follow.

The Rich Man and the Cost of Discipleship (Mark 10:17–31)

In Mark 10:17–31, a man runs up to Jesus and asks what he must do to inherit eternal life. He claims to have kept all the commandments from youth. Jesus looks at him with love and says: “One thing you lack. Go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow me.” The man goes away sad, because he had great wealth. Jesus then says: “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the kingdom of God.”

This passage shows the cost of discipleship in concrete terms: it may require surrendering wealth, status and security. It connects to the Kingdom of God — present discipleship and future reward are linked. The disciples are astonished and ask who can be saved; Jesus replies: “With man this is impossible, but not with God; all things are possible with God.” Peter then notes that they have left everything — Jesus assures him of reward “in this present age” and in “the age to come.”

Key Fact

In Mark 10:17–31, Jesus tells the rich man to sell all his possessions, and then says “it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the Kingdom of God.” This striking image shows that discipleship may demand the surrender of everything that competes with God.

The Failure and Problems of Discipleship

Mark’s account of discipleship is unflinchingly honest about human failure. In Mark 9:14–29, the disciples who remained behind while Jesus was on the Mount of Transfiguration are unable to drive out a spirit from a boy. The father cries: “I asked your disciples to drive out the spirit, but they could not.” Jesus heals the boy and privately tells the disciples: “This kind can come out only by prayer.” Their failure is a lesson in the limits of disciples acting on their own authority without relying on God.

Most dramatically, Peter — the first and most prominent disciple — denies Jesus three times in Mark 14:66–72. A servant girl twice identifies him as a follower of Jesus; bystanders also challenge him. Each time Peter denies it, the last time with curses. The rooster crows. Peter “broke down and wept.” This is the same Peter who confidently declared “You are the Messiah.” His failure shows that discipleship is not a matter of confidence or strength but of grace. For Christians, Peter’s later restoration (implied by Mark 16:7 — the angel says “tell the disciples and Peter”) shows that failure is not the end.

In Mark 10:41–45, the disciples argue about which of them is the greatest. Jesus gathers them and says: “Whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” This teaching on servant leadership defines the purpose of discipleship: not status but service, modelled on Jesus himself.

Women in the Ministry of Jesus

Mark’s Gospel gives significant attention to women as disciples, which was countercultural in the first century. In Mark 7:25–30, a Greek (Syrophoenician) woman approaches Jesus and persistently argues for her daughter’s healing. Jesus initially responds with what sounds like a rebuff, but she persists. Jesus praises her response and heals her daughter. She shows tenacity and faith in a context where Gentile women would not normally address a Jewish rabbi. Many scholars read her as a model disciple — persistent, faithful, willing to engage with rejection.

In Mark 14:3–9, an unnamed woman breaks an alabaster jar of expensive perfume and pours it over Jesus’s head. The disciples are indignant at the “waste.” Jesus defends her: “She has done a beautiful thing to me… wherever the gospel is preached throughout the world, what she has done will also be told.” Her act anticipates Jesus’s burial anointing. It is a profound act of devotion that the disciples fail to recognise.

In Mark 15:40–47 and 16:1–8, it is women — Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Salome — who are present at the crucifixion, witness the burial, and are the first to hear the resurrection proclamation. The male disciples have fled. This pattern of female faithfulness at the cross and tomb is significant for Christian understandings of women’s role in the Church.

Mark 8:34 contains Jesus’s definition of discipleship: “Whoever wants to be my disciple must deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me.” Three modern Christians are studied as examples of costly discipleship.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer (1906–1945) was a German Lutheran pastor and theologian. His book The Cost of Discipleship (1937) argued that “cheap grace” — Christianity without cost or commitment — was a heresy. Genuine discipleship required what he called “costly grace.” He put his beliefs into practice: he joined the resistance against Hitler’s Nazi regime and was arrested in 1943. He was executed at Flossünbürg concentration camp on 9 April 1945, just weeks before the end of the war. His example embodies Mark 8:34 — he literally took up a cross.

Oscar Romero (1917–1980) was the Archbishop of San Salvador in El Salvador. In a deeply divided society, he became an outspoken advocate for the poor and the victims of state violence. His outspokenness made him a target. He was assassinated on 24 March 1980, shot while celebrating Mass at a hospital chapel. He was canonised by Pope Francis on 14 October 2018. His life shows discipleship as prophetic witness even at the cost of death.

Mother Teresa (1910–1997) was an Albanian-Indian Catholic nun who founded the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata in 1950. She devoted her life to serving “the poorest of the poor” — the sick, the dying, and those abandoned on the streets. She connected her service explicitly to Mark 10:45 — the one who came “not to be served, but to serve.” She was canonised by Pope Francis on 4 September 2016.

Key Fact

The three modern disciples all embody Mark 8:34 (“deny themselves and take up their cross”): Bonhoeffer (German Lutheran pastor, executed 1945 for resisting Hitler), Romero (Archbishop of El Salvador, assassinated 1980 while defending the poor), Mother Teresa (Albanian-Indian nun, founded Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata 1950, canonised 2016). All three were canonised or recognised by the Church as heroes of faith.

From an atheist or Humanist perspective, religious observance such as discipleship can be seen as unnecessary. Humanists argue that compassion, service and ethical commitment do not require a religious framework — Bonhoeffer’s courage against the Nazis, or Mother Teresa’s care for the dying, reflects universal human values that anyone can hold regardless of belief. They might also question whether religious motivation can sometimes lead people in the wrong direction — history contains examples of harmful actions done in the name of following religious commands.

Christians respond that the examples of Bonhoeffer, Romero and Mother Teresa show discipleship producing exactly the kind of self-giving, justice-seeking, care-for-the-marginalised that Humanists also value — and that the explicit connection to Jesus’s teaching in Mark provides both motivation and a consistent framework for costly action that secular ethics can also affirm.

lesson_title: Allah in the Qur'an: Al-Fatiha, Tawhid and the 99 Names
content_html:
Al-Fatiha: The Opening of the Qur’an

Surah al-Fatiha (Surah 1) is the first chapter of the Qur’an and its spiritual heart. Its name means “the Opening.” It consists of seven verses and is recited in every raka’a (unit) of the daily prayer — meaning a devout Muslim recites it at least seventeen times a day. It begins: “In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.” This opening formula, known as the Bismillah, begins 113 of the 114 surahs of the Qur’an.

Al-Fatiha moves through praise of Allah as Lord of all worlds, the Gracious and the Merciful, the Master of the Day of Judgement, before turning to a declaration of total dependence: “You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.” It closes with a petition to be guided on “the straight path” — the path of those Allah has blessed, not those who have gone astray.

For Muslims, al-Fatiha is a summary of the whole Qur’an in miniature: it establishes who Allah is (the Lord, the Merciful), what the human relationship with Allah should be (worship and dependence), and what the goal of human life is (guidance on the straight path, leading ultimately to the bliss of paradise). Its brevity and comprehensiveness make it uniquely powerful as a daily act of worship.

Tawhid: The Oneness of Allah

The central theological concept of Islam is Tawhid. It means that Allah is one — absolutely and uniquely.
