This is not simply numerical oneness (the idea that there is one God rather than many) but a qualitative uniqueness: nothing in creation can be compared to Allah, nothing shares his divine nature, and he has no partners, no equals, no offspring and no rivals.

Surah al-Anaam (Surah 6), verses 13–24, expresses this powerfully. It condemns those who “ascribe partners to Allah” and affirms that everything in heaven and earth belongs to him. Allah is described as the Knower of hidden and open things, as the Master of everything. For Muslims, belief in Tawhid shapes every aspect of life: it means that ultimate loyalty belongs to Allah alone, that no human authority can override divine command, and that every act of worship must be directed to Allah and no one else.

Key Fact

Tawhid — the absolute oneness of Allah — is Islam’s foundational belief. The Shahadah (the declaration of faith) expresses it: “There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is his messenger.” Every Islamic practice flows from Tawhid: prayer is directed to Allah alone, shirk (ascribing partners to Allah) is the gravest sin, and all other beliefs are orientated around this central affirmation of divine uniqueness.

The 99 Beautiful Names of Allah

The Qur’an refers to Allah by many names and attributes. Muslim tradition identifies 99 of these as the 99 Beautiful Names (Asma ul-Husna). Each name is both a description of Allah’s nature and a guide to how believers should relate to him. Reciting the names is itself a form of worship — the Prophet Muhammad is reported to have said that Allah has 99 names, and whoever memorises them will enter paradise. The specification focuses on six specific names, each anchored in a Qur’anic verse.

Ar-Rahman (Surah 55:1) — the All-Merciful. This name refers to Allah’s universal, overflowing mercy that extends to all creation, believer and non-believer alike. It is the mercy that sustains the world in existence, the mercy behind creation itself. Ar-Rahim (Surah 3:31) — also translated “the All-Merciful,” but with a different shade: where Ar-Rahman is broad and universal, Ar-Rahim refers to the specific, particular mercy Allah shows to believers who turn to him. Both names open al-Fatiha, establishing that Allah’s fundamental character is merciful.

As-Salam (Surah 59:23) — the Source of Peace. Allah is not simply at peace; he is the source and origin of all peace. The Arabic greeting “as-salamu alaykum” (peace be upon you) derives from this same root, connecting everyday Muslim social life to the divine attribute. Al-Khaliq (Surah 6:102) — the Creator. Allah alone is the originator of all things. Nothing in creation created itself; everything owes its existence to Allah’s creative act. This name underpins the Islamic doctrine of creation.

Al-Ghaffar (Surah 2:173) — the All-Forgiving, or the One who repeatedly forgives. This name emphasises that Allah’s forgiveness is not a single act but a continuous attribute — he covers and forgives sins again and again for those who sincerely repent. Ar-Razzaq (Surah 51:58) — the Sustainer, or the One who provides. Allah is the provider of all sustenance — physical food, spiritual nourishment, and everything a creature needs. This name encourages Muslims to trust Allah’s provision and to be generous, since ultimately all wealth comes from him.

Both Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim come from the Arabic root r-h-m, related to the word for womb (rahim) — suggesting mercy that is as fundamental and enveloping as a mother’s care for a child.

The distinction: Ar-Rahman (active participle, intensive) expresses Allah’s ongoing, universal mercy — the mercy that creates the world, provides rain, and sustains all life regardless of belief. It is often said that Ar-Rahman is exclusively an attribute of Allah — it cannot be used as a name for a human being. Ar-Rahim (intensive adjectival form) expresses the specific mercy Allah directs towards believers who turn to him in faith and repentance. While Ar-Rahman covers the whole creation, Ar-Rahim is the mercy of the hereafter, the reward of the faithful.

Together, the two names at the start of al-Fatiha — and at the start of virtually every surah — announce that the God who speaks in the Qur’an is, before everything else, a God of mercy.

Key Fact

The six specified names with their Qur’anic anchors: Ar-Rahman = universal mercy (Surah 55:1); Ar-Rahim = specific mercy for believers (Surah 3:31); As-Salam = Source of Peace (Surah 59:23); Al-Khaliq = the Creator (Surah 6:102); Al-Ghaffar = the All-Forgiving (Surah 2:173); Ar-Razzaq = the Sustainer (Surah 51:58). Knowing the name, meaning and surah reference is the full exam answer for the 5-mark source question.

Muslims recite the 99 names using prayer beads (subha or tasbih) in a practice called dhikr (remembrance of Allah). Repeating the names is itself an act of worship — meditating on each name deepens understanding of who Allah is and how to relate to him. Different names are called upon in different contexts: Al-Ghaffar (the All-Forgiving) is invoked in prayer for forgiveness; Ar-Razzaq (the Sustainer) in prayers for provision; As-Salam (the Source of Peace) in prayers for peace of heart.

The names also shape Islamic ethics: because Allah is As-Salam, Muslims are called to be instruments of peace; because Allah is Al-Ghaffar, Muslims are encouraged to be forgiving; because Allah is Ar-Razzaq and provides all sustenance, Muslims are encouraged to give generously to those in need. The 99 names are not just theology — they are a programme for living.

lesson_title: Believers, Creation and Humanity as Khalifah
content_html:
Believers and Non-Believers in Surah al-Baqarah

Surah al-Baqarah (Surah 2) is the longest chapter in the Qur’an and one of the most important. Its name, meaning “the Cow,” refers to the story of Moses and a miraculous cow in verses 67–73. The surah opens with a description of three groups of people, presenting a moral map of humanity from the Qur’an’s perspective.

Those who believe are described as people who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, give from what Allah has provided, believe in what was revealed to Muhammad and in earlier revelations, and are certain of the hereafter. For them, the Qur’an says, “such are on guidance from their Lord and such are the successful.” Their faith is active: it manifests in prayer, generosity and moral seriousness, not merely in intellectual assent.

Those who disbelieve are described as people for whom warning makes no difference — their hearts are sealed, their hearing and sight are covered. This language uses the Qur’anic concept of the “sealed heart” — not a physical sealing but a description of a state of moral hardening caused by repeated rejection of truth. A third group, the hypocrites, claim to believe but do not. The Qur’an treats hypocrisy as more dangerous than open disbelief, because it corrupts the community from within.

Key Fact

In Surah al-Baqarah, the believer is someone who: (1) believes in the unseen, (2) establishes prayer, (3) gives from what Allah has provided. Their faith is not passive — it is expressed through worship, generosity and moral action. This portrait of the believer shapes Islamic practice: faith and action cannot be separated.

The Qur’anic Account of Creation

The Qur’an does not give a single unified creation narrative like Genesis 1–2. Instead, creation references are spread across many surahs, each emphasising a different aspect. Several key verses are specified. In Surah 21:30, Allah declares: “Do not the unbelievers see that the heavens and the earth were joined together (as one unit of creation), before We clove them asunder?” This verse is often cited in discussions of whether the Qur’an anticipates modern scientific theories about the origins of the universe. Muslim scholars debate the significance of this verse in relation to cosmology.

Surah 41:11 describes Allah addressing the heavens while they were “smoke” and commanding them and the earth to come into existence willingly or unwillingly — they replied: “We come, in willing obedience.” This passage emphasises that creation is an act of divine command (the Qur’anic concept of Kun fa-yakun — “Be! And it is”). Surah 7:54 states that Allah created the heavens and earth in six “days” (the Arabic word ayyam can mean periods or eras rather than 24-hour days) and then “established himself on the Throne”.

In Surah 45:3–5, creation itself is presented as a sign (ayah) of Allah’s existence and power: the alternation of night and day, the provision of rain, the diversity of languages and colours — all are described as signs “for people of understanding.” This approach — reading the natural world as a testimony to Allah — is a central feature of Qur’anic theology. The universe is not an accident but a deliberate act of communication from the Creator.

Humanity as Khalifah: Surah 2:30–39

One of the most important theological concepts in the Qur’an about human beings is the idea of khalifah. In Surah 2:30–39, Allah announces to the angels: “I will create a vicegerent on earth.” The word khalifah means successor, steward or vicegerent — someone who acts on behalf of another. The angels protest: “Will you place therein one who will spread corruption and shed blood while we glorify your praise?” Allah replies: “I know what you do not know.”

Adam is then created and taught the names of all things — a privilege not given to the angels. When Adam demonstrates this knowledge, Allah commands the angels to bow to Adam. They all do, except Iblis, who refuses out of pride. Iblis becomes the tempter of humanity. Adam and his wife are placed in the garden but warned not to eat from one tree; Iblis deceives them, they eat, and they are sent to live on earth. Allah, however, forgives Adam when he repents — showing that human beings are created weak but capable of repentance and restoration.

The concept of khalifah has profound ethical implications. If humanity is Allah’s steward on earth, then human beings are accountable for how they treat the environment, other creatures and other people. They are trustees, not owners. This forms the Qur’anic basis for environmental ethics in Islam — the earth belongs to Allah, and humans must care for it accordingly.

Both the Qur’an and the Bible present creation as the deliberate act of one God, who creates humanity with a special status above other creatures. Both have a story of a garden, a temptation, a fall and expulsion. Both use six “days” or periods of creation.

Key differences: In the Qur’anic account, Adam repents and is forgiven — there is no concept of “original sin” passed to all humanity. In Islamic theology, human beings are born in a state of fitrah (natural purity) rather than sinfulness. The Qur’an does not name Adam’s wife in these passages. Responsibility for the disobedience is shared more equally between Adam and his wife in the Qur’an than in some readings of Genesis 3, where the woman is often held more responsible.

Modern Muslim scholars and activists draw on the concept of khalifah to argue for Islamic environmental ethics. If humanity is entrusted with the earth as Allah’s steward, then environmental destruction is a form of betrayal of that trust — a spiritual as well as an ethical failure. The Islamic Foundation for Ecology and Environmental Sciences (IFEES) has developed this theology in practical work on conservation.

The concept of khalifah also extends to social justice: as stewards, humans are accountable for how they treat the poor, the marginalised and the oppressed. The same Surah 2 that establishes the believer’s identity also contains laws on just economic dealings, care for orphans and widows, and the payment of zakah (almsgiving). Stewardship is both environmental and social.

Key Fact

Khalifah means vicegerent, steward or successor. In Surah 2:30–39, Allah appoints humanity as his khalifah on earth. This means human beings are trustees, not owners, of the natural world — accountable to Allah for how they treat creation. This is the Qur’anic basis for Islamic environmental ethics and social justice.

lesson_title: Justice, Shirk and Shari'ah Law
content_html:
Justice in Surah An-Nisa (Surah 4:105–135)

Surah An-Nisa (Surah 4, “The Women”) is one of the longest chapters in the Qur’an and covers a wide range of legal and social teachings. Verses 105–135 focus particularly on justice. The Qur’an’s vision of justice is comprehensive — it covers legal fairness in courts, economic fairness, treatment of the poor, and the rights of women, orphans and prisoners.

In Surah 4:135, Allah commands: “O you who believe! Stand out firmly for justice, as witnesses to Allah, even if it be against yourselves, your parents, or your relatives, or whether it be against the rich or the poor.” This is a demanding standard — justice must be impartial even when it is personally costly. A Muslim is expected to testify truthfully even against their own family.

The Qur’an also connects justice to the character of Allah. Because Allah is Just (Al-‘Adl, one of the 99 names), human beings as his khalifah on earth are required to mirror that justice in their institutions and relationships. In Shi’a Islam, Adl (divine justice) is one of the Five Roots of faith, making it even more central to that tradition’s theology.

The Hadith traditions also illustrate justice in practice. The Prophet Muhammad’s recorded sayings and actions (Hadith) show him returning stolen goods, insisting that even a powerful person should be punished for wrongdoing, and declaring that “whoever does not show mercy will not be shown mercy.” These traditions show justice as lived, practical and applied, not merely theological.

Key Fact

Surah 4:135 commands Muslims to “stand out firmly for justice… even if it be against yourselves, your parents, or your relatives.” This makes justice a binding obligation that overrides personal loyalty. It connects to the Islamic concept of Adl (divine justice) — because Allah is Just, Muslims must be just even at personal cost.

Shirk: The Greatest Sin

Shirk means to ascribe partners to Allah — to associate anything or anyone with his divine nature. It is the opposite of Tawhid (the oneness of Allah) and is considered the gravest sin in Islam. The Qur’an states repeatedly that Allah may forgive any sin except shirk for those who die without repenting.

Shirk takes several forms. The most obvious is idol worship — worshipping statues or images as gods. Surah 7:148–150 recounts the story of the Israelites who made and worshipped a golden calf while Moses was receiving the Torah on Sinai. Moses returned to find the people in this act of shirk and was furious. The story is a vivid illustration of how easily human beings fall into substituting a visible, created thing for the invisible, eternal God.

More subtle forms of shirk include: placing ultimate trust or fear in human beings or institutions rather than Allah; following desires (the “lower self”) as if they were divine commands; and giving to human relationships the devotion that belongs only to Allah. Muslim scholars have also identified “hidden shirk” — performing religious acts for human approval rather than sincerely for Allah.

For Muslims today, the condemnation of shirk shapes their approach to other religions. Some Muslim scholars argue that Christian Trinitarian theology — which speaks of God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit — approaches shirk by attributing a partner (Jesus) to Allah. Most Muslims, however, engage respectfully with Christians and Jews as “People of the Book,” recognising the partial truth in their scriptures while maintaining the Islamic insistence on strict divine unity.

The story of the golden calf in Surah 7:148–150 parallels the account in Exodus 32 but with some differences. In the Qur’anic version, the Israelites made the calf in Moses’s absence and worshipped it; they “could not see that it could not speak to them or guide them any way.” Moses returned, cast down the calf and rebuked his brother Aaron for allowing it. The idols’ inability to speak, guide or help their worshippers is a recurring Qur’anic argument against idolatry: only Allah can respond, guide and provide.

The story teaches that shirk is a moral as well as a theological failure — it involves a refusal to reason carefully about what is worthy of worship. The Qur’an repeatedly challenges idol-worshippers to explain how a created thing can have divine attributes. Ibrahim’s famous destruction of his people’s idols (discussed in a later lesson) makes the same point with dramatic action.

Shari’ah Law

Shari’ah means “path” or “way” in Arabic — the path that Allah has revealed for human beings to follow. It is not simply a legal code but a comprehensive guide to how a Muslim should live in relationship with Allah, with other people, and with the natural world. Shari’ah covers worship (ibadat), relationships and family (muamalat), criminal law (uqubat), and social ethics.

Surah 4:59–60 is one of the foundational Qur’anic verses for Shari’ah: “O you who believe! Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. And if you disagree about anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger.” This verse establishes the hierarchy of Islamic legal authority: first the Qur’an (Allah), then the Sunnah (the Prophet’s practice and sayings), then the rulings of qualified scholars.

Surah 33:21–36 reinforces the idea that the Prophet Muhammad is the model for the Muslim community. Verse 21 states: “Certainly you have in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example.” This is the Qur’anic basis for the Sunnah as a source of Islamic law alongside the Qur’an — if you want to know how to live, look at how the Prophet lived.

From an atheist or Humanist perspective, following a religious legal code such as Shari’ah is problematic for several reasons. First, they would argue that laws should derive from democratic consent and human reason, not from texts claimed to be divine revelation. Second, they might point to specific rulings in classical Shari’ah (on gender equality, religious freedom, or punishments) that appear in tension with modern human rights standards. Third, they would question the principle that God’s command is a sufficient basis for law without independent moral justification.

Muslims respond in a number of ways. Many distinguish between the unchanging core of Shari’ah (the principles of justice, compassion and care for the vulnerable) and the specific rulings that were developed in a historical context and can be reinterpreted. Modern Muslim scholars such as Tariq Ramadan argue that Shari’ah is best understood as an ethical framework rather than a rigid legal code. Muslims in democratic societies typically observe the personal dimensions of Shari’ah (prayer, fasting, halal food) while living under civil law.

Key Fact

Shari’ah means “path” — the comprehensive guide to Muslim life. Its sources are the Qur’an and the Sunnah (the Prophet’s practice). Surah 4:59 establishes the hierarchy: “Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority.” Shari’ah covers worship, family, ethics and legal matters, and is understood differently by different Muslim communities around the world.

lesson_title: The Prophets: Nuh, Ibrahim, Ismail and Yusuf
content_html:
The Prophets in Islam

In Islam, Allah has sent a series of prophets to guide humanity. All share the same core message: submit to Allah, worship him alone, and live justly. Each prophet faces opposition, suffers for his message, and ultimately depends on Allah rather than human approval. The Qur’an’s prophet stories are not simply biographical — they are theological templates for how every believer should respond to Allah’s call.

The Prophet Nuh (Noah)

Nuh is one of the earliest prophets in Islamic tradition. He is described in Surah 17:3 as a “grateful servant” (shakur) — his defining characteristic is thankfulness to Allah even when his mission was almost entirely rejected. Surah 71 (Nuh) is devoted entirely to his story. He preached to his people for 950 years (a figurative number expressing the duration of his mission). He called them day and night, publicly and privately, offering them forgiveness if they would turn to Allah.

They refused. They mocked him. They blocked their ears and put their fingers in them so as not to hear. Only a small group believed. Allah then commanded Nuh to build the Ark. The flood came, destroying the rest — including Nuh’s own son, who refused to board the ark and drowned. This detail is unique to the Qur’anic account: Nuh’s son is separated from him by his disbelief, and Allah tells Nuh that the son is not “of your family” because his actions were not righteous. Faith, not biology, defines the community of Allah.

After the flood, Nuh is told to disembark with “peace and blessing from us on you and on some of the peoples who will descend from you.” His significance as a messenger is confirmed in Surah 17:3: he is “a grateful servant” — a description that, in the Qur’an, connects thankfulness (shukr) with faith. To be ungrateful is a form of denial of Allah; to be grateful is a form of worship.

The Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham)

Ibrahim is the most important of the earlier prophets in Islam. He is described in Surah 37:109–111 as receiving Allah’s “peace and salutations” because he proved faithful, and as one who “tended always towards good deeds.” He is known as Khalilullah — the “Friend of Allah.”

Ibrahim’s story involves multiple tests. He was raised in a community of idol-worshippers — including his own father, who made idols. Ibrahim recognised the absurdity of worshipping created objects and challenged his community. In Surah 21:57–58, he is described as destroying the idols of his people, leaving only the largest standing so that people would have to ask “who did this?” — a dramatic act designed to make people think critically about what they were worshipping.

With his wife Hajra (Hajra) and son Ismail, Ibrahim established the sacred site of Makkah. In Surah 2:127–129, Ibrahim and Ismail together raise the foundations of the Ka’ba and pray: “Our Lord, accept this service from us… Our Lord, make us Muslims submitting to you, and of our descendants a Muslim nation submitting to you.” The prayer is answered in the community of Islam itself.

Ibrahim is also commanded to sacrifice his son. The Qur’an does not name which son in the sacrifice narrative itself (Surah 37:99–111). Most Muslim scholars traditionally identify the son as Ismail rather than Isaac (as in Genesis 22), based on the context of the narrative which places Ibrahim in the land of Makkah with Ismail. However, some Muslim scholars across history have argued it was Isaac, following the identification of the earlier revelation in the Tawrat. The debate is acknowledged in the spec. At the moment of sacrifice, Allah intervenes and ransoms the son with a great sacrifice — both are spared. This event is commemorated annually in Id-ul-Adha.

Key Fact

The Qur’an does not name the son in Ibrahim’s sacrifice (Surah 37). Most Muslim scholars traditionally identify him as Ismail based on context (Ibrahim is in Makkah with Ismail when this happens). Some scholars, however, have argued it was Isaac. The spec notes this as a “possible debate” — students should know both positions without asserting that the Qur’an definitively says one or the other.

The Prophet Ismail

Ismail is mentioned in Surah 21:5–86 among the earlier prophets. His characteristics as described in the Qur’an include patience and perseverance. He is also described as obedient to his parents and as commanding his family to pray and give zakah. In the Ka’ba-building narrative (Surah 2:127–129), he works alongside his father, symbolising both physical labour in service of Allah and the passing of faith from one generation to the next.

Ismail’s place in the prophetic chain is significant: Islamic tradition holds that Muhammad descended from Ismail through the Arab line, fulfilling the prayer Ibrahim and Ismail made when building the Ka’ba: “Send among them a messenger from among them.” Ismail thus links the story of Ibrahim to the coming of the Prophet Muhammad.

Key Fact

Nuh’s defining virtue is shukr (gratitude), shown in Surah 17:3. Ibrahim’s Ka’ba prayer (Surah 2:127–129) explicitly asks Allah to “send among them a messenger from among them” — Muslims understand this fulfilled in Muhammad. The son in the sacrifice (Surah 37) is unnamed; most classical Muslim scholars identify him as Ismail, but the debate exists and examiners award marks for acknowledging it.

The Prophet Yusuf (Joseph)

Yusuf’s story is told in Surah 12 — the only surah of the Qur’an devoted entirely to one prophet’s life. The opening verse calls it “the best of stories.” The narrative is rich with human emotion: jealousy, betrayal, temptation, imprisonment, patience, forgiveness and reunion.

Yusuf has the gift of dream interpretation. His brothers, jealous of their father’s love for him, throw him into a well and lie to their father Jacob, telling him Yusuf was eaten by a wolf. Yusuf is found by a passing caravan and taken to Egypt where he is bought as a slave. He is wrongly accused and imprisoned, but his faith and patience sustain him. In prison he interprets the dreams of fellow prisoners correctly.

Pharaoh has a dream that no one can interpret. Yusuf’s ability is remembered, and he interprets it: seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine. Pharaoh releases and honours him, placing him in charge of Egypt’s food stores. The famine brings his brothers to Egypt seeking food. After a series of tests, Yusuf reveals himself and forgives them: “No reproach on you this day; Allah forgives you, and He is the Most Merciful of those who show mercy.”

Each prophet embodies a virtue that Muslims are called to imitate. Nuh: perseverance and gratitude despite near-total rejection. Ibrahim: courage, rational faith and total submission to Allah even when it costs everything. Ismail: patient obedience across generations. Yusuf: moral integrity under pressure, patience in suffering, and generous forgiveness of those who wronged him. The Qur’an repeatedly draws explicit lessons from these stories for the current reader, using the phrase “in this is a sign for those who reflect.”

The prophet stories also emphasise that prophets were human beings, not divine. They suffered, they wept, they were tested. This is important for Islamic theology: the prophets are honoured and their example is followed, but they are not worshipped. Only Allah is worthy of worship (Tawhid). Venerating a prophet to the point of directing worship to them would itself be a form of shirk.

Many of the Qur’anic prophet stories have parallels in the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament. Muslims believe the Qur’an is the final, uncorrupted revelation — where the Bible’s version differs, the Qur’an provides the authoritative account. The key differences in these four prophets include: Nuh’s son who dies (not in Genesis); Ibrahim’s idol-smashing (not in Genesis); the identification of the sacrifice son as Ismail (Genesis says Isaac); Yusuf’s moral emphasis on forgiveness and gratitude to Allah (which echoes the Genesis narrative very closely — one of the clearest instances of the Torah being confirmed by the Qur’an). Muslims use the term Tawrat for the Torah, acknowledging it as an earlier divine revelation while affirming that the Qur’an is the final, preserved revelation.

lesson_title: Dawud, Maryam, Isa and the Mission of Muhammad
content_html:
The Prophet Dawud (David)

Dawud is one of the great prophet-kings of Islam. His story begins in Surah 2:249–251, where the young Dawud fights in the army of Saul (Talut in the Qur’an) against Goliath (Jalut). The narrative closely parallels 1 Samuel 17 but with theological emphasis: Dawud’s victory is not a result of his personal courage but of Allah’s power working through him. The verse states: “So they routed them by Allah’s leave, and Dawud killed Jalut; and Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom.” Victory belongs to Allah; the role of the warrior is to be a willing instrument.

Dawud is also famous as a craftsman: he made armour. The Qur’an mentions this as a divine gift — Allah taught him to make coats of mail. This detail connects practical skill and craftsmanship to prophethood, showing that the prophets were fully engaged in the world rather than withdrawn from it.

Dawud is the author of the Zabur. Surah 17:55 affirms: “And We gave the Psalms to Dawud.” Muslims regard the Zabur as a genuine earlier revelation from Allah, alongside the Tawrat (Torah revealed to Moses) and the Injil (Gospel revealed to Isa). All three earlier scriptures are regarded as authentic in their original form, though Muslims believe they have been altered or corrupted over time, which is why the Qur’an was sent as the final, preserved revelation.

Maryam and the Birth of Isa

Maryam holds a unique position in Islam. She is the only woman mentioned by name in the Qur’an. An entire surah — Surah 19, which bears her name — is devoted to her story. This alone indicates her exceptional status: she is honoured as among the greatest women of all time and as a model of purity, devotion and submission to Allah.

Surah 19 describes the annunciation. The angel Jibril (Gabriel) appears to Maryam in the form of a man. He tells her Allah will give her a pure son. She asks: “How shall I have a son when no man has touched me, and I have not been unchaste?” Jibril replies: “So it will be. Your Lord says: It is easy for Me. And We will make him a sign to the people.” Isa is born miraculously, without a human father, by Allah’s direct creative command.

When Maryam presents the newborn Isa to her people, they accuse her of immorality. The infant Isa speaks from the cradle — a miracle unique to Islamic and certain apocryphal Christian traditions — declaring: “I am indeed a servant of Allah. He has given me the Book and made me a prophet.” This declaration is significant: even as a newborn, Isa affirms his status as a servant and prophet of Allah, not divine.

From a Humanist or atheist perspective, visions such as the visitation of Jibril to Maryam are not real supernatural events and provide no proof that Allah exists. They might argue that angelic visitations are a common feature of ancient religious narratives and reflect the way pre-scientific cultures explained unusual births or the founding of religious movements. A naturalistic reading would explain Maryam’s experience as a vision, a dream, or a later legendary development in the tradition.

Muslims respond that the annunciation is attested in both the Qur’an and the earlier Christian scriptures (the Gospel of Luke), giving it corroboration across revelation traditions. For Muslims, the miracle of Isa’s birth is a sign (ayah) of Allah’s power — just as he created Adam from dust with no father and no mother, he created Isa from Maryam with no father. Both are signs of the same creative power that sustains the universe.

The Prophet Isa: Life, Mission and Ascension

Isa is one of the five greatest prophets in Islam (the Ulu l-Azm, or prophets of firm resolve). He performed miracles: healing the blind and the leper, raising the dead, and breathing life into clay birds. He received the Injil (Gospel) as a revelation from Allah. In Surah 61:6, Isa is recorded as foretelling: “And remember when Isa son of Maryam said: ‘O Children of Israel! I am Allah’s messenger to you, confirming the Torah before me and bringing good news of a messenger to come after me whose name shall be Ahmad.’” Muslims read “Ahmad” (another name for Muhammad) as Isa’s prophecy of the final prophet.

The most theologically significant passage about Isa is Surah 4:157–158, which deals with the manner of his death or departure from the world. The verse states: “And for their saying, ‘We have killed the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, the messenger of Allah’ — they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them. Those who disagree about it are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it except conjecture. They certainly did not kill him. Rather, Allah raised him up to Himself.”

This passage is the basis for the Islamic teaching that Isa was not crucified. Most Muslim scholars throughout history have interpreted the verse to mean that Allah raised Isa to himself before the crucifixion took place, and that someone else (or an illusion) was crucified in his place. This is a carefully held theological position — it does not deny that crucifixions happened in Roman Palestine, or that Jewish and Roman authorities sought to kill Jesus. It affirms that Allah protected his messenger from death in this way.

Key Fact

Surah 4:157–158 states that Isa “was not killed, nor was he crucified, but it was made to appear so.” Most Muslim scholars interpret this to mean Allah raised Isa before crucifixion occurred. This is an Islamic theological position — not a denial of history. Christians believe Isa (Jesus) died and rose; Muslims affirm he was raised to Allah without dying. This is the central Muslim–Christian divergence on Isa.

The Mission of Muhammad

The Prophet Muhammad received his first revelation in 610 CE in the cave of Hira near Makkah. Surah 26:213–217 records Allah’s command to Muhammad to begin preaching openly: “And warn your nearest kin.” This was the beginning of the public mission — Muhammad first approached his own clan and family, many of whom rejected him. The Qur’an records both the command to preach and the resistance he encountered.

Muhammad’s mission was to deliver the final and complete revelation from Allah, restoring the pure Tawhid that earlier prophets had taught but which human communities had corrupted. The Qur’an describes him as the “Seal of the Prophets” (Khatam al-Nabiyyin) — the last and final messenger, after whom no further prophet will come. His preaching met fierce opposition from the Quraysh tribe of Makkah, who had economic and social interests in maintaining the polytheistic religion of the Ka’ba.

The Islamic mission to call others to submission to Allah (Islam means “submission”) raises questions for non-religious thinkers about religious freedom and pluralism. Humanists would argue that in modern, pluralistic Britain, trying to convert other people to one’s religion shows a lack of respect for their autonomy and right to their own beliefs. They might also question the assumption that one religion possesses the final, complete truth.

Muslims respond that the Qur’anic command to preach is a command to invite and persuade — not to compel. Surah 2:256 states: “There is no compulsion in religion.” The model of Muhammad’s preaching in Makkah — enduring persecution for thirteen years before any military defence was permitted — shows that the Islamic approach to mission is fundamentally one of patient witness, not force. Divergent Muslim communities today interpret “calling to Islam” differently: some emphasise personal moral example; others engage in formal da’wah (invitation); others focus on social justice work as a form of witness.

Key Fact

In Surah 61:6, Isa foretells the coming of “a messenger after me whose name shall be Ahmad” — Muslims interpret Ahmad as another name of Muhammad. This places Isa in the prophetic chain that culminates in Muhammad, and frames the Injil (Gospel) as pointing forward to the final prophet. For Muslims, Christianity and Islam are not competing religions but successive stages of the same divine revelation.
